name: Child workflows with an explicit parent-close policy (and the continue-as-new caveat)
what: A child workflow execution is spawned from inside a parent workflow; the parent must await the spawn and may optionally await the child's result. If the parent does not await it, the child's Parent Close Policy decides what happens to it when the parent closes (cancellation/termination propagation). Child workflows do not carry over when the parent uses Continue-As-New, and if a child itself uses Continue-As-New the parent sees the whole run chain as a single execution.
build: Add a parent_close_policy field (cancel|abandon|terminate) to delegated sub-runs in hday_manifest.py and enforce it in hday_gate.py: when a parent run closes, iterate its children and apply the declared policy, writing a typed ledger row per child with the action taken. Rollover of a parent (see Continue-As-New pattern) must re-attach live children explicitly rather than assume inheritance, matching the documented caveat.
test: tests/test_hday_gate.py: start a parent with three children (one cancel, one abandon, one terminate); close the parent and assert each child's terminal state matches its policy and each produced exactly one ledger row; assert a rollover of the parent leaves the abandoned child alive and re-attaches the cancelled one as already-terminal.

name: Context state store with atomic edits, and resources kept out of state
what: Each run has a Context and each context has a state store: ctx.store.get(key, default=...) and ctx.store.set(key, value) for values steps share during a run (or deliberately carry into a later run by reusing the context). Heavyweight clients, indexes and file handles are documented as belonging in resources, not state, because state must be data you are willing to serialize when you snapshot or resume. Where several steps may mutate state concurrently, edit_state() locks the state so the update is atomic.
build: Add a context store to hday_flow.py: ctx.store.get/set backed by the run's checkpoint segment, an edit_state() context manager taking an exclusive lock for read-modify-write (so two parallel lanes cannot interleave), and a resources registry for non-serializable handles (model clients, browser sessions) that is explicitly excluded from snapshots and rebuilt on resume. Add a hday_gotchas.py check that rejects storing a declared resource in state.
test: tests/test_hday_flow.py: 50 concurrent increment steps through edit_state() and assert the final counter is exactly 50 (no lost updates) while the same test without the lock shows a lower count, proving the lock is load-bearing; assert a resource object placed in state raises a typed error at set() time and that a snapshot taken after the run contains no resource references.

name: Continue-As-New: checkpoint the state and start a fresh run to bound history growth
what: Continue-As-New checkpoints a workflow's state and starts a fresh workflow execution with that state, keeping the same workflow id so the run chain reads as one logical execution while each individual run's history stays bounded. It is the documented answer to unbounded event history and to long-lived workflows that loop forever (for example a workflow that keeps processing a queue).
build: Add a rollover rule to hday_checkpoint.py: when a run's ledger segment exceeds a configured row or byte budget, write a rollover checkpoint (carrying the live state forward), close the segment, and start a new segment under the same logical run id, linked by a continuation pointer. hday_replay.py treats a run chain as one execution, and hday_ctxscore.py can score the compressed chain instead of the raw rows.
test: tests/test_hday_checkpoint.py: drive a synthetic run past the configured budget and assert a rollover happened at the boundary, the new segment's first row points at the previous segment, the logical run id is unchanged, and a full replay of the chain yields the same final state as an unrolled run of the same inputs.

name: Durability modes as a per-run cost/latency dial (exit / async / sync)
what: invoke/stream accept durability='exit' | 'async' | 'sync'. 'exit' persists changes only when the run exits (success, error, or interrupt): best performance, no recovery from a mid-run process crash. 'async' persists while the next step executes: good performance, small window where a crash loses the last checkpoint. 'sync' persists synchronously before the next step starts: every checkpoint is written before execution continues, at some performance cost.
build: Add a durability field (exit|async|sync, default async) to the run manifest in hday_manifest.py, resolved from the risk/impact judgment hday_gate.py already computes (high-risk or irreversible tool class -> sync, read-only -> exit). hday_checkpoint.py honours it: sync = append+fsync the ledger row before dispatching the next tool call, async = flush from a writer thread at step boundaries, exit = buffer and flush once at run end. Every run records the mode and the reason as a ledger row so the cockpit can show why a run was slow.
test: tests/test_hday_checkpoint.py: parametrise over the three modes with a fake writer that counts flush calls and can be told to fail after the Nth write; assert sync flushes before each subsequent step, exit flushes exactly once at run end, and a simulated crash after a sync flush leaves the last completed super-step readable while an exit-mode crash leaves nothing; assert the ledger contains one row naming the mode and the reason.

name: Durable sleeps that hold no compute (step.sleep / step.sleepUntil)
what: step.sleep and step.sleepUntil tell the platform to resume the function at a future time; the code does not run during the interval, so sleeps work in any environment including serverless, and a sleeping function does not count against plan concurrency limits or against any concurrency policy set on the function (the documented maximum is a year).
build: Add a durable wait to hday_steps.py: sleep_until(run_id, at, reason) records a wake row {run_id, at, reason, resume_token} and returns control immediately; a runner (CLI subcommand or the existing scheduler hook) scans due wake rows, resumes the run at the recorded step, and writes a ledger row for the wait (planned vs actual wake). Rate-limit backoff in hday_router.py uses it instead of time.sleep, so a throttled lane releases its slot.
test: tests/test_hday_steps.py: with a frozen clock, schedule a wake 2 hours out and assert no process is blocked (the call returns in <50ms), the run is marked waiting, and a scan before the due time resumes nothing; advance the clock past the due time, run the scanner, and assert exactly one resume with the original resume_token and one ledger row recording the wait duration.

name: Extension negotiation: `extensions` capability maps + graceful degradation
what: Extensions are identified as `{vendor-prefix}/{extension-name}`, e.g. `io.modelcontextprotocol/oauth-client-credentials`, `io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`. Clients advertise support inside `_meta['io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities'].extensions` on every request (each extension's settings object is its own schema; `{}` = no settings); servers advertise theirs in the `server/discover` response under `capabilities.extensions`. Official extensions live in modelcontextprotocol/ext-* repos; experimental ones in experimental-ext-* tied to a working group. The rules: an extension MUST NOT remove/rename fields, change types, alter existing semantics, or add new required fields; unsupported peers must get core-protocol fallback or an explicit error if the extension is mandatory.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `ExtensionRegistry` mapping identifier -> {client_settings, server_settings, mandatory: bool, fallback: callable}. Stamp the client's supported set into every request `_meta`. Add `hday_manifest.py` awareness: the plugin's own manifest gains a `protocol_extensions` block so a deployment can declare which extensions it requires, and startup fails loudly if a required extension is absent rather than degrading. Desktop: the service-wall panel shows per-server extension support as chips.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_extensions.py — assert the client's extensions map is present on every outgoing request (including ones unrelated to the extension), that a mandatory-but-unsupported extension produces an explicit startup error, that a non-mandatory one degrades to core behavior, and that a third-party prefix not matching `{reverse-dns}/{name}` is rejected at registration.

name: Loop termination owned by the loop plus sub-agent escalation (the exit_loop tool pattern)
what: LoopAgent(sub_agents=[...], max_iterations=N) iterates its sub-agents in order, calling each one's run; crucially the loop itself does not decide when to stop - termination must come from either max_iterations or from a sub-agent that signals termination (the documented example gives the loop a tool-based "exit tool" that a sub-agent calls when the condition is met; the mechanism is described as raising a custom event, setting a flag in a shared context, or returning a specific value).
build: Add to hday_compose.py: Loop with max_iterations plus an escalation channel on the child context (child.escalate(reason) / skip_summarization equivalents), so a lane can end the loop with a typed reason. Record the terminating condition for every loop in the ledger (max_iterations | escalated:<reason>) so 'why did this stop' is answerable, and make the escalation a first-class judgment row in hday_gate.py rather than free text.
test: tests/test_hday_compose.py: a writer/critic loop where the critic escalates on iteration 3; assert exactly 3 iterations, the terminating reason is 'escalated:quality_ok', and each iteration has its own ledger row; a second run with a critic that never escalates stops at max_iterations with reason 'max_iterations' and a typed warning row (not a silent truncation).

name: Per-step independent retry counters with an attempt index, plus non-retriable and retry-after errors
what: By default a function or step is retried up to 4 times after the initial attempt (5 attempts total), with a documented backoff schedule; the handler receives an attempt argument that is zero-indexed, increments on each retry, and is reset when steps complete. Each step.run() has its own independent retry counter - a function configured with 4 retries gives every step its own 4 retries, so failures do not consume a shared budget. NonRetriableError stops retrying immediately for errors that will never succeed, and RetryAfterError lets a handler demand a specific delay (for example when a third-party rate limit says when to come back).
build: Extend the retry policy from hday_router.py so the budget is per (run, step) rather than per run, with the attempt index injected into the lane's context and a reset on step completion. Add two typed exceptions in hday_gate.py - NonRetriable (stop, record why) and RetryAfter(seconds, reason) - that tools can raise, and record both as typed ledger rows so the cockpit can distinguish 'flaky', 'never retriable' and 'rate limited'.
test: tests/test_hday_router.py: three steps in one run, each failing its own number of times; assert each step gets its full independent budget (total attempts = sum, not min), the attempt index resets after a step completes, a NonRetriable raise stops after one attempt with the reason recorded, and RetryAfter(30) schedules the next attempt exactly 30s later on the frozen clock.

name: Step memoization with stable step IDs and per-ID counters (loops reuse one ID)
what: Every step method takes an id as its first argument; the step's ID is hashed as the state identifier used to look the result up in later executions, and the step's index (0, 1, ...) is included in the recorded result, so the memo key is effectively (hashed id, occurrence index) and the same step id can be reused inside a loop. Each step executes as a separate request, and any non-deterministic logic (database or API calls) must be placed inside step.run() for the execution model to be correct. When step.run() finishes successfully its response is saved in the run state and the step will not re-run; step.run() acts as a code-level transaction where the entire step must succeed to complete. Non-deterministic side effects (database writes, API calls) belong inside step.run() so they are checkpointed and not repeated during a retry.
build: Add hday_steps.py: a step(id, fn) helper that hashes (run_id, id, occurrence_counter) into a memo key, stores the JSON result in the run's ledger segment, and returns the stored result on a re-execution instead of calling fn. The occurrence counter is per (run_id, id) so loops are safe; side-effecting helpers in hday_gate.py wrap their bodies in step() so a resumed run never re-fires a decided tool call. Expose a step-view in the cockpit: id, occurrence, status, duration.
test: tests/test_hday_steps.py: call a step that increments a counter inside a loop of 5 iterations and assert the memo keys are (id, 1..5) and the counter ends at 5; re-run the same run id with the memo present and assert fn is never called (call-count instrumentation) and results match; assert a step whose body raises mid-way leaves no memo entry and re-runs on resume.

name: externalize-dont-delete
what: Manus treats the file system as the ultimate context: unlimited, persistent, directly operable by the agent, and used not just as storage but as structured externalized memory. Their compression strategies are always designed to be RESTORABLE — a web page's content can be dropped from context as long as the URL is preserved, and a document's contents can be omitted if its path remains available in the sandbox — so context shrinks without permanently losing information. They explicitly reject irreversible compression: an agent must predict its next action from all prior state, and you cannot reliably predict which observation becomes critical ten steps later. The companion rule is 'keep the wrong stuff in': leave failed actions and the resulting stack traces in the context, because erasing failure removes the evidence and the model then cannot update its beliefs away from the bad action; they call error recovery one of the clearest indicators of true agentic behaviour. Anthropic's framing matches from the other side: prefer just-in-time retrieval over pre-loading, keep lightweight identifiers (file paths, queries, links) and load data at runtime, with the file tree itself acting as a signpost system.
build: Make every compression in hday_ctxscore restorable by construction: replace payloads with typed pointers {kind: file|url|tool_result|episode, ref, sha, bytes} and never drop the pointer. Add a hard rule (enforced in code, not convention) that gate vetoes, failed checks and error traces are never eligible for clearing or summarization — they are pinned like decisions. Add a rehydrate(pointer) tool so any cleared payload can be pulled back on demand, and count rehydrations in the ledger: a high rehydration rate on a specific pointer kind is evidence the compressor is dropping something it should have kept.
test: tests/test_restorable_compression.py::test_every_cleared_payload_keeps_a_working_pointer_and_failures_are_pinned — clear a long transcript and assert every dropped payload has a pointer that rehydrates byte-identically; assert gate vetoes and failed checks are still verbatim in context; assert rehydration counts land in the ledger.

name: observation-tree
what: Observations (LLM calls, tool calls, retrieval steps, spans, events) nest under a trace that shares one trace_id; sessions group traces. Trace-level attributes (user_id, session_id, tags, metadata) are copied onto every observation row so aggregation stays fast on one table.
build: Add trace_id (one per session turn) and observation_id to every row emitted by hday_gate.decide / hday_ctxscore.score / hday_router.suggest, and copy turn-level attrs (session_id, mandate, cwd, model) onto each row. Extend the day-ledger command with --trace <id> and make the cockpit ledger view group by trace_id (root = turn, children = lane decisions). No new store: the flat rows stay authoritative.
test: Unit (tests/test_hday_lanes.py style): rows from three lanes in one turn share trace_id and carry session_id; day-ledger --trace returns them ordered; node:vm view-model test groups 3 fixture rows under 1 trace and renders an unknown id honestly.

name: procedural-memory-type
what: memory_type on add() selects the kind of memory. Only procedural_memory is actually implemented: it stores step-by-step task knowledge (how an agent performs a workflow) rather than facts about a user, and requires an agent_id. The docs state plainly that semantic_memory and episodic_memory exist in the enum but are NOT wired into the extraction pipeline, are rejected by validation, and have no documented roadmap. Sync add() raises Mem0ValidationError; async raises ValueError.
build: Add a procedures store keyed by agent/lane (not by user): a successful run's tool sequence, its preconditions and its outcome becomes a retrievable procedure. Wire it into hday_router.suggest so a repeated task shape recalls the procedure that worked, and expose the count of procedures in the cockpit. Reject unknown memory types at the API boundary with a typed error rather than silently accepting them — the documented failure mode here is exactly that class of bug.
test: tests/test_procedures.py::test_unknown_memory_type_is_rejected_and_procedure_recall_is_agent_scoped — assert an unknown memory_type raises a typed error naming the valid value; assert a procedure stored for lane A is not returned for lane B.

name: retry-budget-multiplication
what: The docs decompose worst-case request volume into three independent multipliers: N = model requests per logical call (initial attempt, one follow-up per tool call — even a successful tool call queues another request — plus retry prompts); M = attempts per model request inside the provider SDK client (e.g. an OpenAI client with max_retries=2 allows 3); K = attempts per request on the wire (transport stop strategy, e.g. stop_after_attempt(2) means 2 total). The worked example: retries={'output': 2} x SDK max_retries=2 x stop_after_attempt(2) puts 3 x 3 x 2 = 18 requests on the network, each carrying its own timeout, i.e. 180 seconds of request time worst case before backoff. The docs also warn that UsageLimits.request_limit (default 50) bounds only N and never sees the wire requests added beneath it.
build: Add a worst-case request estimator to the cost guard: given (turns, tools per turn, output_retries, sdk_max_retries, transport_attempts, timeout) compute N*M*K and the worst-case wall time, and refuse configurations above a declared ceiling before the run starts. Surface the estimate on the cockpit card for long-running lanes. This is a pure function and needs no network to test.
test: tests/test_retry_math.py::test_worst_case_request_count_and_refusal — assert (3,3,2) computes 18 and the derived wall time; assert a configuration above the ceiling is refused before any request is issued.

name: tool-result-clearing
what: The cookbook's three context levers are compaction, tool-result clearing and memory. Tool clearing caps in-session token growth when the context is dominated by large, re-fetchable tool results (file reads, API responses). The API table gives the concrete knobs: clear_tool_uses_20250919, triggered by a server-side token threshold, with trigger (default 100K tokens), keep (default 3 tool uses), clear_at_least, exclude_tools and clear_tool_inputs. Compaction (compact_20260112) is separately triggered (default 150K, server-side minimum 50K) and exposes trigger, instructions and pause_after_compaction. The memory tool (memory_20250818) is different again: it is driven by the MODEL as a tool call, and the client implements the operations view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, rename against a /memories path. The cookbook's framing is that these are distinct primitives for distinct problems — bulky re-fetchable reads (clearing), long analytical conversations (compaction), knowledge that must survive between sessions (memory) — and it recommends replacing the default compaction prompt to preserve what your agent needs.
build: Extend hday_ctxscore's vacuum with a clearing stage that runs BEFORE any summarization: when the transcript crosses a token trigger, drop tool results older than the last N (start with 3), never touching assistant text, decisions or gate events; support an exclude list for tools whose results are not re-fetchable (e.g. one-shot probes) and a clear_at_least floor so clearing actually fires rather than no-oping. Keep the cleared payloads in the existing archive (hday_ctxscore already preserves hidden chunks) and leave a one-line pointer with the tool name + arguments so the agent can re-fetch.
test: tests/test_tool_clearing.py::test_old_tool_results_are_cleared_but_decisions_and_excluded_tools_survive — build a transcript with 6 tool results, assert the oldest 3 are replaced by pointers, assert assistant decisions and an excluded tool's result are intact, and assert the cleared payloads are still readable from the archive.

name: 2026 stateless MCP: server/discover + per-request _meta, no initialize handshake
what: The initialize/notifications-initialized handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header are REMOVED. Every request carries its own protocol version and client capabilities in `params._meta`: `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`, `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`, `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo`. Servers SHOULD identify themselves in each result's `_meta` under `io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo`. `server/discover` MUST be implemented by servers and returns {resultType:'complete', supportedVersions:[...], capabilities:{...}, instructions?, ttlMs, cacheScope, _meta:{...serverInfo}}; it is cacheable. Version mismatch -> `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`. On stdio, `server/discover` doubles as the backward-compatibility probe against legacy handshake servers. serverInfo is self-reported, unverified, and MUST NOT drive security decisions.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `MCPNegotiator` that (1) calls server/discover first, (2) caches DiscoverResult keyed by server with `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` respected, (3) falls back to the legacy initialize handshake when discover fails on stdio, and (4) stamps every outgoing request's `_meta` with protocolVersion + clientCapabilities + clientInfo. Capability checks read from the per-request stamped set, never from a module-global. Record the negotiated version in the gate ledger so a post-hoc audit can tell which protocol revision a decision was made under.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp2026_discover.py — assert discover is called exactly once per TTL window (not per request), that a 2026 server never receives an initialize request, that a legacy stdio server is detected and driven through the handshake fallback, that an unsupported version raises UnsupportedProtocolVersionError rather than degrading silently, and that serverInfo never appears in any authorization decision.

name: A2A streaming: SSE of TaskStatusUpdateEvent / TaskArtifactUpdateEvent with final-chunk semantics
what: SendStreamingMessage (formerly message/stream) returns a StreamResponse: an initial Task OR Message, then a stream of TaskStatusUpdateEvent {taskId, contextId, status{state, message?, timestamp}, metadata?} and TaskArtifactUpdateEvent {taskId, contextId, artifact, append?, lastChunk?, metadata?} (spec sections 3.1.2, 3.2.3, 4.2). `append:true` means the artifact content should be appended to a previously sent artifact with the same artifactId; `lastChunk:true` marks the final chunk of that artifact. The stream carries a final completion indicator. Streaming unsupported by the agent -> UnsupportedOperationError (check `agentCard.capabilities.streaming` first — capability validation is required). SubscribeToTask (formerly tasks/resubscribe) re-attaches to an existing task's stream, which is how a reconnecting cockpit recovers a task it lost track of.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `A2AStreamConsumer` — asserts `capabilities.streaming` before calling; maintains an artifactId -> buffer map; on append:true concatenates, on lastChunk:true seals and emits one finished artifact. Status updates mutate the task's section in place (never append a new row per update). On stream drop, re-attach via SubscribeToTask and reconcile by taskId+artifactId rather than restarting. Desktop: in-flight cards render the live artifact buffer with a chunk counter; a sealed artifact moves to the review queue.
test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_stream.py — fixture stream emitting 3 artifact chunks (2 append:true, then lastChunk:true) interleaved with 4 status updates. Assert exactly one artifact is produced (not 3), that 4 status updates cause 1 card mutation and 0 new rows, that calling stream without `capabilities.streaming` never issues the RPC, and that a mid-stream drop + SubscribeToTask reconciles to the same artifactId without duplicating content.

name: A2A task lifecycle: contextId/taskId, eight TaskStates, blocking vs non-blocking
what: An agent responds to a message with either a stateless `Message` (trivial/transactional) or a stateful `Task`. `contextId` groups multiple Tasks and Messages into one conversation; `taskId` identifies one task. Exact `TaskState` enum values: `TASK_STATE_UNSPECIFIED`, `TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED`, `TASK_STATE_WORKING`, `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` (terminal), `TASK_STATE_FAILED` (terminal), `TASK_STATE_CANCELED` (terminal), `TASK_STATE_REJECTED` (terminal), `TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED` (interrupted), `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` (interrupted). SendMessageConfiguration.returnImmediately controls execution mode: false/unset = blocking, the call MUST wait until a terminal or interrupted state and return the latest state with all artifacts; true = return immediately after task creation and the caller polls (GetTask), subscribes (SubscribeToTask), or relies on push notifications. Sending a message to a task in a terminal state is UnsupportedOperationError. Tasks are immutable in the sense that refinements produce new artifacts/versions rather than mutating prior ones; artifacts are referenced and tracked by artifactId. v1.0 adds canonical errors via google.rpc.Status/ErrorInfo, ISO 8601 timestamps, cursor pagination on ListTasks (pageSize 1..100, default 50), and `A2A-Version` / `A2A-Extensions` HTTP headers.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `A2ATask{task_id, context_id, state, status_message, artifacts[], timestamp}` with a strict state->section mapping: WORKING/SUBMITTED -> in-flight, INPUT_REQUIRED/AUTH_REQUIRED -> needs-you (AUTH_REQUIRED gets an auth card, not a question card), COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELED/REJECTED -> review queue. Always send `returnImmediately: true` from the cockpit (never let a UI action block on a remote agent) and drive updates via SubscribeToTask; keep a blocking path only for explicit one-shot calls. Parse google.rpc.Status errors into {code, message, details} and render the canonical code, not a raw string. Send `A2A-Version` on every request.
test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_task.py — assert each of the eight states lands in exactly one cockpit section (table-driven, including UNSPECIFIED which must not silently look like WORKING); that AUTH_REQUIRED produces an auth card and not a question card; that a message sent to a COMPLETED task surfaces UnsupportedOperationError; that a non-blocking send returns within the timeout with no artifacts; and that a google.rpc.Status error renders its canonical code.

name: A2A v1.0 wire contract: PascalCase methods, unified Part, discriminator stream events, A2A-Version
what: v1.0 renames JSON-RPC methods from lowercase slash form to PascalCase: message/send -> SendMessage, message/stream -> SendStreamingMessage, tasks/get -> GetTask, tasks/list -> ListTasks, tasks/cancel -> CancelTask, tasks/resubscribe -> SubscribeToTask, plus the four push-notification-config operations and GetExtendedAgentCard. Part is unified into a single object with OneOf {text, raw(base64), url, data} plus optional metadata/filename (previously separate TextPart/FilePart/DataPart — CRITICAL breaking change). Stream events adopt a discriminator pattern instead of a union that must be sniffed. AgentCard restructured (capabilities.streaming / pushNotifications / extendedAgentCard all under AgentCapabilities). Errors standardized on google.rpc.Status/ErrorInfo. Timestamps ISO 8601. Pagination is cursor-based (pageToken/next_page_token). Two HTTP headers are registered: `A2A-Version` and `A2A-Extensions`; media type is `application/a2a+json`; a well-known URI is registered for the card. Clients SHOULD send A2A-Version and negotiate; SDKs are expected to support multiple versions during migration.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: a `Part` normalizer handling all four OneOf arms (raw -> base64 decode to bytes with size guard, url -> deferred fetch, data -> structured), a stream-event discriminator switch (exhaustive, with an explicit unknown-variant branch that logs rather than crashes), and a shared `negotiate_headers()` used by both the MCP and A2A clients to emit version + extensions headers. Never sniff a stream event's shape by key presence; switch on the discriminator. Add a compatibility test fixture set for both v0.3.0 and v1.0 payloads.
test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_wire.py — assert all four Part arms normalize (including a 10MB raw part being refused rather than loaded), that an unknown stream discriminator logs and skips instead of raising, that A2A-Version and A2A-Extensions are present on every request, that Content-Type is application/a2a+json, and that a v0.3.0-shaped payload is detected and reported as version skew with an actionable message.

name: AG-UI capability discovery: getCapabilities() and feature gating
what: AbstractAgent exposes an optional `getCapabilities(): Promise<AgentCapabilities>` returning a typed snapshot of what the agent currently supports. Principles: discovery only (no negotiation), dynamic (reflects current state), optional (agents that don't implement it return undefined), and absent-means-unknown (only declare what you support). AgentCapabilities categories: identity {name, type, description, version, provider, documentationUrl, metadata}, transport {streaming, websocket, httpBinary, pushNotifications, resumable}, tools {supported, items, clientProvided}, output {structuredOutput, mimeTypes}, state {snapshots, deltas, persistence}, multiAgent {delegation, handoffs, subagents}, reasoning {supported, encrypted thinking}, multimodal (by direction), execution {code execution, timeouts, iteration caps}, humanInTheLoop {approvals, interventions, feedback, interrupts, approveWithEdits}, and a `custom` escape hatch. Clients use it for adaptive UI and feature gating, and must gate on explicit equality (capabilities?.output?.structuredOutput === true) because an omitted field means undeclared, not unsupported.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: an `AgentCapabilities` dataclass set mirroring the AG-UI categories, implemented per surface (desktop / TUI / Discord) and per connected agent, with `get_capabilities()` on both sides. `desktop/plugin.js` gates every affordance on explicit truthiness (never on falsiness of an omitted field): no approval UI unless humanInTheLoop.approvals === true, no reasoning panel unless reasoning.supported === true, no live artifact streaming unless transport.streaming === true. `custom` carries hermes-day specifics (e.g. {'com.hermes-day/surfaces': [...]}). Serve the capability document over the same AG-UI endpoint the event stream uses.
test: tests/test_capabilities_gating.py — assert an omitted field and an explicit false behave identically for gating (both hide the affordance); that a capability added at runtime is reflected on the next call; that each surface declares a distinct transport set; and that a client asking for structured output when the agent's output.structuredOutput is absent falls back to text rather than erroring.

name: AG-UI shared state: STATE_SNAPSHOT + STATE_DELTA (RFC 6902 JSON Patch) and the two-way channel
what: State is a structured object that persists across interactions, is readable by both agent and frontend, and is mutable from both sides. Two sync methods: STATE_SNAPSHOT {type, snapshot} delivers a complete state and the frontend must REPLACE its model entirely; STATE_DELTA {type, delta: JsonPatchOperation[]} carries RFC 6902 ops ({op: add|remove|replace|move|copy|test, path: JSON Pointer (RFC 6901), value?, from?}) to be applied in sequence. Snapshots are for establishing a baseline, post-interruption resync, and major changes; deltas for high-frequency small updates. The reference implementation applies patches with fast-json-patch non-mutatingly and catches failures (logging state + patch) rather than corrupting state; if inconsistency is detected the frontend can request a fresh STATE_SNAPSHOT. MESSAGES_SNAPSHOT carries the complete conversation history. State is run-scoped. Best practices include explicit conflict resolution between agent and frontend writes and never storing sensitive data in shared state.
build: `hday_state.py` (new): a `SharedDayState` document (queues, mutes, pins, focus mode, filters) with `apply_snapshot`, `apply_delta` (RFC 6902, applied non-mutatingly, all-or-nothing, failure logged with the full patch), and `request_resync()` on detected inconsistency. Both the Python hook layer and `desktop/plugin.js` read/write it; UI writes emit deltas that are also sent to the agent. Conflict policy: user-authored keys (mutes, pins) are UI-authoritative and agent writes to them are rejected with a logged warning; agent-authored keys (summaries, derived badges) are agent-authoritative. Sensitive fields (tokens, session content) are excluded from the shared document by an explicit allowlist.
test: tests/test_state_patch.py — assert snapshot fully replaces prior state (no merge residue); that a delta whose 3rd op is invalid leaves state byte-identical to before (all-or-nothing); that applying a valid sequence of 200 ops yields the same result as the equivalent snapshot; that an agent write to a UI-authoritative key is rejected and logged; and that no allowlisted-out field ever appears in the serialized shared state.

name: AG-UI subagents: subagentRunId attribution and suspension
what: AG-UI does NOT orchestrate subagents — it only attributes events to the subagent that produced them. Three events: SubagentStarted {subagentRunId (required), name (required), description?, parentSubagentRunId?, parentToolCallId?, parentMessageId?}, SubagentFinished {subagentRunId, result?, outcome? {type:'success'} | {type:'suspended', interruptIds?[]}}, SubagentError. `subagentRunId` is an opaque handle for ONE INVOCATION (like runId), never a reusable definition — use `name` for 'which kind of subagent'. The one exception: a subagent that finished with outcome {type:'suspended'} MAY reuse its id on a resuming run, and the client must treat that later SubagentStarted as a continuation (waiting -> running), never as a duplicate. Every started subagent closes before RunFinished; a paused subagent emits SubagentFinished with outcome 'suspended' so the UI can render 'waiting' not 'done'. Attribution transfers to messages and tool results, which carry their own attribution. parentToolCallId/parentMessageId exist for the agents-as-tools pattern so the subagent's output can render inside the tool-call card. A version shim strips subagent fields in both directions against older peers, which flattens attribution. Known limits: protobuf covers 19 of 36 event types; .NET loses the second owner on parallel tool calls from different subagents.
build: `hday_events.py`: map Hermes subagent_start/stop into SUBAGENT_STARTED/FINISHED with a freshly minted `subagentRunId` (never the profile or agent name), keeping `name` for display. Key all transient UI state (spinner, collapsible group, progress row) by subagentRunId and persist NOTHING by it. Implement the suspension rule: a subagent that paused on an approval emits outcome {type:'suspended', interruptIds:[...]} and the cockpit renders 'waiting'; a later SUBAGENT_STARTED with the same id is a continuation, not a duplicate row. Desktop: group cards by parentToolCallId when present so an agents-as-tools subagent nests inside its tool card.
test: tests/test_subagents_attribution.py — assert two invocations of the same-named subagent get distinct subagentRunIds and produce two rows; that a suspended subagent renders 'waiting' and not 'done'; that a resumed SUBAGENT_STARTED with a reused id updates the existing row instead of creating a second; that no UI state is persisted keyed by subagentRunId; and that output from a nested subagent lands inside its parentToolCallId card.

name: Activities as the side-effect boundary: declarative retry policy plus heartbeat checkpointing
what: An Activity is a normal function that executes one well-defined action, registered by name on a worker; activity code may be non-deterministic and is recommended to be idempotent so retries do not duplicate side effects. Activities are retried automatically under a Retry Policy (default: exponential backoff with coefficient 2.0, 1s initial interval, 100s maximum interval, max attempts 0 = unlimited, no non-retryable errors), and each attempt starts from the initial state unless the code uses a Heartbeat detail payload for checkpointing, in which case the last recorded heartbeat details are handed to the next attempt so it can continue where it left off. Larger functionality should be split into multiple activities for shorter timeouts and easier recovery.
build: Define the side-effect contract in hday_gate.py: every tool call is executed as an activity record {name, input, attempt, idempotency_key, heartbeat}, with the retry policy and non-retryable set declared per tool in hday_manifest.py. Add heartbeat support to long-running lanes: the lane reports progress payloads, hday_checkpoint.py stores the last heartbeat per activity, and a retry hands the stored payload back to the lane. Emit a typed judgment when a tool is declared non-idempotent and gets retried.
test: tests/test_hday_lanes.py: a fake activity that fails on attempt 1 after recording a heartbeat and succeeds on attempt 2 by resuming from the heartbeat payload; assert it processed only the remaining items (no duplicated side effects), assert the ledger shows attempt 1/2 with the same idempotency key, and assert a non-idempotent tool that fails produces a typed 'retry_of_non_idempotent' judgment rather than a silent second execution.

name: Actor with durable state: c.state plus createState, persisted and restored across restarts
what: Each actor instance holds state in memory for instant reads and writes; state on c.state is simple serializable data that is automatically persisted and restored across restarts, and createState computes the initial state (optionally from the input passed at creation). Actions mutate c.state directly and changes are persisted automatically.
build: Add hday_actors.py: an Actor class with declare state schema (JSON-serializable only), createState(input) for initialization, action methods that mutate and return values, and an automatic persist hook that snapshots state to a per-actor file at action boundaries (reusing the checkpoint writer so the storage format stays single-source). Map actors onto existing lanes: one actor per bot profile / session / repo, addressable by key, with state restored on first touch after a process restart.
test: tests/test_hday_actors.py: create an actor with input-derived state, run 3 mutating actions, simulate a process restart (drop the in-memory object, re-instantiate from disk), and assert the state and the action results continue from the persisted values; assert a non-serializable state field is rejected at declaration time with a typed error, and that two actor keys never share state.

name: Callback hooks at eight lifecycle points that block, rewrite, or observe
what: ADK defines eight hooks - before/after agent, model and tool, plus on_model_error and on_tool_error - each with a documented parameter list (for example before_tool_callback(tool, args, tool_context) and after_tool_callback(tool, args, tool_context, tool_response)); only the two agent callbacks are fields on every BaseAgent while the six model/tool hooks are LlmAgent-only, and a callback may be a plain or an async function. Returning a predefined response (an LlmResponse or a dict/Map) from a before_ hook blocks the operation and prevents the underlying call, while returning nothing lets execution continue - documented as the guardrails/policy pattern, alongside caching (return the cached result from before_, store the new one in after_) and request/response modification (mutate llm_request, llm_response, tool args or tool_response). State written inside a callback is tracked in the following Event.actions.state_delta and persisted by the SessionService.
build: Add hday_hooks.py with eight named hook points (before/after x run/lane/model/tool, plus on_model_error/on_tool_error) and our own list semantics (stop at first truthy result; None continues), then re-express the existing free regex honesty guard and the gate's mandate checks as hooks rather than inline branches - adding enforcement, never subtracting it. Hook decisions write ledger rows (hook name, index in the chain, decision, reason) so a blocked call is attributable to a specific hook.
test: tests/test_hday_hooks.py: register three before_tool hooks returning None, None, and a deny verdict; assert all three ran, the third short-circuited the chain, the tool never executed, and the ledger has three rows naming each hook; assert a hook returning an empty dict continues the chain while one returning a truthy rewrite replaces the args and stops it; assert the legacy honesty guard still fires through the hook path (regression test on the existing cases).

name: CopilotKit HITL hooks: useHumanInTheLoop (interactive tool) and useInterrupt (AG-UI standard interrupts)
what: Two distinct HITL mechanisms. (1) useHumanInTheLoop(tool, deps?) registers an interactive tool with NO handler: an internal status machine (ToolCallStatus.InProgress -> Executing -> Complete) supplies a `respond` callback to the render component during Executing, and the agent stays paused until respond(value) is called — exactly once per invocation. Built on useFrontendTool; registered on mount, removed on unmount; returns void. (2) useInterrupt(config) handles agent interrupts and resumes execution. It supports the AG-UI standard flow (RUN_FINISHED with outcome.type === 'interrupt' carrying interrupts[]) AND the legacy custom-event flow (`on_interrupt`), with standard taking precedence when both appear in one run. Callbacks receive `interrupt` (the primary) and `interrupts` (the full open set); `resolve(payload)` resumes, `cancel()` cancels; responses accumulate one per open interrupt and the resume run starts only once every open interrupt is addressed. Expired interrupts (past expiresAt) are NOT resumed — the hook logs an error and clears pending state. Interrupt UI renders inside <CopilotChat> by default; `renderInChat:false` returns the element for manual placement. Starting a new run clears pending interrupt state. `event.value` is typed any and must be narrowed.
build: In `desktop/plugin.js`: the approval card is a useHumanInTheLoop-shaped component — while status is Executing the card shows a/d buttons and `respond` is called exactly once (disable after first call); after Complete the card renders the recorded result inline. Wrap the whole board in a useInterrupt-shaped handler so interrupts raised anywhere (including inside subagents, via subagentRunId) surface in 'Needs you' with a resolve/cancel pair, and hold the resume until the open set is fully addressed. Treat an expired interrupt as a distinct visual state ('expired — re-ask') that never silently resumes. Keep the legacy on_interrupt path behind a capability check for older agents.
test: tests/test_copilotkit_hitl.py + plugin.js harness — assert respond is callable once and a second call is a no-op; that the agent stays paused (no resume emitted) until respond fires; that resolve() on 2 of 3 open interrupts emits no resume run; that cancel() on all open interrupts resumes with statuses 'cancelled'; that an expired interrupt logs and clears rather than resuming; and that a legacy on_interrupt event is handled when the standard outcome is absent but ignored when present.

name: CopilotKit: useAgent + useAgentContext as the two-way shared-state client
what: `useAgent(options?) -> {agent: AbstractAgent, isReady: boolean}` returns a live AG-UI AbstractAgent and re-renders on state/message/status change. Exactly two option shapes are valid: bind to the shared registry instance ({agentId} or nothing), or bind a PRIVATE agent to a thread — all three of {agentId, runtimeAgentId, threadId} required; partial combinations are type errors (a runtime agent registered under an id is a singleton, so a per-hook threadId on it would let two hooks clobber each other). `updates: [UseAgentUpdate.OnStateChanged | OnMessagesChanged]` throttles re-renders. `agent.state` is plain data; `agent.setState({...})` writes back and the agent reads it on its next turn. `isReady` is false while the runtime connects, with `agent` being a fully-constructed provisional stand-in — guard one-time subscriptions on isReady. `agent.subscribe({onRunStartedEvent, onRunFinalized})` returns `{unsubscribe}`. `useAgentContext` is the one-way, UI-owned, auto-unregistering read-only channel (current user, selected record, scroll position) for values the agent should read but never write. Server side, `CopilotKitMiddleware` picks up CopilotKit state alongside the app's own; `copilotkit_emit_state` pushes state to the frontend; `StateStreamingMiddleware(StateItem(state_key=..., tool=..., tool_argument=...))` streams a tool argument token-by-token into state[key] while the call is still in flight — and the frontend's subscription indexes partial-JSON-parsed args by `state_key`, so the tool argument name MUST equal state_key. The older `useCoAgent` name now resolves to `useAgent`.
build: In `desktop/plugin.js`: use the thread-scoped form ({agentId: `day-${threadId}`, runtimeAgentId: 'default', threadId}) so multiple cockpit panes against one runtime agent don't clobber threads; subscribe with `updates: [UseAgentUpdate.OnStateChanged]` to avoid re-render storms on a board with many rows; guard the one-time interrupt subscription on `isReady`. Publish read-only cockpit context (active profile, focused pane, filter text, mute set) through the useAgentContext equivalent (the plugin's context-registration API) rather than writing it into shared state. On the Python side, mirror StateStreamingMiddleware for hermes-day's long-running evidence runs so a partial test log streams into state['evidence'] as it is produced, with the tool argument named `evidence`.
test: tests/test_copilotkit_bindings.py + a node:vm plugin.js harness — assert partial option combinations are rejected (type-level and runtime), that a board with 200 rows and OnStateChanged-only subscription re-renders once per state change rather than per message, that a subscription registered before isReady does not bind to the provisional agent, and that a streamed tool argument lands under state[key] exactly when the argument name equals state_key and never otherwise.

name: Deterministic replay from a recorded event history, with replay-safe primitives
what: A workflow execution emits commands and processes events, all recorded in an ordered event history. On resume, Temporal does not restore memory from a snapshot: it re-runs the workflow code from the beginning and replays the history step by step so the code reaches the same state (it may start from a cached point). Because code is re-executed, non-deterministic calls are unsafe (Date.now() or a random number could differ and send the run down a different path); the platform supplies replay-safe replacements (workflow time from the context, timers recorded as events that do not wait again, randomness captured once and reused). Activity results are recorded in history and reused during replay, so activities are not executed again.
build: Add hday_replay.py: a deterministic executor that runs a recorded ledger segment through the gate's decision functions with all non-determinism injected (now() from the log, ids from the log, RNG seeded from a logged seed) and asserts the replayed decisions equal the recorded ones. Anything not injectable is a typed violation ('non_deterministic_call') naming the call site, so new lanes get caught in CI instead of in production.
test: tests/test_hday_replay.py: record a 20-row ledger segment from a synthetic run, replay it and assert a byte-identical decision sequence; then patch one decision function to call a real clock and assert replay reports a non_deterministic_call violation with the offending call site and the run is marked failed, not silently divergent.

name: Event-driven steps: typed events are the edges, plain Python is the logic
what: A workflow is a set of steps; a step receives an event, does work, and returns another event, and that returned event triggers the next step whose type annotation accepts it - the event types describe the edges and ordinary code describes the logic inside. Branches are plain if statements returning different event types, loops are steps returning an event handled by an earlier step, and a step that returns list[Event] fans out. StartEvent and StopEvent are the two special-case events the framework provides out of the box (events themselves are user-defined Pydantic objects), and the validator plus the visualization connect each producer step to the steps that consume its events.
build: Add hday_flow.py: a step decorator whose signature (accepted event types -> returned event type) is inspected at registration to build the routing table, so hday_router.py routes by event type instead of a hand-maintained map. Define StartEvent/StopEvent equivalents (run_started, run_finished) plus typed lane events, and make every lane emit typed events that land in the ledger. Validate at registration that a workflow has exactly one start and one stop path, failing fast with a typed error.
test: tests/test_hday_flow.py: register a 4-step workflow with one branch and one loop; assert the derived routing table matches the declared annotations, that an event with no consumer raises a typed 'unroutable_event' error naming the event, and that a workflow missing a stop path fails validation at registration (not at run time); assert the loop terminates after the declared iteration bound.

name: Fan-out/fan-in encoded in step signatures, with three separate concurrency limits
what: Return a list from a step and it fans out, one event per element; take a list parameter and the step fans in, firing once on the whole batch - the decorator reads those types and the validator and visualisation connect producers to consumers automatically. Dynamic emission uses ctx.send_event. Concurrency is controlled at three distinct levels: num_concurrent_runs on the workflow caps how many run() calls are active at once (per process), @step(num_workers=...) caps how many copies of one step process events at once inside a run, and a shared asyncio.Semaphore caps a step across all runs (the documented way to protect an external API).
build: Add to hday_flow.py: a step that returns a list produces N child work items and a step accepting a list consumes the batch exactly once (join semantics), both recorded as typed rows so the ledger shows the batch boundary. Add the three limit knobs (run-level concurrency, per-step workers, cross-run semaphore keyed by resource) to the lane manifest and enforce them in hday_router.py's scheduler with an injectable clock so tests stay deterministic.
test: tests/test_hday_flow.py: a fan-out of 5 items into a join; assert the join step ran exactly once with 5 items (not 5 times with 1), that the ledger records one batch row plus 5 item rows, and that with num_workers=2 at most 2 items are in flight at any instant (instrumented concurrency high-water mark); assert a resource semaphore of 1 across two concurrent runs serialises the protected step.

name: Handoff between steps through named state keys (output_key) with scoped state prefixes
what: In a sequential workflow, earlier agents write results to session state (often via output_key) and later agents read them from context.state, with instruction templating like {draft_text} or {validation_status} pulling those values into prompts. State keys are strings and values must be serializable; prefixes define scope and persistence: no prefix = the current session only, user: = shared across all sessions for that user, app: = shared across all users of the app, temp: = scoped to the current invocation only. In Python, get_user_state(app_name, user_id) reads user-scoped keys before any session exists.
build: Add a scoped state API to hday_actors.py: set(key, value) with mandatory prefixes (run: default, session:, user:, app:, temp:) validated against the actor/session in scope, plus get(key, default). Lanes declare which keys they produce (output_key equivalents) in hday_manifest.py, and hday_ctxscore.py can then score prompt size against the keys actually used. Templating in lane prompts resolves {key} from scoped state with a typed error on a missing key.
test: tests/test_hday_actors.py: write one key per scope and assert lifetimes (temp: gone at run end, run: visible to later steps in the same run, session: visible to a new run in the same session, user:/app: visible to other sessions/users as declared); assert an undeclared prefix raises a typed error and that a prompt template referencing a missing key fails with the key name rather than rendering an empty string.

name: Human-in-the-loop as a pair of ordinary events (input required / human response)
what: HITL needs a run to pause, tell the caller what input is needed, and continue when the caller responds - and the documented pattern needs no special API: one step returns InputRequiredEvent (carrying the prompt), another step consumes HumanResponseEvent, the caller watches the stream and sends the response back into the same handler with handler.send_event(HumanResponseEvent(response=...)). Both events can be subclassed when the prompt or response needs more structure.
build: Add input_required(prompt, schema, timeout) and human_response(value, responder) events to hday_flow.py, wired into hday_gate.py as the escalation path: a gate decision that needs a human emits an input-required event with a typed schema, the run pauses at a checkpoint, and any surface (cockpit, TUI, Discord) can send the response event into the same run. Record who responded, when, and against which prompt as a ledger row so approvals are attributable.
test: tests/test_hday_flow.py: a run that pauses on input_required; assert no downstream step executes while paused and the checkpoint exists; send a human_response from a simulated surface and assert the run continues with the value, one ledger row names the responder and prompt id, and a second response for the same prompt id is rejected as already-answered (typed, no duplicate continuation).

name: Interrupt + Command(resume=...) as the HITL pause primitive, with replay re-triggering
what: interrupt(value) inside a node pauses execution and surfaces the value to the caller; the run resumes with graph.invoke(Command(resume=answer), config) and the node's interrupt() call returns that answer, so the node re-executes from its start with the resume value injected. Interrupts are always re-triggered during time travel: replaying or forking before the interrupt pauses again for a new Command(resume=...). With several interrupts in one thread (a multi-step form), you can fork from between them and change a later answer without re-asking earlier questions.
build: Add an interrupt capability to hday_gate.py: a gate decision that needs a human returns an Interrupt object (id, prompt, payload, node) instead of raising, and the run's state is checkpointed at that boundary via hday_checkpoint.py. Resume is a single function resume_run(thread_id, interrupt_id, value) that loads the checkpoint, injects the value, and re-enters the same decision function; interrupts carry stable ids so a multi-question approval resolves each answer independently. The cockpit and Discord surfaces both render the same interrupt payload and post the same resume call.
test: tests/test_hday_gate.py: a two-question approval flow; assert the first invoke returns two pending interrupts with stable ids and does not execute the gated tool; resume question 2 first and assert only that answer is recorded and question 1 is still pending; then resume question 1 and assert the tool executes exactly once and the ledger has one decision row per interrupt id.

name: Lifecycle hooks with a defined order, plus shutdown cancellation via an abort signal
what: Actor startup runs onMigrate (every start, before anything touches the database, told whether this is the first creation), createState, onCreate, createVars, onWake, then run (background, non-blocking); sleeping waits for run to complete with a timeout, then calls onSleep; destroy calls onDestroy; waking after sleep/restart/crash runs onMigrate, createVars, onWake, run. Separately, actions run in parallel by default and long-running ones can be cancelled with an AbortController chained to c.abortSignal so actor shutdown aborts them (queues are the documented tool when ordering, not parallelism, is needed).
build: Add a lifecycle contract to hday_actors.py with the same hook names and order (migrate -> createState -> onCreate -> createVars -> onWake -> run), each optional and each able to be asserted in tests; add a shutdown signal that lanes must respect (pass an abort signal into long lanes, cancel on actor sleep/destroy, and record a typed 'aborted_on_shutdown' ledger row). Expose the current lifecycle stage in the cockpit so a stuck actor shows which hook it is in.
test: tests/test_hday_actors.py: an actor recording hook order into a list; assert first-start order is migrate, createState, onCreate, createVars, onWake, run and post-restart order is migrate, createVars, onWake, run; assert sleep waits for run to finish (a slow run delays onSleep and is killed at the configured timeout with a typed row); assert a long lane observes the abort signal on destroy and writes 'aborted_on_shutdown' rather than a partial result.

name: Node retry policy, node timeouts, and routing failures back into the graph
what: add_node(..., retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3)) re-runs a failed node attempt based on exception type and backoff settings; defaults are max_attempts 3, initial_interval 0.5s, backoff_factor 2.0, max_interval 128s, jitter on, retrying any exception except ValueError and friends (HTTP errors only on 5xx). set_node_defaults configures retries/timeouts/error handlers once for all nodes, and the mechanisms compose in a fixed order: on an exception (including a timeout) the retry policy decides whether to retry, and only after retries are exhausted does the error handler run. Failures can be routed back into the graph with Command, and the page documents resume-safe failures and drain semantics.
build: Extend hday_router.py with a retry/timeout policy per lane node: RetryPolicy(max_attempts, initial_interval, backoff_factor, max_interval, jitter, retry_on) plus a node timeout, applied by the same executor that dispatches tool calls. On exhaustion, route to an error handler node via the same decision path the gate uses, and write one ledger row per attempt (attempt index, error class, next delay) so the cockpit can show flapping tools. Non-retryable classes (validation/ValueError-equivalents) short-circuit with no retry rows.
test: tests/test_hday_router.py: a fake tool that fails N times then succeeds, with a monkeypatched clock; assert attempt count equals max_attempts, delays follow the declared backoff exactly (deterministic because jitter is seeded off), and the ledger has one row per attempt; assert a ValueError-equivalent fails after exactly one attempt with reason 'non_retryable', and that a node timeout routes to the handler node only after the retry budget is exhausted.

name: OTel GenAI events + MCP semantic conventions: opt-in content events, context propagation via params._meta, and MCP metrics
what: Events: `gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details` (opt-in, requirement level Opt-In) carries the same attribute set as inference spans including chat history and parameters, and exists so input/output details can be stored independently of traces; `gen_ai.evaluation.result` carries gen_ai.evaluation.name (required), score.value, score.label, explanation, and gen_ai.response.id. MCP conventions (RECOMMENDED over generic RPC/HTTP conventions, because one HTTP request can carry multiple MCP messages and one streamable-HTTP request can serve several): context propagation by injecting W3C Trace Context into the MCP request `params._meta` property bag — keys `traceparent`, `tracestate`, `baggage` written UNPREFIXED even though `_meta` keys are normally DNS-prefixed (SEP-414 defines this explicit exception); the receiver extracts from `params._meta` and uses it as the remote parent, linking (not parenting) ambient HTTP context, since MCP and transport contexts are independent. MCP spans: kind CLIENT, name `{mcp.method.name} {target}` where target matches gen_ai.tool.name or gen_ai.prompt.name (resource URIs only on opt-in, to avoid cardinality), with attributes mcp.method.name (required), mcp.protocol.version, mcp.session.id, mcp.resource.uri, jsonrpc.request.id, rpc.response.status_code, network.protocol.*. Metrics: mcp.client.operation.duration, mcp.server.operation.duration, mcp.client.session.duration, mcp.server.session.duration.
build: `hday_telemetry.py`: inject traceparent/tracestate/baggage UNPREFIXED into every MCP request's `params._meta`, and extract on the server side using `_meta` as remote parent with a span LINK (not parent) to the ambient HTTP context. Emit the four mcp.* metrics with mcp.method.name and mcp.session.id labels; the Sources panel renders p95 duration per server from them. Emit `gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details` events (opt-in) so content can be shipped to a separate store without polluting the trace; emit `gen_ai.evaluation.result` for the honesty-guard verdicts (name='hermes-day.evidence', score.label in {verified, no_evidence, checks_failed, guard_violation}) so evidence quality is queryable alongside the traces.
test: tests/test_telemetry_mcp.py — assert traceparent is written unprefixed into params._meta (a DNS-prefixed key fails the test), that the server span's parent is the MCP client span and the HTTP span appears as a link, that all four mcp.* metrics are emitted with method name labels, that gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details is absent unless opted in, and that a guard violation emits gen_ai.evaluation.result with the expected label.

name: OTel GenAI: agent/framework spans (create_agent, invoke_agent, invoke_workflow, plan) and the execute_tool span
what: Agent conventions extend and override the inference conventions. `gen_ai.create_agent.client` (operation name create_agent, span name `create_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}`, kind CLIENT) carries gen_ai.agent.id (a STABLE provider-assigned identifier — AWS Bedrock agent ARN, GCP Agent Registry identifier; in-memory instance ids are explicitly NOT recommended), gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.agent.description, gen_ai.agent.version, plus the usual model/server attributes. Other operation names: invoke_agent, invoke_workflow, plan (agent planning or task decomposition phase), retrieval, fetch_response (retrieve a prior response by id WITHOUT inference — and instrumentations SHOULD NOT report token usage for it). Agent spans support span creation-time attributes (gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.operation.name) so sampling decisions can be made on them. Tool execution uses the shared `execute_tool` span; MCP tool-call spans are explicitly compatible with it and an MCP instrumentation that detects outer GenAI tool tracing SHOULD NOT create a second span but add MCP attributes to the existing one.
build: `hday_telemetry.py`: emit create_agent / invoke_agent / invoke_workflow / plan spans for profile spawns, subagent dispatch, and mission plans, using gen_ai.agent.id = the stable profile/subagent-definition identifier and gen_ai.agent.name for display. Set agent.name and operation.name at span creation so sampling can use them. Add a dedupe guard: if a Hermes pre_tool_call span already exists for a given tool invocation, the MCP layer MUST annotate it rather than open a second execute_tool span (key on (server, jsonrpc_id) or (session, tool_call_id)). Never report token usage on fetch_response operations.
test: tests/test_telemetry_agent_spans.py — assert agent.id is the stable definition id and not a per-run instance id; that a tool call observed by both the Hermes hook layer and the MCP layer produces exactly one execute_tool span with both attribute sets; that fetch_response spans carry no usage attributes; and that agent.name/operation.name are present at span creation time.

name: OTel GenAI: inference client spans and the content-capture contract
what: Moved out of the main semconv repo into open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai (the old opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/ pages are stubs pointing there; status Development). Span type `gen_ai.inference.client`: kind CLIENT (INTERNAL allowed for in-process models), span name `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}`, and a span SHOULD cover the logical operation including automatic retries. Required attributes: `gen_ai.operation.name` (chat | generate_content | text_completion | embeddings | execute_tool | invoke_agent | invoke_workflow | plan | retrieval | fetch_response | create_agent | memory ops ...), `gen_ai.provider.name` (openai | gcp.gen_ai | aws.bedrock | ... — a discriminator selecting the provider-specific telemetry flavour). Conditionally required: error.type, gen_ai.conversation.id, gen_ai.output.type, gen_ai.prompt.name/version, gen_ai.request.choice.count/model/seed/stream/top_k, server.port. Recommended: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, frequency/presence_penalty, stop_sequences, reasoning.level, response.id/model/finish_reasons, and `gen_ai.response.time_to_first_chunk` (seconds, streaming only). Content capture is opt-in and three-tiered: `gen_ai.system_instructions`, `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages` follow fixed JSON schemas (model/gen-ai/gen-ai-input-messages.json, -output-messages.json, -system-instructions.json); they may be recorded structured on events, or JSON-serialized on spans where structured attributes aren't supported; instrumentations MAY expose an in-process hook that fires regardless of the sampling decision to upload content to external storage and enrich the span.
build: `hday_telemetry.py` (new): emit OTel-shaped span records into the decision ledger alongside the existing entries — span name `{operation} {model}`, required attributes always present, provider-specific attributes namespaced under the provider prefix, and `gen_ai.conversation.id` set from the Hermes session id so a cockpit row can join telemetry to sessions. Content capture is OFF by default and gated behind an explicit config flag with a per-field truncation option that preserves JSON structure. Implement the upload hook as a no-op-by-default callable so a deployment can wire content to its own storage without changing the ledger schema.
test: tests/test_telemetry_genai.py — assert every emitted span carries gen_ai.operation.name and gen_ai.provider.name; that no content attribute is present when capture is disabled; that enabling truncation preserves JSON structure while shortening contents; that a retried request produces one span (not N); that time_to_first_chunk is emitted only for streaming requests; and that provider-specific attributes never appear on a span whose provider.name is a different provider.

name: Prompts as user-invoked slash commands with typed arguments
what: prompts/list returns {name, title, description, arguments[{name, description, required}]} with pagination; prompts/get takes {name, arguments{}} and returns messages[] whose content is one of text, image (base64+mimeType), audio (base64+mimeType), or an embedded `resource` block. Arguments can be auto-completed through the completion utility. Capability `prompts:{listChanged?}`. Invalid name / missing required arg is -32602. The spec's own interaction model is a slash command in the client UI.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `list_prompts()`, `get_prompt(name, arguments)` -> `PromptInvocation{messages[], description}`. Map each prompt to a cockpit action: `desktop/plugin.js` filter field gains `:` prefix routing (e.g. `:code_review`) that opens an argument form generated from `arguments[]` (required ones block submit). Render returned messages through the same card pipeline as sessions, tagging the card with the owning server. Cache prompt lists with TTL; honour prompts/list_changed by invalidating.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_prompts.py — assert required-argument enforcement happens client-side before any RPC is sent, that an embedded resource block survives round-trip without base64 corruption, that -32602 from prompts/get surfaces as a form-validation error (not a crash), and that list_changed invalidates the cached list exactly once.

name: Queue with completable messages: request/response, durable delivery, sender timeout
what: Actors consume work from a queue with a run loop (for await (const message of c.queue.iter())), and messages have three documented properties: realtime (delivered to a live actor as soon as possible), durable (persisted and surviving actor sleep/restart), and request/response (clients can wait for a completion response). With completable: true the handler calls message.complete(...) and a waiting sender gets the value, with a sender-side timeout that surfaces status 'timedOut'; if processing fails before complete() the message is not redelivered and the sender times out rather than receiving a completion. next/nextBatch pull one or many messages with an optional timeout.
build: Add a durable queue to hday_actors.py: enqueue(actor_key, payload, {completable, wait, timeout}), a per-actor run loop that processes messages strictly in order, and complete(message_id, result) which resolves any waiting caller. Persist queue contents through the checkpoint writer so a restart resumes pending messages, and record a ledger row per message with status (completed | timedOut | failed_before_complete) so timeouts are visible rather than silent.
test: tests/test_hday_actors.py: enqueue 3 messages while the actor is asleep, wake it, and assert they are processed in order and durably (queue empty only after completion rows exist); assert a waiting caller receives the completed value; assert a handler that raises before complete() yields status 'timedOut' for the caller, exactly one ledger row, and no redelivery on restart.

name: Resources: URI-addressed context, templates, subscribe/list_changed
what: resources/list (paginated), resources/templates/list for RFC 6570 URI templates, resources/read -> contents[] of {uri, mimeType, text} or {uri, mimeType, blob(base64)}. Capability `resources:{subscribe?, listChanged?}` — both optional and independent. Subscribed URIs push `notifications/resources/updated`; list mutations push `notifications/resources/list_changed`. Missing resource is -32002. Standard schemes: https://, file://, git://; custom schemes MUST follow RFC 3986. Resources are application-driven (host decides inclusion), unlike prompts which are user-driven.
build: In `hday_protocols.py`: `list_resources()`, `list_resource_templates()`, `read_resource(uri) -> ResourceContent{uri, mime_type, text|blob_b64, size}`. Add `ResourceSubscriber` that issues resources/subscribe and routes `notifications/resources/updated` into `hday_ctxscore.py` as an invalidation event (re-score that URI's contribution, do not full-recompute). Handle -32002 as `ResourceGone` and drop the cache entry. Desktop: resource reads render in the existing terminal block style; blob content shows size + mime only, never inline base64.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_resources.py — server advertises resources:{subscribe:true,listChanged:false} only; assert the client does not expect list_changed, that reading a missing URI raises ResourceGone (not a generic error), and that a resources/updated notification triggers exactly one ctxscore invalidation for that URI and zero for others.

name: Roots: client-declared filesystem scope + list_changed
what: Client declares capability `roots:{listChanged:true}`. Server issues a `roots/list` request; client answers `{roots:[{uri:'file:///abs/path', name:'Display'}]}` — uri MUST be a file:// URI in this revision, name optional. On change the client MUST send `notifications/roots/list_changed`. Unsupported -> -32601; internal error -> -32603. Clients MUST validate root URIs to prevent path traversal and MUST only expose roots with appropriate permissions; servers SHOULD validate all paths against provided roots. NOTE: SEP-2577 deprecates roots in the 2026-07-28 revision.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `RootProvider` with `set_roots(list[Path])` (normalizes to file:// absolute URIs, rejects symlink escapes and any path outside configured workspaces), `handle_roots_list()`, and `notify_roots_changed()`. Wire into `hday_gate.py`: every pre_tool_call decision record gains `in_scope: bool` computed against the active root set; out-of-scope writes escalate rather than auto-approve. Desktop: the escalation matrix panel shows the root set and per-root write counts. Implement roots as the *legacy* path behind a version check — see mcp2026-stateless-discover.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_roots.py — assert path traversal (`file:///workspace/../../etc`) is rejected, that a root removal emits exactly one list_changed, that in_scope is false for a path outside all roots and the gate escalates instead of allowing, and that a client without the capability answers roots/list with -32601.

name: Signals vs Updates vs Queries as three distinct message channels (plus Signal-With-Start)
what: Signals are asynchronous, fire-and-forget messages to a running workflow, sendable from a client, the CLI, or another workflow; Signal-With-Start lazily initializes a workflow while signaling it (signal the running one if it exists, otherwise start and immediately deliver). Updates are synchronous: the call invokes an update handler and can return its result, with startUpdate letting the caller await either Accepted (the worker was contacted, so the update is persisted - the point where Update Validators run) or Completed, and Update IDs giving exactly-once processing. Queries are read-only requests that do not mutate history.
build: Add hday_messages.py with three typed channel kinds: signal(run_id, kind, payload) (append-only, no response, may start the run if absent), update(run_id, kind, payload) (validated synchronously by the same judgment functions the gate uses; returns a typed result, rejects before persistence when validation fails, carries an update_id for exactly-once), and query(run_id, kind) (pure read of the ledger, never writes). Wire the desktop cockpit and Discord surface to query() for status and update() for approvals, both reading the same ledger rows.
test: tests/test_hday_lanes.py: assert a signal to a missing run creates it (signal-with-start) and appends exactly one row; assert an update with a payload that fails validation returns a rejection and leaves no ledger row while a valid one returns a result and appends one row; assert replaying the same update_id does not append a second row; assert query() on a ledger never grows the file (mtime + row count unchanged).

name: Snapshot and resume a run across processes via context serialisation
what: Workflows are ephemeral by default: once run() returns, state is gone. Because a run advances by reducing events in a controlled way, its state at any step boundary is well defined - the events still in flight plus the state store - and Context.to_dict() serialises it while Context.from_dict() rebuilds it, so run(ctx=...) continues from there, even in a different process. The documented motivation is a fan-out over hundreds of documents that should not restart from zero when the process is killed halfway.
build: Add to_dict()/from_dict() to the run context in hday_flow.py, covering exactly two things: in-flight (undelivered) events and the state store - with the pending-write and checkpoint rows from hday_checkpoint.py as the durable substrate. Add a resume_run(thread_id) entry point that rebuilds the context and continues, and make every resumed run write a 'resumed' ledger row carrying the originating checkpoint id.
test: tests/test_hday_flow.py: run a 100-item fan-out, kill it at item 40 by serialising the context and dropping the process state, rebuild with from_dict() in a fresh object graph, and assert items 1-40 are not recomputed (per-item call counters) and the run completes with all 100 results; assert the resumed run's ledger row points at the checkpoint it resumed from.

name: Storage tiers per actor: durable state, ephemeral vars, and a per-actor SQLite database
what: Rivet splits actor storage by lifetime and shape: durable c.state for serializable data that must survive restarts, ephemeral vars (declared in the actor's vars constant, must be structuredClone-able) for runtime-only data that is not persisted and is recreated on wake, and an embedded SQLite database per actor instance for relational data, queried with raw SQL and transactions, with compute and storage kept together to avoid network round trips. The state page is written as a guide to choosing between c.state and SQLite.
build: Document and enforce the tier rule in hday_manifest.py: each actor field is declared as durable | ephemeral | sqlite, and hday_actors.py materialises them accordingly (durable -> persisted snapshot, ephemeral -> rebuilt on wake from a declared factory, sqlite -> a per-actor sqlite3 file with a migration hook). Add a lint to hday_gotchas.py that flags durable state growing past a size threshold or fields declared durable that are not JSON-serializable, suggesting the sqlite tier instead.
test: tests/test_hday_actors.py: an actor with one field per tier; mutate all three, restart, and assert durable survived, ephemeral was rebuilt by its factory (not restored), and the sqlite rows are intact and transactional (a rolled-back transaction leaves no rows); assert the gotchas lint fires on an oversized durable field with the sqlite suggestion.

name: Subgraph persistence modes and checkpoint_ns namespacing
what: A subgraph is a compiled graph used as a node in another graph, and the subgraph's compile(checkpointer=...) selects its persistence: None (per-invocation, the default) starts fresh each call but inherits the parent's checkpointer for interrupts and durable execution within that call; True (per-thread) accumulates state across calls on the same thread; False (stateless) runs like a plain function with no interrupts or durable execution.
