Each checkpoint carries checkpoint_ns: '' for the root graph, 'node_name:uuid' for a subgraph invoked as that node, and nested namespaces joined with '|'. Per-thread subgraphs cannot be called in parallel because both calls would write the same namespace and conflict.
build: Add a namespace field to hday_checkpoint.py keyed like checkpoint_ns ('', 'lane:uuid', joined with '|' for nesting) plus a per-sub-run persistence mode (per_invocation|per_thread|stateless) declared in hday_manifest.py for each delegated sub-run. The gate refuses (typed judgment, not a boolean) to run two per_thread sub-runs of the same lane concurrently on one thread, returning the conflict as a routing decision instead of a crash.
test: tests/test_hday_checkpoint.py: spawn a parent run with two nested lanes; assert the nested checkpoints carry 'lane:<uuid>' namespaces and that a nested run's state is invisible to its sibling; assert stateless mode writes no checkpoint rows; assert requesting two concurrent per_thread sub-runs of the same lane yields a typed refusal with reason 'namespace_conflict' and no partial rows written.

name: Tasks extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks): polling, mid-flight input, durable handles
what: Long-running operations as first-class async: a server MAY return a task handle unsolicited (no per-request opt-in, unlike 2025-11-25), clients poll with `tasks/get`, send input with `tasks/update`, and cancel with `tasks/cancel`. `tasks/result` is REMOVED (clients calling it MUST receive -32601), `tasks/list` is REMOVED, and the `task` parameter on CallToolRequest is removed (servers MUST ignore it). Results are polymorphic — a plain CallToolResult and a task handle are both valid for any augmented request, and a client that negotiated the extension MUST handle both. Task IDs MAY be bearer tokens for server-side state and MUST be unguessable. Authz MUST be re-checked on every task-related request. Removing tasks/list is an explicit anti-leak measure: no cross-caller task enumeration.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `TaskHandle{task_id, server, created_at, status, last_polled}`; `poll_task()` with backoff, `update_task()`, `cancel_task()`. A task handle arriving where a tool result was expected is detected by shape (polymorphic result) and registered as an in-flight item rather than rendered as a tool result. Desktop: tasks render in the In-flight section with a distinct source chip and a cancel affordance. Never persist task IDs in a place that leaks them into logs; treat them as secrets in the ledger.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_tasks.py — assert a polymorphic result (handle where a CallToolResult was expected) registers an in-flight item and does not error; that tasks/result is never called and -32601 is handled; that a task ID is redacted from log output; that tasks/list is never used for discovery; and that a second profile cannot enumerate another profile's tasks.

name: Template workflow agents: deterministic sequential/parallel/loop orchestration with no model in the control loop
what: Template workflow agents operate on predefined logic and determine their execution sequence by type - sequential, parallel or loop - without consulting an AI model for orchestration, which the docs state results in deterministic and predictable execution patterns. They are presented alongside graph-based workflows (a declarative graph of nodes and edges with explicit routing) and dynamic workflows (programmatic orchestration in your own code) as three complementary ways to compose multi-step work.
build: Add hday_compose.py with three deterministic composites over lanes - Sequence([...]), Parallel([...]), Loop(body, max_iterations, until) - each returning a typed result and each writing one ledger row per child invocation plus one composite row (so the tree is reconstructible). hday_router.py keeps choosing which lanes run, but the composites own the ordering, which makes lane order testable without a model call.
test: tests/test_hday_compose.py: assert Sequence runs lanes in declared order and stops on first failure, Parallel runs all children and reports partial results with per-child rows, and Loop respects max_iterations exactly (a body that never satisfies 'until' stops after N iterations with a typed 'loop_exhausted' row); assert no composite ever calls a model (a stub model client records zero invocations).

name: Thread-scoped checkpointer with super-step snapshots and pending-write resume
what: A checkpointer snapshots graph state at every super-step (one tick where all nodes scheduled for that step run, possibly in parallel), keyed by a thread_id that is the primary key for storing and retrieving checkpoints. Each snapshot is a StateSnapshot carrying values, next (nodes still to run), config (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id), metadata (source = input|loop|update, writes = node outputs, step = super-step counter) and parent_config. When a node fails mid-super-step, the writes of the sibling nodes that already completed are kept as pending writes, so resuming from that super-step does not re-run the successful nodes.
build: Add hday_checkpoint.py implementing a Checkpointer over the existing ledger store: put(thread_id, checkpoint_ns, step, values, next_nodes, writes), put_writes(thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, task_id, writes) for per-node partial output, get_tuple(thread_id, checkpoint_id=None) and list_thread(thread_id) returning StateSnapshot-shaped dicts (values/next/config/metadata/parent_config). hday_gate.py writes one checkpoint per gate super-step (the batch of tool calls decided in one tick) and, on startup, rebuilds 'next' + pending writes from the ledger so a resumed run re-decides nothing already recorded. Keep it file-backed and offline; no network path.
test: tests/test_hday_checkpoint.py: drive a fake 3-node pipeline in-process; inject a failure after node A writes and node B raises; assert get_tuple returns the super-step whose values contain A's write and whose pending writes contain B's partial output; resume and assert A's side-effect counter is still 1 and the run reaches the terminal state. A second test asserts one checkpoint per super-step with strictly increasing metadata['step'] and a parent_config chain that walks back to the first checkpoint.

name: Time travel: state history plus explicit forks (update_state with checkpoint_id and as_node)
what: get_state_history(config) returns the thread's checkpoints newest-first, each exposing next (the nodes that would run) so you can find the boundary you want. update_state(prior_checkpoint_config, values=..., as_node=...) does not roll back the thread: it creates a new checkpoint branching from that point and execution resumes from the chosen node's successors (as_node picks which node 'produced' the update, needed for parallel branches, fresh threads, or skipping nodes). invoke(None, fork_config) then continues from the fork while the original history stays intact.
build: Add history and fork to hday_checkpoint.py: history(thread_id) returning snapshots with next/as_node candidates, and fork(thread_id, checkpoint_id, values, as_node=None) writing a new branch (new checkpoint_id, parent_config pointing at the fork point) without mutating the original chain. Expose it through a hday_replay CLI subcommand and a cockpit action, so a reviewer can fork a decided run, change one judgment input, and diff the resulting decisions against the original ledger rows.
test: tests/test_hday_checkpoint.py: run a 3-step pipeline to completion, capture the checkpoint before step 2, fork it with a changed input value and as_node set to the step-1 node; assert the forked run's step-2 output differs, the original thread's history is byte-identical before and after the fork, and the new checkpoint's parent_config points at the fork point; assert a second history() call sees both branches.

name: Wait-for-event with timeout and a correlation expression (plus wait-for-signal for unique waits)
what: step.waitForEvent(id, {event, timeout, if}) pauses the run until a matching event arrives and resolves with the event data or null if the timeout elapses first; the if expression correlates the incoming event against the triggering event's data (for example event.data.userId == async.data.userId), and race-condition guidance is documented separately. The docs position events as the preferred pause/resume mechanism because a single event fans out to many functions at once, events decouple the resumer from the resumed code, and events carry audit trails (they are stored in an OLAP store). Inside a parallel group a losing waitForEvent is not cancelled - it keeps the run active until its timeout, so timeouts should be tight.
build: Add wait_for(run_id, matcher, timeout) to hday_steps.py where matcher is a small declarative expression over {run_id, lane, kind, payload fields} (not eval'd code - a field/op/value triple), persisted as a wait row; incoming ledger events are tested against pending matchers, and the first match resumes the run with the event payload. On timeout the run resumes with None and a typed 'wait_timeout' judgment. Parallel groups register their waits in one row with an explicit on_loser policy (cancel|let_expire) so a loser cannot keep a run alive by accident.
test: tests/test_hday_steps.py: two concurrent runs waiting on the same event kind but different correlation ids; deliver one matching event and assert exactly the correlated run resumes with the payload while the other stays pending; assert the loser of a parallel race is cancelled under on_loser=cancel and that under let_expire the run is still open at the timeout with one timeout row.

name: adapter-layer-coercion
what: A signature only DECLARES types; coercion happens in the adapter layer. dspy/adapters/utils.py::parse_value tries json_repair first, falls back to ast.literal_eval, then validates against TypeAdapter(annotation); for custom dspy.Type subclasses it retries with the raw string when pydantic validation fails so the type's own parser can take over. The stated reason for the split: multiple adapters (Chat, JSON, XML, TwoStep) must coerce the same Signature differently — a JSON adapter leans on the model's JSON mode, an XML adapter parses from tags — so keeping coercion in the adapter keeps signatures lean and avoids duplicated parser logic. Field values arrive as strings and are cast at the edge.
build: Add hday_adapters.py with a 3-rung parse chain (json_repair -> ast.literal_eval -> TypeAdapter) plus per-provider adapters: JSON-mode for providers that support it, a tag-based adapter for providers that do not, and a prompted-schema adapter as the last resort. Record which rung succeeded in the ledger — a rising share of json_repair hits is an early warning that a provider's structured output is degrading.
test: tests/test_adapters.py::test_parse_chain_recovers_malformed_json_and_records_the_rung — feed trailing-comma and single-quoted payloads and assert both coerce; assert the ledger row records the rung; assert a value that no rung can repair raises rather than silently returning None.

name: bitemporal-edge-validity
what: Edges carry a temporal validity window in BOTH event time and ingestion time: t_valid/t_invalid describe when the fact was true in the world, and t'_valid/t'_invalid describe when the system learned and superseded it. When a new edge contradicts an existing one, the existing edge is INVALIDATED — its t_invalid is set to the new edge's t_valid — rather than deleted or overwritten. The README frames the same model as a 'context graph': every fact has a validity window ('Kendra loves Adidas shoes (as of March 2026)'), entities evolve with updated summaries, and everything traces back to episodes. Retrieval filters expired edges; history is preserved for as-of queries.
build: Extend ledger rows with four timestamps: valid_from/valid_to (when the decision was in force) and created_at/expired_at (when hermes-day recorded and superseded it). Add a supersede(old_id, new_id, reason) op that sets valid_to = new.valid_from and expired_at = now WITHOUT deleting the row. Default recall filters expired rows; add memory_as_of(ts) for point-in-time recall. Surface 'superseded' as a distinct cockpit badge so a stale belief is visible rather than silently absent.
test: tests/test_ledger_bitemporal.py::test_supersede_invalidates_without_deleting — write fact A, supersede it with B, assert A still exists with valid_to == B.valid_from, assert default recall returns only B, assert memory_as_of(before_B) returns only A.

name: compaction-with-preserve-list-and-recitation
what: Compaction takes a conversation nearing the context limit, summarizes it, and reinitiates a new context window with the summary. In Claude Code the message history is passed to the model to summarize and compress the most critical details: the summary PRESERVES architectural decisions, unresolved bugs and implementation details while DISCARDING redundant tool outputs and messages, and the agent then continues with that summary plus the five most recently accessed files. Tuning advice: start by maximizing recall so the compaction prompt captures every relevant piece, then iterate to improve precision — over-aggressive compaction loses subtle context whose importance only appears later. The companion technique is structured note-taking (agentic memory): the agent writes notes persisted OUTSIDE the context window and pulls them back later, which is what lets an agent read its own notes and continue multi-hour work after a context reset.
build: Replace hday_ctxscore's generic vacuum with a compaction pass that takes an explicit preserve list (open decisions, vetoed commands and their reasons, unresolved failures, file paths touched, the current mandate) and discards raw tool payloads. Always re-inject the live plan/notes file AFTER the summary so it lands in the recent attention span (this is Manus's recitation trick: rewriting the todo list at the end of context pushes the global plan into the recent attention window and mitigates lost-in-the-middle). Add a compaction recall probe: a small set of questions whose answers must survive the summary, run in tests.
test: tests/test_compaction_recall.py::test_preserve_list_survives_and_plan_is_recited_last — compact a synthetic long trace and assert the open decision, the veto reason and the touched paths are present; assert the plan block is the LAST block in the rebuilt context; assert the recall probe passes.

name: episode-provenance
what: Every derived fact traces back to an EPISODE — the raw data as ingested, the ground-truth stream. The graph is built from episodes (text and structured JSON), and the ingestion pipeline is: initialize indices/constraints, add episodes, search edges with hybrid search, rerank by graph distance, search nodes with predefined search recipes. The paper's ingestion section adds that entity extraction processes the current message plus the last n messages (n=4 in the paper, i.e. two complete turns) for context, and that writes go through predefined Cypher queries rather than LLM-generated database queries, to keep schema formats consistent and reduce hallucination.
build: Give every memory row and every ledger row a source_episode_id pointing at an immutable episode record (session id, turn index, tool call id, or an explicit ingested artifact path). Episodes are append-only and never rewritten. Add memory_provenance(memory_id) -> episode chain for the cockpit, and a memory_rebuild(episode_id) that re-runs extraction for one episode. Keep the extraction write-path as fixed, typed operations (no model-authored SQL/JSON writes).
test: tests/test_provenance.py::test_every_memory_has_an_immutable_episode_and_rebuild_is_idempotent — assert no memory row can be created with a null source_episode_id; mutate the extractor prompt, re-run memory_rebuild for one episode and assert the episode record is byte-identical while derived rows changed.

name: extraction-pipeline-with-dedup
what: add() runs a four-stage write pipeline: (1) context lookup — check related existing memories so the same fact is not stored twice; (2) fact extraction — an LLM extracts preferences, decisions, plans and reusable details; (3) deduplication and embedding — redundant facts are removed, each memory is embedded for semantic search; (4) entity extraction — pull the people/places/orgs/concepts each memory mentions, stored for entity matching at search time. Writes are ADDITIVE by default (new facts never silently rewrite old ones); infer=False stores raw content verbatim; corrections require explicit update/delete. Messages are the input, extracted facts are the storage unit, and scope is user_id / agent_id / run_id plus metadata filters.
build: Give the decision ledger a memory_add(messages, *, scope, infer=True, metadata) that runs: related-lookup (lexical + embedding over existing rows) -> extract (typed judgment returning a list of candidate facts) -> dedupe (drop near-duplicates by normalized-text hash then similarity) -> store with {scope, metadata, source_episode_id}. Keep infer=False as an escape hatch for verbatim capture. Never rewrite on add; expose memory_update/memory_delete as separate, ledger-logged ops. All writes go through the gate so an unmandated write is vetoed like any other side effect.
test: tests/test_memory_add.py::test_duplicate_facts_are_dropped_and_old_facts_survive — add the same preference twice and assert one row; add a contradicting preference and assert BOTH rows exist with distinct episode ids until an explicit update runs.

name: kv-cache-stable-prefix-and-mask-dont-remove
what: Two rules from the Manus post. (1) Design around the KV-cache: the cache hit rate is called the single most important metric for a production agent, and cached input tokens can cost ~10x less than uncached. Practices: keep the prompt PREFIX stable (a common mistake is a second-precision timestamp at the top of the system prompt, which kills the cache from that token on), make the context APPEND-ONLY (avoid modifying previous actions/observations; ensure deterministic serialization, since many JSON serializers do not guarantee stable key ordering), and mark cache breakpoints explicitly when the provider needs them, at minimum covering the end of the system prompt. Agent workloads are prefill-dominated (they cite a ~100:1 input-to-output token ratio). (2) Mask, don't remove: avoid dynamically adding or removing tools mid-iteration, because tool definitions live near the front of the context so any change invalidates the cache for everything after it, and because previous actions referring to now-undefined tools confuse the model into schema violations or hallucinated actions. Instead mask token logits during decoding, or use response prefill — auto (prefill the assistant prefix), required (prefill to the tool-call token), specified (prefill into the function name). They also keep consistent action-name prefixes (browser_, shell_) so a whole group can be enforced without stateful logits processors.
build: In the prompt assembler: freeze the prefix (system + tool definitions) across turns, move anything volatile (clock, counters, current file) BELOW the stable block, and assert deterministic serialization (sorted keys) in a test. Add a cache-bust detector that hashes the prefix each turn and logs a warning to the ledger when it changes without a declared reason — the same shape as the existing 'warn on cache busts' idea. For routing, keep the full tool list in the prefix permanently and let hday_router express availability as a mask/allowlist applied at selection time rather than by rewriting the tool block; enforce group-level availability through consistent name prefixes.
test: tests/test_prefix_stability.py::test_prefix_hash_is_stable_across_turns_and_mask_does_not_rewrite_tools — run three turns with a changing clock and assert the prefix hash is identical; assert the rendered tool block is byte-identical while the router's allowed set changes; assert a deliberate prefix change logs a cache-bust event.

name: llm-validator-with-context
what: Two mechanisms combine. (1) llm_validator(rule, client=...) plugs a model-based check into the same pydantic pipeline via BeforeValidator, so a semantic rule ('don't say objectionable things') raises a ValidationError like any other validator — and the docs note the resulting error message is generated by the LLM, not the code, 'so it'll be helpful for re-asking the model'. (2) The context parameter passes runtime data to validators, read via ValidationInfo (info.context): the worked example validates that a supporting_quote actually appears in a supplied source_text, after whitespace normalization — a deterministic, non-LLM check against ground truth.
build: Wire the ledger's evidence into validation context: any judgment that cites a file, a test name or an evidence id is validated against the real artifact (path exists, test name appears in the run output) via ValidationInfo-style context, deterministically. Reserve llm_validator-style checks for genuinely subjective rules and mark them as such in the ledger so a model-judged failure is never confused with a code-judged one.
test: tests/test_grounded_validation.py::test_citation_validators_check_real_artifacts_and_are_marked — assert a cited file that does not exist fails validation with a code-generated message; assert the ledger distinguishes code-judged from llm-judged failures.

name: output-retry-budgets-retrypromptpart
what: Retries are budgeted separately for tools and output: Agent(retries=3) sets both, Agent(retries={'tools': 5, 'output': 1}) sets them individually, and a bare int sets both; unspecified keys keep a default of 1. A retry is a MODEL REQUEST carrying a RetryPromptPart that holds the failure as a string (from ModelRetry) or a list of pydantic error details (from ValidationError) and renders with 'Fix the errors and try again.' appended; its tool_name is set for a tool-call retry and None for an output retry. Tool retries are triggered by a ValidationError on the arguments, by the tool/args_validator/hook raising ModelRetry, by a tool timeout, or by the model calling a tool that does not exist. Counter semantics are precise: the counter is keyed by tool name and RESETS ON SUCCESS (so a tool alternating fail/success never exhausts a budget of 1), max_retries=N means N retries / N+1 attempts, and a hallucinated tool name gets its own budget under the invented name, bounded by the agent-wide tools budget. Budget exhaustion raises UnexpectedModelBehavior. ToolFailed is the deliberate opposite of a retry: it records a ToolReturnPart with outcome='failed' and does NOT consume the budget, so repeated failures are bounded by UsageLimits instead. Retry prompts stay in the history, so reusing that history replays earlier failures to the model (filter them with a ProcessHistory capability if unwanted).
build: Give hermes-day's typed judgments a retry budget object {tools: N, output: M} with the same counter keying (per tool name, reset on success) and the same two failure channels: a repair prompt that replays the pydantic error list, and an explicit 'failed, do not retry' result that bypasses the budget. On budget exhaustion raise a typed error naming the tool/budget. Store the retry prompt in the transcript so a resumed session sees its earlier mistakes, and expose the per-tool retry counts in the ledger.
test: tests/test_retry_budgets.py::test_counters_reset_on_success_and_exhaustion_raises — drive a tool fail/succeed/fail/succeed with budget 1 and assert no exhaustion; drive fail/fail with budget 1 and assert a typed budget error; assert the 'failed' channel never increments the counter.

name: path-addressed-memory-blocks
what: Memory is a git-backed repository owned by the agent and projected onto the runtime filesystem (MemFS / 'context repository'). Each memory is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter and is addressed by path: the memory labelled 'system/persona' projects to system/persona.md. Files under system/ are loaded into the system prompt on every turn; everything else stays out of context until read. The file TREE is always in the system prompt, so directory and file names act as signposts the agent follows. Edits are local until committed and pushed, at which point they become the agent's memory everywhere.
build: Add hday_memory.py exposing a memory root (default .hermes-day/memory/, env override) with the layout system/{persona.md,human.md} + reference/*. Each file: YAML frontmatter (description) + body. pre_llm hook composes: (1) every file under system/ verbatim, (2) a deterministic tree listing (sorted, one line per path, no bodies) for everything else. Expose memory_read(path)/memory_write(path, body, frontmatter) tools that refuse paths outside the root. Persist via `git -C <root> commit -am <summary>` when git is present, else plain writes; never fail the turn on git errors. Emit a token count for the system/ section into the ledger so drift is visible.
test: tests/test_hday_memory.py::test_system_blocks_always_in_prompt_and_tree_is_paths_only — write system/persona.md + reference/deep.md, run a pre_llm pass, assert the prompt contains the persona body and the string 'reference/deep.md' but NOT its body; assert memory_read('../../etc/passwd') raises.

name: procedural-prompt-optimizer
what: Procedural memory encodes how the agent should behave; it starts as the system prompt and then EVOLVES through feedback. create_prompt_optimizer(model, kind='metaprompt', config={'max_reflection_steps': 3}) takes trajectories paired with feedback (e.g. {"trajectories": [(trajectory, {"user_score": 0})], "prompt": prompt}) and returns a rewritten prompt. In the documented example the optimiser turns a bare 'You are a helpful assistant.' into a numbered behavioural rule list derived from the failure in the trajectory.
build: Add an offline optimiser job that reads ledger rows for a lane, pairs each with a scalar outcome (verified=1, checks-failed=0, guard-veto=-1) plus the failure text, and rewrites that lane's instruction block via a metaprompt loop with max_reflection_steps capped (start at 3). Never auto-apply: write the candidate prompt + a diff to runs/prompt-candidates/<lane>-<ts>.md and require an explicit promote. Cap reflection steps and record token cost in the ledger.
test: tests/test_prompt_optimizer.py::test_optimizer_proposes_but_never_auto_applies — run the job over seeded ledger rows, assert a candidate file exists containing a diff against the live prompt, assert the live prompt file is byte-identical afterwards, and assert a promote step is required to change it.

name: profiles-vs-collections
what: Semantic memory is stored in one of two shapes. A PROFILE is a single structured document holding current state (e.g. a user profile with preferences and other_preferences lists); it excels when you need quick access to current state, when you have data requirements about what may be stored, and it is easy to hand to a user for manual editing. A COLLECTION is many individual documents; it is right when you want to track knowledge across many interactions WITHOUT loss of information and when you want to recall information contextually rather than every time. The docs frame the choice as a decision, not a default.
build: Implement both stores in hday_memory: a bounded profile document (system/profile.md, with a declared field schema and a hard token cap enforced at write time) and a collection table (many rows, retrieved on demand). Route writes by intent: corrections/preferences -> profile; observations/decisions/artifacts -> collection. Expose the profile in the cockpit as a human-editable pane, since that is its stated advantage.
test: tests/test_memory_shapes.py::test_profile_is_capped_and_collection_is_not — write past the profile's token cap and assert the write is rejected (or must evict a named field), while the collection accepts unbounded appends and only surfaces rows on query.

name: step.invoke for typed sub-function calls and step.sendEvent for fan-out without a result
what: step.invoke(id, {function, data}) asynchronously calls another function (in any language SDK) and awaits its typed result, with its own configuration such as concurrency limits - the documented way to compose functionality and build map-reduce style jobs. step.sendEvent(id, {name, data}) emits an event that triggers matching functions when you want fan-out and do not need the result.
build: Add invoke(lane, payload) and emit(kind, payload) to hday_steps.py: invoke creates a child run (namespace from the subgraph pattern), waits for its terminal row, and returns its typed result, all under a step memo key so a resumed parent reuses the stored child result; emit appends an event row that the dispatcher fans out to matching lanes with no parent wait. Both write ledger rows linking parent and child (or event) ids so the cockpit can render the run tree.
test: tests/test_hday_steps.py: a parent invoking two children and emitting one event; assert children are memoized (second parent resume does not re-create them), the parent result equals the children's typed outputs, the emitted event row exists with no parent-child link, and the rendered run tree in the ledger view shows exactly one parent with two children plus one detached event.

name: subagent-context-isolation-and-shared-traces
what: Anthropic: specialized sub-agents handle focused tasks with clean context windows while the main agent coordinates with a high-level plan; a subagent may explore with tens of thousands of tokens but returns only a condensed, distilled summary (often 1,000-2,000 tokens), so the detailed search context stays isolated and the lead agent synthesizes. Cognition argues the complementary constraint: PRINCIPLE 1 — share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages; PRINCIPLE 2 — actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results. Their worked failure: two parallel subagents given the same task produce a Super-Mario background and a non-Flappy-Bird bird, because each acted on assumptions the other could not see. Their default is a single-threaded linear agent; their scaling answer is a dedicated model that compresses a history of actions and conversation into key details, events and decisions — 'hard to get right', and something they have fine-tuned a smaller model for. They also observe that Claude Code's subagents never run in parallel with the parent and are usually only asked to answer a question, not write code.
build: Codify two subagent classes in hermes-day: (a) read-only investigators (recall/history/artifact search) that may run in parallel and MUST return a bounded summary (cap it — start at ~1.5K tokens) plus cited evidence ids; (b) writers that run single-threaded against the shared trace and are never parallel with a peer that touches the same artifact. Dispatch for a writer carries the full parent trace (not a paraphrase). Add a summary-size assertion so an investigator that returns a transcript is rejected. Surface the class (investigator vs writer) on the cockpit card.
test: tests/test_subagent_contract.py::test_investigators_are_bounded_and_writers_serialize — assert an investigator returning an over-cap summary is rejected; assert two writers touching the same artifact cannot be scheduled concurrently; assert a writer's dispatch payload contains the parent trace, not a summary.

name: subagent-frontmatter-memory-blocks
what: Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter in .letta/agents/ (project) or ~/.letta/agents/ (global): name, description, tools (allowlist, e.g. 'Glob, Grep, Read'), model, and memoryBlocks (which memory blocks the subagent may see, e.g. 'human, persona'). Built-ins are curated per-purpose: fork (inherits the parent conversation with full context and tools, model=inherit), general-purpose (read/write), recall (read-ONLY search of conversation history), reflection (background sleep-time consolidation), memory (reorganizes memory blocks into a cleaner hierarchy with less redundancy), init and history-analyzer. Each built-in has a recommended model tier (auto / auto-fast / inherit) and a read/write vs read-only access level.
build: Define subagent specs as .hermes-day/agents/*.md with frontmatter {name, description, tools, model, memory_blocks, access: read|read-write}. A loader parses them into typed dicts validated at startup (unknown tool or block name = hard error). The router consults memory_blocks to decide which system/ blocks to inject into that subagent's context. Ship built-ins: recall (read-only, ledger+memory search), memory (reorg/dedupe blocks), reflection (background consolidation), fork (inherit parent trace). Mirror the frontmatter in the desktop cockpit so the agent roster is inspectable.
test: tests/test_agent_specs.py::test_recall_agent_is_read_only_and_unknown_block_fails_closed — load the shipped specs, assert the recall spec's access is read and its tool list contains no write tool; assert a spec naming memory_blocks: nonexistent raises at load time.

name: subscriptions/listen: one long-lived stream with a negotiated notification filter
what: Replaces the HTTP GET endpoint and resources/subscribe|unsubscribe. Client sends `subscriptions/listen` with params.notifications = {toolsListChanged?:bool, promptsListChanged?:bool, resourcesListChanged?:bool, resourceSubscriptions?:[uri]} — all optional, omitted means not subscribed. Server MUST send `notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged` as the FIRST message, carrying `_meta['io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId']` (the JSON-RPC id of the listen request) and the subset it agreed to honour, and MUST NOT send anything on that subscription before it. Every subsequent notification carries the same subscriptionId. Multiple concurrent subscriptions are allowed and demultiplexed by that id. Graceful closure = a normal completion response to the original listen request; an abrupt transport close is a reconnect trigger, and on stdio the client MUST re-send subscriptions/listen after reconnect (no server-side subscription state survives).
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `SubscriptionStream` with `open(filter) -> SubscriptionId`, an `acknowledged` gate (no notification is dispatched before ack is seen), per-subscriptionId dispatch table, and reconnect logic that re-sends the exact original filter. Map toolsListChanged -> invalidate the mcp.tools panel cache; resourceSubscriptions -> ctxscore invalidation; promptsListChanged -> prompt cache. Desktop: a source row shows `subscribed: 2/3 types` from the acknowledged filter, so a server silently dropping a type is visible.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp2026_subscriptions.py — assert a notification arriving before acknowledged is dropped and logged (not dispatched), that two concurrent subscriptions on one stdio channel demultiplex correctly by subscriptionId, that a server dropping resourcesListChanged from the ack results in the UI showing 2/3 rather than a hang, and that after a simulated transport drop the client re-sends the identical filter.

name: tools/list + tools/call with cursor pagination and capability negotiation
what: Server declares capabilities.tools (optionally listChanged) in the initialize response. Client discovers via tools/list (supports `cursor` -> `nextCursor` pagination) and invokes via tools/call with params {name, arguments}. Tool results carry `content` (text/image/audio/resource blocks) and an `isError` boolean; unknown tool is JSON-RPC -32602, unknown method -32601. Lifecycle: client MUST send `notifications/initialized` after the initialize response before normal traffic; on HTTP every subsequent request MUST carry `MCP-Protocol-Version: <version>`.
build: New module `hday_protocols.py` with `MCPClient` class: `initialize()` -> capability dict, `list_tools()` draining cursors, `call_tool(name, arguments, _meta=None)`. Emit a normalized `ToolDescriptor{server, name, title, description, input_schema, annotations}` and a `ToolResult{is_error, content_blocks, server, duration_ms}`. Feed both into the existing gate ledger (`hday_gate.py` decision records gain `server`, `tool`, `jsonrpc_id`). Desktop: `desktop/plugin.js` gains a `mcp.tools` panel section rendering ToolDescriptor rows with an `isError` chip. Never conflate -32602/-32601 with a tool's own isError=true.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_tools.py — fixture JSON-RPC server (in-process, stdio and HTTP modes) that returns two pages of tools/list with nextCursor, a -32602 for an unknown tool, and an isError=true tool result. Assert: cursor drained exactly once, ToolDescriptor count == expected, isError surfaced separately from JSON-RPC errors, MCP-Protocol-Version header present on every HTTP request.

name: typed-deps-runcontext
what: The Agent takes deps_type=<a type> (the TYPE, not an instance — it is not used at runtime, it exists for full type checking), and each run passes the matching instance as deps=. Dependencies are accessed through RunContext[Deps], which must be the first parameter of system-prompt functions, tools and output validators; accessing them is ctx.deps.<field>. RunContext is parameterised with the deps type so a mismatch is a static type error, and it also exposes .agent (name, output_type) and realtime properties. Synchronous dependency functions are run via run_in_executor in a thread pool; deps fields can be referenced in instructions via template strings (TemplateStr('Hello {{name}}')). Dependencies can be overridden, which is what makes the agent testable.
build: Introduce a DayDeps dataclass {repo_root, ledger, config, clock, embedder} and make every hermes-day tool/hook take ctx: RunContext[DayDeps] as its first argument instead of reading module globals or env. Declare deps_type once at registration so a mismatch fails type-check. Use override to inject a frozen clock and an in-memory ledger in tests — this removes the monkeypatch-heavy setup visible in the current test suite.
test: tests/test_day_deps.py::test_tools_take_typed_deps_and_override_replaces_them — assert a tool invoked without ctx raises; run a lane with overridden deps (frozen clock, in-memory ledger) and assert no real filesystem or clock access occurred.

name: typed-step-memory-and-planning-step
what: Every agent in smolagents derives from a single MultiStepAgent class implementing the ReAct cycle (Yao et al., 2022). The loop is precisely specified: initialization stores the system prompt in a SystemPromptStep and the user query in a TaskStep; then, while the task is unsolved, the agent (a) calls agent.write_memory_to_messages() to serialize the agent logs into LLM-readable chat messages, (b) sends them to a Model and parses the completion into an action (a JSON blob for ToolCallingAgent, a code snippet for CodeAgent), (c) executes the action and logs the result as an ActionStep, and (d) runs every callback in agent.step_callbacks. When planning is activated the plan is PERIODICALLY REVISED and stored in a PlanningStep, which also feeds facts about the task into memory. Memory is therefore a typed, ordered log of step records rather than a message list, and serialization is an explicit, replaceable method. The docs also note the two variants fit different work: CodeAgent for code actions, ToolCallingAgent (JSON) when the work needs waiting between actions, e.g. web browsing with page-interaction latency.
build: Replace the ad-hoc message list in a session with typed step records: SystemPromptStep, TaskStep, ActionStep {thought, action, observation, outcome}, PlanningStep {plan, facts}. Persist them in the ledger and render through one write_memory_to_messages() function that hday_adapters can vary per provider. Expose step_callbacks as the single hook surface (folding in post_tool_call), and emit a PlanningStep on a cadence (or when the plan drifts) that re-states the plan and the facts — the same recitation mechanism as 9.1, but recorded as a typed step so it is auditable.
test: tests/test_step_memory.py::test_steps_are_typed_ordered_and_planning_recites — run a 3-step task and assert the log order is [SystemPrompt, Task, Action, Action, Planning, Action]; assert dropping ActionStep observations leaves PlanningStep and failed ActionSteps intact; assert every step round-trips through write_memory_to_messages.

name: Approval-gated tools that fail closed when no human channel exists
what: approval_required() is a built-in tool middleware that gates execution on human approval: when the model calls a decorated tool, the user is prompted to approve or deny before it runs, and a denial returns a message the agent can adapt to rather than an error. It takes message, denied_message, timeout, and allow_always, and returns an ApprovalRequired instance that reports its settings via describe().config (message, denied_message, timeout, allow_always) - while approval memory (which tools the user answered 'always' for) lives in context.variables and therefore never appears in the description. The fail-closed rule is the important one: approval_required() relies on the agent's hitl_hook to collect input, and with no hitl_hook configured there is nobody to ask, so context.input() raises HumanInputNotProvidedError and THE TURN ENDS - the gated tool does not run and, critically, the model is not handed a tool failure it could route around. The same applies on timeout: the turn ends with HumanInputTimeoutError, and a late answer arriving after the deadline does not release the approval. The docs also record a fixed bug pattern: timeout used to default to 30 and never fired because the hook ran inline so the clock only started after it returned; it now binds and defaults to None (wait indefinitely) so enabling a timeout does not silently start failing turns.
build: Port into hday_gate as middleware approval_required(message=None, denied_message=None, timeout=None, allow_always=False) returning an ApprovalRequired instance with describe().config. Gate on the turn context's hitl channel: if no hitl hook is registered, raise HumanInputNotProvidedError and END THE TURN (no tool result, no assistant continuation) rather than returning an error the model can route around. On timeout, end the turn with HumanInputTimeoutError and record the late answer as ignored. Keep approval memory in turn/session variables keyed by tool name, never on the middleware instance, and assert that describe() never contains it. Set timeout default None and document that a timeout only works because the approval channel is genuinely async.
test: Deterministic: (a) with no hitl hook, assert the turn ends with HumanInputNotProvidedError and the model receives NO message (assert the message list is unchanged); (b) with timeout=1 and no answer, assert HumanInputTimeoutError and that a late 'y' does not run the tool; (c) assert allow_always records 'always' in variables and a second call needs no prompt, while describe().config still reports allow_always=False as configured; (d) assert a denial returns denied_message to the model and the tool did not run; (e) regression: assert the timeout clock starts when the prompt is emitted, not when the hook returns (fixture where the hook sleeps past the timeout).

name: Session as a five-method pluggable store with a merge callback and a per-run fetch limit
what: A session is a narrow interface, not a framework feature: get_items(limit=...) -> list, add_items(items), pop_item(), clear_session(), and the session_id key. Runner.run(..., session=session) merges session history with the current call's input before the model call; RunConfig.session_input_callback receives the two lists and returns the merged list, which is the sanctioned seam for 'keep recent history only' style policies. RunConfig.session_settings=SessionSettings(limit=None|N) controls how much history is fetched before each run (None = all, N = most recent N). Implementations ship as a matrix over the same interface - SQLiteSession (file-backed or in-memory), AsyncSQLiteSession (aiosqlite), AdvancedSQLiteSession (branching/analytics) - and SQLiteSession(session_id, db_path) takes an optional database file. pop_item() is documented for corrections: pop the assistant item then the user item to undo a turn. Session stores items as a list of message-shaped dicts, and the runner is responsible for writing back what happened.
build: Define hday_sessions.SessionStore protocol {get_items(session_id, limit=None), add_items(session_id, items), pop_item(session_id), clear_session(session_id)} with a SqliteSessionStore implementation on the existing sqlite handle plus an in-memory store for tests. Add HdayRunConfig.session_input_callback(existing: list, new: list) -> list invoked before every lane call, and session_settings=SessionSettings(limit=...). Wire the cockpit's 'undo last turn' button to pop_item twice (assistant then user) and record the undo as a decision-ledger entry so the ledger stays the audit source of truth while the session stays the working set.
test: Deterministic: (a) with SessionSettings(limit=3) and 10 stored items assert the callback receives exactly 3; (b) assert a custom session_input_callback's return value is what reaches the model (capture via a fake provider); (c) assert pop_item twice then get_items yields the original prefix; (d) assert clear_session leaves the decision ledger untouched.

name: Task guardrails as a (passed, value) contract with feedback-as-retry and bounded retries
what: A Task can carry guardrail (single) or guardrails (a list, executed sequentially). Each guardrail is either a callable or a natural-language string; a string is turned into an LLM guardrail automatically. The callable contract is a tuple: (bool, Any) - True with the (possibly transformed) output means proceed, and False with a value means the value is treated as feedback and the task is retried with that feedback, which is why the same hook both validates and repairs output. guardrail_max_retries bounds the loop. Because guardrails are a list, validation and transformation compose: an early guardrail can normalize the output that later guardrails then check.
build: Add hday_gate.TaskGuardrail = Callable[[TaskOutput], tuple[bool, Any]]. Task(guardrails=[...], guardrail_max_retries=N). Runner: run guardrails sequentially over the candidate output; each guardrail returning (True, v) replaces the working output with v; (False, feedback) aborts the chain and re-runs the task with `feedback` appended to the prompt; after guardrail_max_retries exhausted, fail the turn with a typed GuardrailExhausted carrying the last feedback and the full guardrail history. Accept a plain string guardrail by compiling it into an LLM guardrail that asks the judgment lane for a (bool, reason) verdict. Record every attempt in the ledger {attempt, guardrail, passed, feedback}.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a guardrail returning (True, transformed) mutates the output seen by the next guardrail in the list; (b) assert (False, 'needs a citation') re-runs the task with that exact feedback in the prompt and succeeds on attempt 2; (c) assert guardrail_max_retries=2 stops after exactly 3 attempts and raises GuardrailExhausted; (d) assert a string guardrail is compiled and its verdict is routed through the fake judgment lane; (e) assert the ledger holds one record per attempt in order.

name: evaluation-result-events
what: gen_ai.evaluation.result is an event carrying gen_ai.evaluation.name (required), gen_ai.evaluation.score.label (e.g. pass/fail, relevant/not_relevant) and gen_ai.evaluation.score.value, parented to the GenAI span being evaluated, or carrying gen_ai.response.id when the span id is unavailable.
build: Emit evaluation-result rows from the scorer API and from every judge verdict: name = scorer name, label = categorical verdict, value = numeric score, parent = the ledger row id being evaluated (falling back to the turn id). Cockpit renders evaluation events as annotations on the decision row; the count of evaluation events equals the count of scored rows.
test: Unit: an evaluation event with neither a parent id nor gen_ai.response.id is rejected; label/value survive a ledger file round-trip; a fixture run with N scored rows yields exactly N evaluation events.

name: events-only-scores
what: In Langfuse v4 events_only deployments the legacy endpoints (/api/public/traces, /sessions, /scores v1, /metrics) 404. Scores still work through exactly two routes: POST /api/public/ingestion with score-create events, and GET /api/public/v3/scores. Ingestion is queued (rows appear after ~5-20s), so a single read after a 207 looks like a silent drop.
build: Vendor the client shape into hday_scores.py (stdlib only, cron-safe): push_scores(rows, run_key) builds uuid5(NAMESPACE, run_key|name) ids, encodes BOOLEAN as 1/0, posts one ingestion batch, then --verify polls v3/scores with a deadline. Score names are stable across runs; the date lives only in run_key/metadata so a trend line exists.
test: Unit with a fake transport: re-sending the same run_key yields identical ids (row count unchanged); a 207 with errors raises non-zero exit with one stderr line; verify polls until the deadline then fails loudly instead of reporting success.

name: nemo-rails-taxonomy
what: Five rail types: input rails (on user input), dialog rails (influence how the LLM is prompted), retrieval rails (on retrieved chunks in RAG), execution rails (on tool input/output), and output rails (on the generated response). A rail can reject OR alter the content (e.g. mask sensitive data, rephrase) rather than only block.
build: hday_rails.py mapping the taxonomy to hook points, with rail_action in {allow, deny, alter}; an alter rail records before/after hashes plus the reason as a ledger row (never a silent rewrite). Document the mapping in the README so new hooks land in the correct rail and the taxonomy does not drift.
test: Unit: every registered rail declares type and action; an alter rail records both hashes and the diff reason; an unknown rail type fails registration loudly; a rail that raises fails open with an unjudged row.

name: span-naming
what: Span names follow a grammar: inference spans are `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}`; agent spans are `create_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}` and `invoke_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}`; tool spans are `execute_tool {gen_ai.tool.name}`. Span kind is CLIENT for remote GenAI calls, INTERNAL for in-process tool execution.
build: hday_trace.py producing deterministic names per lane: `gate.decide {model}`, `ctxscore.score {model}`, `router.rank bm25`, `execute_tool {tool}`. Store operation_name, span_name and span_kind on each row; the cockpit groups by operation_name. Document the fallback for a missing model (e.g. `gate.decide unknown`) so names are never empty.
test: Grammar test over every lane: span_name matches ^[a-z_]+ \S+$; a missing model yields the documented fallback; a row with a free-form name fails the suite.

name: span-type-taxonomy
what: Traces are composed of typed spans (eval, task, llm, function, tool, score, and more), each type meaning one thing (e.g. task = a unit of application logic, tool = a model-issued tool call, score = a scorer result), which is what makes a trace readable at a glance and filterable.
build: Map ledger rows onto a small closed taxonomy stored as data (rules/span-types.json): turn (root), gate.regex, gate.judge, ctxscore.judge, router.rank, tool.call, score, evidence. Every row carries span_type plus parent_id; the cockpit view-model renders type-specific badges and collapses score/evidence rows under their parent. Unknown types render as unknown, never silently coerced.
test: node:vm view-model test: a fixture ledger renders correct badges; an unknown span_type renders unknown; parent linkage nests score rows under the row they graded; a row with a missing parent falls back to the turn root.

name: typed-scores
what: Four score data types: NUMERIC (float), CATEGORICAL (value from a predefined set), BOOLEAN (0/1), TEXT (free-form 1-500 chars). Five creation paths: LLM-as-a-judge, code evaluators, UI, annotation queues, SDK/API. TEXT scores are explicitly excluded from experiments, LLM-judge runs and score analytics because they cannot be aggregated.
build: Add a score row type to the ledger writer: {name, value, dataType, comment, metadata, observation_id, source}. Ship rules/score-configs.json enumerating allowed names and category sets (gate.verdict in {allow,deny,unjudged}, judge.confidence NUMERIC 0-1, evidence.present BOOLEAN). Cockpit: day-scores command plus a score column; TEXT rows render in a notes column only and are excluded from every rollup.
test: Unit: NUMERIC with a string value rejected; CATEGORICAL with an unknown category rejected; rollups skip TEXT rows; score rows never mutate the decision row they annotate; existing 267 tests still pass.

name: validator-chain-onfail
what: Guardrails AI composes validators into a chain with per-validator failure policy: `Guard().use(Validator, on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION)`, installable validators from a hub (regex match, competitor check, toxic language), and structured output generated from a Pydantic model.
build: hday_validate.py with validators [json_schema, kind_enum, confidence_range, reason_nonempty], each with a policy declared in rules/rails.yml. REASK is exactly one bounded retry to the judge; after that the row becomes unjudged (never a block). Every validation failure lands in the ledger with validator name and reason.
test: Malformed JSON triggers exactly one reask then unjudged with a reason; out-of-range confidence is rejected; a passing chain returns the parsed dict with no silent coercion; the retry counter cannot exceed 1.

name: A2A push notifications: TaskPushNotificationConfig + webhook auth (JWT/JWKS)
what: When the client is offline the agent POSTs to a registered webhook (spec section 4.3, Push Notification Objects). TaskPushNotificationConfig = {tenant?, id?, taskId?, url (required), token?, authentication?{scheme, credentials?}}. The notification is an HTTP POST to `url` with `Content-Type: application/a2a+json` and an `Authorization: {scheme} {credentials}` header, and the body is a StreamResponse containing exactly one of task | message | statusUpdate | artifactUpdate — i.e. push carries the same event types as the SSE stream. Config CRUD: CreatePushNotificationConfig / GetPushNotificationConfig / ListPushNotificationConfigs / DeletePushNotificationConfig. Server-side security: don't leak tokens, protect webhook URLs, validate the client webhook. Receiver-side: validate the source, use allowlists, verify signed tokens. Recommended flow is an asymmetric JWT: the agent signs with its private key including iss/aud/iat/exp/jti/taskId, publishes JWKS, and the webhook verifies the signature and claims; reject stale notifications by timestamp and dedupe by jti/event id.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `PushNotificationReceiver` — HTTP endpoint with a per-config shared token, JWT verification against a cached JWKS (with key rotation), claim validation (iss/aud/iat/exp/jti), timestamp freshness window, and jti replay cache. Reject by default when `authentication` is absent and the server is not on a local allowlist. Register configs on task creation, delete on terminal state. Feed verified payloads into the same event pipeline as SSE (one consumer, two sources). Desktop: a push-notification badge per source showing last-verified-at and rejected count.
test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_push.py — assert (a) an unsigned POST is rejected, (b) a JWT signed by the wrong key is rejected, (c) an expired/nbf-violating JWT is rejected, (d) a replayed jti is rejected exactly once, (e) a valid notification mutates the same task card a stream would, and (f) no token or credential appears in logs.

name: AG-UI event stream: the typed event catalogue and its flow patterns
what: A streaming, typed event protocol. Base properties on every event: type, optional timestamp, optional rawEvent, optional metadata. Categories and members: Lifecycle (RUN_STARTED, RUN_FINISHED, RUN_ERROR, STEP_STARTED, STEP_FINISHED); Text messages (TEXT_MESSAGE_START/CONTENT/END, plus a TEXT_MESSAGE_CHUNK shorthand); Tool calls (TOOL_CALL_START/ARGS/END/RESULT, plus TOOL_CALL_CHUNK); State (STATE_SNAPSHOT, STATE_DELTA, MESSAGES_SNAPSHOT); Activity (ACTIVITY_SNAPSHOT, ACTIVITY_DELTA); Reasoning (REASONING_START, REASONING_MESSAGE_START/CONTENT/END/CHUNK, REASONING_END, REASONING_ENCRYPTED_VALUE); Subagent (SUBAGENT_STARTED/FINISHED/ERROR); Special (RAW, CUSTOM); drafts (MetaEvent). Three canonical flow patterns: Start-Content-End (streaming content), Snapshot-Delta (state sync), Started/Finished|Error (lifecycle). Events should be processed in receipt order; events sharing an id (messageId, toolCallId) belong to one logical stream; implementations should be resilient to out-of-order delivery. Transport-agnostic (SSE, WebSockets, webhooks) and the agent interface is `run(input: RunAgentInput) -> Observable<BaseEvent>`.
build: `hday_events.py` (new): an internal `CockpitEvent` union mirroring the AG-UI catalogue (lifecycle/text/tool/state/activity/reasoning/subagent/custom) with a single `reduce(state, event)` reducer, plus adapters Hermes-hook -> CockpitEvent (agent_loop_stopped -> RUN_FINISHED, subagent_start/stop -> SUBAGENT_STARTED/FINISHED, pre_tool_call/post_tool_call -> TOOL_CALL_START/END) and CockpitEvent -> AG-UI wire (so hermes-day can serve its own state to an AG-UI client). The reducer is pure and order-tolerant: a TOOL_CALL_ARGS for an unknown toolCallId opens an implicit START rather than dropping the event. Desktop: plugin.js subscribes to the reducer's output instead of ad-hoc hook payloads.
test: tests/test_events_reducer.py — golden-stream tests: feed a recorded event sequence and assert the reduced cockpit state; feed the same sequence shuffled within a messageId group and assert the same final state; feed a TOOL_CALL_ARGS with no START and assert an implicit start; assert every AG-UI event type maps to exactly one CockpitEvent variant (no silent drops) with an explicit `unmapped` counter that the test asserts is zero.

name: AG-UI interrupts: RunFinished outcome=interrupt, the Interrupt type, and resume
what: Runs are interrupt-aware: RunFinishedEvent gains an optional `outcome` discriminated union — omitted (legacy, treat as normal completion), {type:'success'}, or {type:'interrupt', interrupts:[...]} where interrupts is non-empty. Interrupt = {id, reason, message?, toolCallId?, responseSchema?, expiresAt?, metadata?, subagentRunId?} — id is the correlation key across interrupt/resume/idempotency/audit; reason is a categorical routing hint (core values plus custom); responseSchema is a JSON Schema for the expected resume.payload; expiresAt is an ISO-8601 TTL and stale resumes produce RunError; subagentRunId attributes an interrupt raised inside a subagent. Resume: the next RunAgentInput on the SAME threadId carries `resume: [{interruptId, status:'resolved'|'cancelled', payload?, metadata?}]`. Denials are expressed INSIDE the payload (e.g. {approved:false}), not as a separate status. metadata carries envelope data (e.g. a signature proving the human decision wasn't tampered with) and reserves the `ag-ui` key. Contract rules: same threadId; resume[].interruptId must reference an id from the interrupted run; the resume array must address EVERY open interrupt (partial resumes unsupported). RunStarted also gains optional parentRunId (branching/time travel) and input (exact agent input for the run).
build: `hday_interrupts.py` (new): `Interrupt{id, reason, message, tool_call_id, response_schema, expires_at, metadata, subagent_run_id}` with a reason taxonomy mapped to cockpit kinds (tool_call -> approval card, input_required -> question card, custom -> generic). The cockpit's a/d/s/o keys produce resume entries: `a` -> {status:'resolved', payload:{approved:true}}, `d` -> {status:'resolved', payload:{approved:false, reason:...}} (denial inside payload), `s` -> no resume, snooze locally and re-surface. Enforce all three contract rules in code: thread match, interruptId linkage, and complete coverage of the open set — a partial submit is rejected client-side before any RPC. Reject resumes past expiresAt with a RunError rather than a silent no-op. Sign the metadata envelope with the profile key so an approval is attributable.
test: tests/test_interrupts_resume.py — assert (a) a legacy RunFinished with no outcome is treated as success, (b) a partial resume addressing 2 of 3 open interrupts is refused client-side, (c) resume[].interruptId not present in the interrupted run is refused, (d) a resume on a different threadId is refused, (e) a denial round-trips as payload{approved:false} and never as status:'cancelled', (f) an expired interrupt yields RunError and clears pending state, (g) the metadata signature verifies and a tampered payload fails.

name: Agent Card discovery: well-known URI, skills, capabilities, signatures, caching
what: The Agent Card is a JSON 'business card' describing: identity (name, description, provider), service endpoint (`url`), A2A capabilities (`streaming`, `pushNotifications`, and — after the v1.0 move — `extendedAgentCard`), authentication `schemes` (e.g. Bearer, OAuth2), and skills as AgentSkill objects {id, name, description, inputModes, outputModes, examples}. Three discovery strategies: (1) well-known URI, (2) curated registries / catalog-based, (3) direct configuration / private. Cards may be signed (RFC 7515 JWS + RFC 8785 JCS canonicalization) and clients should verify. Servers should send Cache-Control/max-age and an ETag derived from the card's `version` field or a content hash; clients should use If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since rather than unconditional re-fetch. Sensitive cards are protected by mTLS, IP restrictions, OAuth, or registry selective disclosure — never by embedded static secrets. `GetExtendedAgentCard` retrieves an authenticated, session-scoped extended card.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `AgentCardClient` — fetch the well-known card, verify a JWS signature when present (reject unsigned when policy demands it), honour ETag/max-age, and call GetExtendedAgentCard when authenticated. Normalize into `RemoteAgent{id, name, provider, url, skills[], streaming, push_notifications, auth_schemes, card_version, signature_verified}`. `hday_router.py` uses skills[] + inputModes/outputModes to route a task to a remote agent instead of a local profile. Desktop: remote agents appear in the Sources section with a `signed` / `unsigned` chip and a card-age indicator.
test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_card.py — fixture cards covering: unsigned, validly signed, tampered-payload (must fail verification), and one with an ETag that yields 304. Assert a tampered card is rejected, that a 304 does not re-download the body, that skills/inputModes drive router selection, and that no credential from the card is ever written to disk.

name: Flow control declared on the function: concurrency, multi-tenancy, throttling, debounce, priority, singleton
what: Flow control is configuration on the function rather than code: concurrency limits the number of executing steps across runs (optionally keyed per user/resource), multi-tenancy groups queued work by tenant to reduce head-of-line blocking and give best-effort fairness, throttling caps throughput over a period, debounce collapses bursts, priority orders queued work, and singleton (plus idempotency and rate limiting) round out the set - all available in every environment.
build: Add a flow block to each lane entry in hday_manifest.py: {concurrency: {limit, key}, throttle: {limit, period}, debounce: {period, key}, priority, singleton: {key}, rate_limit: {limit, period}}. Implement enforcement in hday_router.py as a deterministic scheduler over queued run rows (no wall-clock sleeps in tests: the clock is injectable), and write a typed 'flow_deferred' judgment with the rule that deferred a run so the reason is visible.
test: tests/test_hday_router.py: with an injected clock, submit 10 runs against a lane with concurrency key=tenant (limit 2) and assert at most 2 are dispatched at a time per tenant and that a second tenant is not blocked behind the first; assert a debounce window collapses 5 rapid submissions into 1 dispatch and records 4 'flow_deferred' rows naming debounce, and that a priority-9 run dispatches before an earlier priority-1 run.

name: MCP Apps (io.modelcontextprotocol/ui): sandboxed interactive UI inside tool results
what: An official extension (repo modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps) letting a server return interactive UI inline in a conversation. MVP is HTML-only, addressed by MIME type `text/html;profile=mcp-app`; clients declare support as `extensions: {'io.modelcontextprotocol/ui': {mimeTypes: ['text/html;profile=mcp-app']}}`. UI runs in a sandboxed iframe with restricted permissions; UI-to-host communication is JSON-RPC (loggable/auditable), not a global API object; hosts may predeclare/review templates; UI-initiated tool calls can require explicit user consent. An `externalIframes` capability exists for external-URL content (deferred from the MVP). Rejected alternatives: a custom message protocol, and a host-injected global API object (breaks with external iframe sources).
build: `desktop/plugin.js`: an `mcp.app` card type that renders an iframe with `sandbox` set (no allow-same-origin), srcdoc from the predeclared template, `postMessage`-based JSON-RPC bridge, and a hard allowlist of UI->host methods (at minimum: tool-call request, resize, log). Every UI-initiated tool call routes through `hday_gate.py` as its own decision record with `origin: 'mcp-app'` and requires explicit consent by default. Advertise the extension in the client capability map. Never execute UI-provided HTML outside the sandbox and never let it read plugin state directly.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_apps.py + a node:vm/jsdom harness for plugin.js — assert the iframe is created with sandbox lacking allow-same-origin, that an unlisted postMessage method is dropped, that a UI-initiated tool call produces a gate decision record with origin='mcp-app' and is denied without consent, and that a tool result without the extension falls back to plain text rendering.

name: Sampling + elicitation: the two server->client reverse requests (and MRTR in 2026)
what: Sampling: server sends `sampling/createMessage` with messages[], systemPrompt, maxTokens, optional modelPreferences; client returns CreateMessageResult {role, content, model, stopReason}. Elicitation: server sends `elicitation/create` with {mode:'form', message, requestedSchema (JSON Schema object)}; client returns ElicitResult {action:'accept'|'decline'|'cancel', content}. Both are client capabilities (`sampling:{}`, `elicitation:{}`). In 2026-07-28 both are *replaced* by Multi Round-Trip Requests: the server returns InputRequiredResult {resultType:'input_required', inputRequests:{key:{method,params}}, requestState?} and the client retries the ORIGINAL request with inputResponses keyed identically, a NEW JSON-RPC id, and requestState echoed byte-for-byte and never inspected. Server-initiated requests are no longer supported.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `ReverseRequestRouter` that classifies an inbound server request as {sampling, elicitation, mrtr_input_required} and converts it into a cockpit card of kind 'question' with a typed answer form built from requestedSchema. On answer, produce ElicitResult / CreateMessageResult (legacy) or the inputResponses retry (MRTR) — same card, two wire encodings. MRTR contract enforced in code: `request_state_echo` is stored as an opaque bytes blob, asserted equal on retry, and explicitly NOT parsed. Sampling requests MUST route through the gate: a server must not silently spend this profile's model budget.
test: tests/test_protocols_mrtr.py — (a) legacy path: server-initiated elicitation becomes a card and the accept/decline/cancel triple maps to the right ElicitResult actions; (b) MRTR path: requestState round-trips byte-identical, the retry carries a different JSON-RPC id, a tampered requestState is rejected by the fixture server, and a partial inputResponses map is answered with a fresh InputRequiredResult rather than an error; (c) a sampling request without gate approval never reaches the provider.

name: Streamable HTTP transport + OAuth 2.1 resource-server authorization
what: One HTTP endpoint (e.g. POST /mcp) handling all JSON-RPC. Client POSTs with `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`; the server replies either a single JSON response or an SSE stream carrying the response plus any interleaved server requests/notifications. Session management via `Mcp-Session-Id` returned on initialize and echoed thereafter. `MCP-Protocol-Version: <version>` header required on all requests after initialization. Shutdown = closing the HTTP connection. Authorization: the MCP server is an OAuth 2.1 *resource server*; it publishes RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata and returns 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="<url>"`, which drives discovery of the authorization server.
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `StreamableHTTPTransport` — POST with the required Accept header, parse both `application/json` and `text/event-stream` replies from the same code path, persist Mcp-Session-Id per server, attach MCP-Protocol-Version, and demultiplex SSE frames into {response, server_request, notification}. On 401, parse `resource_metadata` from WWW-Authenticate, fetch the PRM document, and surface an auth card in the vault panel with the discovered authorization server + scopes; never store the token in the plugin config.
test: tests/test_protocols_streamable_http.py — fixture server that (a) replies JSON to one request and SSE to the next on the same endpoint, (b) interleaves a server->client sampling request inside an SSE response, (c) returns 401 + WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata on a missing token. Assert the demultiplexer routes each frame correctly, that a missing MCP-Protocol-Version header is a hard client-side error, and that a token is never written into the plugin's on-disk config.

name: ast-walking-interpreter
what: Code execution is not delegated to the vanilla Python interpreter; smolagents ships a LocalPythonExecutor that loads the Abstract Syntax Tree from the code and executes it operation by operation under explicit rules. Documented rules: imports are DISALLOWED unless explicitly added to an authorization list; access to submodules is disabled by default and each must be authorized individually (or a wildcard like 'numpy.*' to allow numpy and all subpackages) — with the noted trap that seemingly innocuous packages like random can expose harmful submodules (random._os); and the total count of elementary operations is capped to prevent infinite loops and resource bloating. The docs enumerate the threat model explicitly: plain LLM error, supply-chain compromise, prompt injection from a browsed page, and exploitation of publicly accessible agents.
build: Implement the code-action executor as an AST walker: no import unless on the allowlist, submodule access denied unless explicitly granted, an operation-count ceiling per action, and no attribute access to dunder names. Record every denied node in the ledger as a guard event so injection attempts are visible rather than silent. Keep the E2B-style remote sandbox as an optional escalation for anything that genuinely needs network or a full filesystem.
test: tests/test_code_executor.py::test_imports_and_submodules_are_denied_by_default_and_op_count_is_capped — assert 'import os' is denied, assert an authorized 'numpy' does not grant 'numpy.random' without the wildcard, assert an infinite loop trips the operation cap, and assert each denial appends a ledger guard event.

name: code-as-action
what: In a CodeAgent the model writes its action as executable code rather than a JSON blob of tool names and arguments; ToolCallingAgent (JSON/text actions) is still supported alongside it. The blog's stated advantages of code actions: composability (you can nest and reuse actions the way you define and call a Python function, which JSON cannot express), object management (storing an action's output such as a generated image), generality (code expresses anything a computer can do), and representation in LLM training data (plenty of quality code is already in the training set, so models are already fluent in it). It cites multiple papers on tool calling in code and points at Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents.
build: Add a code-action lane for multi-step read-only work (triage a batch of findings, aggregate a ledger slice): the model emits one Python snippet against a small, documented API surface, hermes-day executes it in the interpreter below, and only the result enters the transcript. Gate it read-only by default and require the same mandate check as any write.
test: tests/test_code_actions.py::test_one_code_action_replaces_n_calls_and_is_read_only — assert a batch aggregation completes in a single action with one transcript entry, and that a write attempt inside a code action is vetoed by the gate.

name: gepa-reflective-pareto
what: GEPA (Genetic-Pareto, arxiv 2507.19457) evolves textual components using REFLECTION rather than reinforcement. Documented mechanics: it captures full traces of the module's execution, identifies the trace parts corresponding to a specific predictor, and reflects on that predictor's behaviour to propose a new instruction for it. Users supply rich TEXTUAL feedback in addition to scalar metric scores, at the granularity of individual predictors or the whole system. Candidate selection is Pareto-based over per-instance scores (candidate_selection_strategy: 'pareto' | 'current_best'), with reflection_minibatch_size (default 3), auto budgets ('light'|'medium'|'heavy'), max_metric_calls/max_full_evals, skip_perfect_score=True, add_format_failure_as_feedback, and pluggable instruction_proposer/code_proposer. It can also be used as inference-time search (valset=trainset, track_stats=True) returning the Pareto frontier via detailed_results.
build: Build a GEPA-shaped optimiser for the gate's judge instructions: metric returns (score, feedback_text) where feedback quotes the vetoed command and the human-readable reason; the Pareto frontier is tracked per failure family (over-block / under-block / wrong-mandate / honesty-guard). Minibatch = 3 real ledger cases, budget capped by max_metric_calls, skip_perfect_score on. Log the frontier to the ledger; promotion stays manual. Keep the existing deterministic regex honesty guard untouched — optimise only the JUDGE prompt.
test: tests/test_gepa_frontier.py::test_pareto_keeps_slice_best_candidates_and_budget_is_enforced — with two candidate prompts each best on a different failure family, assert both survive the frontier; assert the run stops at max_metric_calls and that no candidate run mutates the live judge prompt.

name: hybrid-retrieval-plus-rerankers
what: Retrieval is search-then-rerank. Three search functions run: cosine semantic similarity, Okapi BM25 full-text (both via Neo4j's Lucene), and breadth-first search over the graph. The paper is explicit about why: full-text finds word similarity, cosine finds semantic similarity, and BFS finds CONTEXTUAL similarity (nodes/edges closer in the graph appeared in more similar conversational contexts); BFS is described as enhancing the initial search results. The rerank stage raises precision: RRF (reciprocal rank fusion) and MMR (maximal marginal relevance) are supported, plus a graph-based episode-mentions reranker that prioritizes results by how often an entity or fact is mentioned in episodes. Graphiti's README exposes the same shape as 'predefined search recipes' and 'rerank by graph distance'.
build: Generalize hday_router.rank_wide into a recall pipeline: channel 1 = lexical_judge (exists), channel 2 = embedding cosine over memory + tool descriptions, channel 3 = BFS over the entity/decision graph (depth 1-2). Fuse with RRF (score = sum 1/(k + rank), k=60) then apply MMR to drop near-duplicates (lambda ~0.7 relevance vs diversity). Add an episode-mentions tiebreak using the provenance counts. Return the per-channel rank vector in Pick so the fusion is auditable, and keep a degraded path (lexical only) when no embedder is configured — mirroring hday_ctxscore's existing head/tail fallback.
test: tests/test_hybrid_recall.py::test_rrf_fuses_channels_and_mmr_drops_near_duplicates — stub three channels with disjoint rankings and assert the fused order matches a hand-computed RRF; feed two near-identical candidates and assert MMR keeps one; assert no-embedder config still returns lexical results.

name: sleep-time-memory-consolidation
what: Two agents exist under the hood: a primary agent that CANNOT edit its own in-context memory, and a sleep-time agent that holds the memory-editing tools and can rewrite BOTH the primary's in-context memory and its own. Memory management therefore happens asynchronously, off the conversation's latency path. The sleep-time agent is typically configured with a stronger/slower model than the primary, and a frequency setting trades tokens for how often it revises learned context. Updates are 'anytime': the primary can read memory while the sleep-time agent is still reasoning. Motivation stated in the post: in MemGPT, memory management, conversation and other tasks are bundled in one agent, making it slower and less reliable, and incremental in-conversation memory formation becomes messy over time.
build: Split the memory tool surface: foreground sessions get memory_read + memory_append_note; only a consolidator lane gets memory_rewrite/merge/delete. Add a consolidator entry point (cron or post-turn, gated by a frequency budget in the ledger) that reads the session ledger + gotchas + notes and rewrites system/*.md. Never let the consolidator block a read: it writes to a temp file and atomically renames. Record each consolidation pass (model, tokens, files touched) in the decision ledger so 'stronger model for consolidation' is measurable.
test: tests/test_memory_consolidation.py::test_foreground_cannot_rewrite_blocks_and_consolidator_is_atomic — assert the foreground tool list excludes memory_rewrite; run a consolidator pass over a seeded ledger and assert system/*.md changed, the rename was atomic (no partial file observed), and a ledger row was appended.

name: typed-signature-contract
what: A Signature is the declarative contract between program and model: input fields, output fields, and instructions. Mechanically, every field is a pydantic FieldInfo and the base Signature extends pydantic.BaseModel, with DSPy metadata in json_schema_extra; any pydantic constraint (gt, lt, min_length) therefore works and gets stringified into json_schema_extra['constraints'] so the ADAPTER mentions it in the prompt. The class docstring becomes the instructions (cleandoc'd; if absent DSPy generates 'Given the fields X, produce the fields Y.'). Instructions live on the signature, not the module — the module (Predict/ChainOfThought/ReAct) supplies only the call-time strategy, so the same signature can be handed to any module. Field ORDER is meaningful: Signature.fields is what the adapter walks when rendering, so reordering changes the prompt.
build: Introduce hday_sig.py: a Signature base class (pydantic) with InputField/OutputField factories carrying desc and prefix, a docstring-derived instructions property, and deterministic field ordering (inputs then outputs). Rewrite the gate judge and router judgments to declare Signatures instead of free-form prompt strings.
