Render via an adapter so the SAME signature can be sent to different providers (see adapter-layer-coercion). Keep field names stable — see immutable-signature-optimizer-safety.
test: tests/test_hday_sig.py::test_signature_is_the_schema_and_the_prompt — declare a signature with a constrained field, assert the rendered prompt contains the docstring as instructions plus the constraint text, and assert a value violating the constraint fails pydantic validation rather than reaching the model.

name: Delegation hooks that can rewrite, bound, or reject a subagent delegation, with a copied request context
what: Subagents are declared on the parent as an agents map, and the parent decides when to delegate using its own instructions plus each subagent's description - the supervisor pattern. Delegation is interceptable through a delegation option (set in the agent's defaultOptions or per call) with onDelegationStart(context), which is called before the parent delegates and returns an object controlling it: proceed: true to allow, proceed: false with a rejectionReason to reject (the reason is handed back to the parent, which can then synthesize instead), modifiedPrompt to rewrite what the subagent receives, and modifiedMaxSteps to bound the subagent's own iteration count. The context exposes primitiveId (which subagent), prompt, iteration (current iteration number) and requestContext - and the iteration field is what lets a hook implement 'reject delegation after N iterations and force synthesis'. Request context is shallow-copied at the delegation boundary, excluding run-scoped identity keys, so entries set or deleted during the subagent run do not affect the parent, and the hook can set entries on context.requestContext to pass values down. There is a further delegation option group beyond onDelegationStart (message filtering and completion scoring are documented alongside it).
build: Add delegation={'onDelegationStart': fn} on the lane group and per call. DelegationContext(primitive_id, prompt, iteration, request_context). The hook returns {proceed: bool, rejection_reason: str|None, modified_prompt: str|None, modified_max_steps: int|None}. Implement: rejection returns the reason to the parent as a tool error it can act on rather than aborting the turn; modified_prompt replaces the child's prompt; modified_max_steps caps the child's loop; and request_context is a SHALLOW COPY at the boundary so child writes never leak to the parent (assert this with a mutation test). Record every delegation decision and its modifications in the ledger.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert proceed=False delivers rejection_reason to the parent and the child lane never runs (spy counter == 0); (b) assert modified_prompt is what the child receives (capture the child's first request); (c) assert modified_max_steps caps the child's iterations at exactly N; (d) assert iteration increments across repeated delegations in one turn and a hook rejecting at iteration > 8 forces synthesis; (e) assert a child setting a request_context key is not visible to the parent afterwards, while a key set by the hook IS visible to the child.

name: Evals as gates plus thresholds with a three-valued verdict
what: Evals add severity semantics to a scored run. runEvals({data, target, gates, scorers}) separates hard requirements from tracked metrics: gates are scorers that must average 1.0 across all data items or the run fails, and scorers are tracked metrics that may carry a threshold. A threshold is either a number (minimum) or an object with min and/or max - max exists specifically for scorers where a high score is bad (hallucination, toxicity) and {min, max} expresses a band. The verdict is computed after all items are processed: 'failed' if any gate averaged below 1.0, 'scored' if all gates passed but some threshold was missed, 'passed' if all gates scored 1.0 and all thresholds were met; the verdict field is OMITTED entirely when no gates or threshold-bearing scorers are configured, or when every configured gate and threshold returned notScorable() (no numeric evidence), in which case scores and summary are still returned. Gates run before regular scorers on each item, and a gate-only run is allowed (scorers is optional when at least one gate is present) which is documented for deterministic CI checks; a run with neither gates nor scorers throws. Results are exposed as gateResults [{id, passed, score}] and thresholdResults [{id, passed, averageScore, threshold}] so CI can print exactly which gate failed.
build: Add hday_evals.run_evals(data, target, gates=[], scorers=[]) with Gate(id, fn) requiring an average of 1.0 and Scorer(id, fn, threshold: float | {'min':..,'max':..}). Compute verdict in {passed, scored, failed} after all items, OMIT the verdict when there are no gates or threshold-bearing scorers or when every one returned not_scorable(), and expose gate_results and threshold_results. Allow a gate-only run (scorers optional) and raise when neither is supplied. Wire a CI entry point that exits 1 on 'failed', warns on 'scored', and prints the failing gate ids. Mirror mastra's naming in the test helpers so existing tests can migrate incrementally.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a gate averaging 0.99 yields verdict='failed' and a gate averaging 1.0 yields at least 'scored'; (b) assert a max-only threshold fails on a high score (toxicity fixture) and a {min,max} band fails outside the band; (c) assert the verdict key is ABSENT when all gates and thresholds return not_scorable() (assert 'verdict' not in result); (d) assert a run with neither gates nor scorers raises; (e) assert a bare scorer appears in scores but does not change the verdict; (f) assert gate_results ids match the failing gate printed by the CI entry point.

name: Event-driven core: topics as (type, source) pairs with typed subscriptions instead of direct agent references
what: Agent-to-agent messaging is decoupled through topics. A topic is identified by a TopicId of (type, source) where source defaults to DefaultTopicId (type='default', source='default'), so broadcasting is publishing to the default topic and direct addressing is publishing to a topic whose source is the target agent's id. Subscriptions are typed: TypeSubscription(topic_type=..., agent_type=...) means every agent of that type receives every message published to that topic type. Because the source is part of the identity, the same message type can be routed to a specific instance without the publisher knowing the instance's object - and an agent id is auto-generated from the topic source when the runtime creates the agent, which is what makes 'publish to topic (T, agent_id)' work as direct messaging. Publish is via the runtime's publish_message with the sender's id, and handlers are declared with @message_handler on a RoutedAgent.
build: Add hday_bus.py: TopicId(type: str, source: str = 'default'), Subscription(protocol) with TypeSubscription(topic_type, agent_type) and a DefaultSubscription for the default topic. Lane agents extend a RoutedLane base with @handler(message_type) methods and an auto-generated lane_id derived from the topic source when registered. Implement publish(topic_id, message, sender_id) and broadcast(message, sender_id) on a Bus that resolves subscriptions to lane instances and records one ledger entry per delivery {topic_type, topic_source, message_type, sender, receiver, ts}. No lane may hold a direct reference to another lane - enforce it with an import/dependency test.
test: Deterministic: (a) two lanes subscribing to the same topic_type both receive a broadcast, in registration order; (b) a direct publish to (type, lane_id) reaches only that lane even when three lanes subscribe to the type; (c) assert lane_id is derived from the topic source on register; (d) static test: no module under lanes/ imports another lane module; (e) assert one ledger entry per delivery and zero entries for a publish with no subscribers.

name: Group chat as a manager-mediated RequestToSpeak protocol with model-based speaker selection
what: The group-chat pattern is implemented as a manager agent that owns the roster and the transcript. Participants are registered with the manager (RegisterAgent carrying the agent's topic type), and the manager runs a loop: publish a RequestToSpeak message to the selected participant, receive a GroupChatRequestPublish, publish the participant's message to the group topic, record it in the conversation, then select the next speaker and repeat until a termination condition holds. Speaker selection is pluggable - the reference implementation uses a model call over the transcript plus the roster - and SelectorGroupChat documents the high-level version of the same loop: it selects the next speaker from conversation context plus each participant's name and description, will not select the same speaker consecutively unless allow_repeated_speaker=True, supports a custom selection_function and a candidate_function that narrows the roster before selection, and supports a custom selector_prompt. Messages are broadcast to all participants, and after a task completes the conversation context is retained by the team and participants so the next task continues from it; BaseGroupChat.reset() clears it.
build: Add hday_groupchat.py: GroupChatManager holding roster (lane_id -> description) and a shared transcript. Protocol messages RegisterAgent(lane_id, topic_type), RequestToSpeak(manager_id, request_id), GroupChatRequestPublish, GroupChatMessage(sender, content). select_speaker(transcript, roster, allow_repeated_speaker=False, candidate_function=None, selector_prompt=None) returns a lane_id; default implementation uses the hday judgment lane, with candidate_function narrowing the roster first. Enforce: no consecutive selection unless allow_repeated_speaker; unknown lane_id raises; every selection writes a ledger entry {kind: speaker_selected, request_id, lane_id, reason}. Expose reset() and keep the transcript across tasks by default.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert the manager never selects the same lane twice in a row while another candidate exists, and does when it is the only candidate; (b) assert candidate_function is applied before selection and a lane excluded by it can never be selected; (c) assert a scripted selector_function drives a fixed 5-message transcript deterministically (golden-file compare); (d) assert reset() empties the transcript while ledger history survives; (e) assert each RequestToSpeak produces exactly one publish from the requested lane and that an out-of-turn publish is rejected.

name: Guardrails as typed verdicts with tripwires, plus a parallel-vs-blocking execution switch
what: Guardrails are decorated functions (@input_guardrail, @output_guardrail) that return GuardrailFunctionOutput(output_info=<any>, tripwire_triggered=<bool>), wrapped by the runner into InputGuardrailResult / OutputGuardrailResult. If tripwire_triggered is true the runner raises InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered / OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered and halts. Two execution strategies: run_in_parallel=True (default) starts the guardrail concurrently with the agent - lowest latency, but the agent may already have consumed tokens and executed tools before cancellation; run_in_parallel=False runs the guardrail to completion BEFORE the agent starts, so a tripwire prevents token spend and tool side effects (output guardrails always run after the agent, so they have no run_in_parallel). Input guardrails run only for the FIRST agent in a chain. The exception carries evidence: exception.guardrail_result identifies the triggering guardrail, and exception.run_data.input_guardrail_results / output_guardrail_results hold every result completed before the stop, including the tripwire. Tool-level guardrails (tool_input_guardrails / tool_output_guardrails) exist on the FunctionTool pipeline and can be attached to every tool of a local MCP server; hosted tools and built-in execution tools do not use that pipeline. A tripwire and an exception raised by the guardrail function behave differently on persistence: a tripwire persists already-completed tool call/output items and reasoning needed for replay while EXCLUDING the rejected candidate final output, substituting the text 'Output withheld by an output guardrail.'; a raised exception is treated as an unknown verdict and persists completed final-turn items. RunConfig.output_guardrail_blocked_message can replace the placeholder with a data-free string or synchronous formatter that never receives the rejected output.
build: Introduce hday_gate.GuardrailResult(guardrail_name, output_info, tripwire_triggered) and a @guardrail(kind='input'|'output', run_in_parallel: bool) decorator registering into a lane's guardrail lists. Gate returns a GuardrailResult instead of raising, and the runner converts tripwire=True into GateTripwire(lane, guardrail_name, run_data). Implement the persistence rule in the ledger writer: on tripwire, append tool_call/tool_output records plus the guardrail result with output_info replaced by a constant placeholder, and never append the candidate output; on a guardrail exception, append the completed final-turn items and mark verdict='unknown'. Add RunConfig.tripwire_placeholder so the placeholder text is configurable but never derived from rejected content. Keep input guardrails first-agent-only, matching the reference semantics.
test: Deterministic: (a) a stub guardrail returning tripwire_triggered=True raises GateTripwire and the ledger contains zero records carrying the rejected payload (assert by substring scan of the serialized ledger); (b) with run_in_parallel=False assert the tool executor was never invoked (spy counter == 0) when the guardrail trips, and was invoked when run_in_parallel=True; (c) assert input guardrails registered on a second lane in a chain never execute; (d) assert GateTripwire.run_data.input_guardrail_results includes the triggering result.

name: Hook system with typed interception points, four interception verbs, and fail-open for unrelated exceptions
what: Execution hooks are typed by InterceptionPoint and registered per agent, per tool, or crew-wide, with agents=/tools= scoping filters. A hook may intercept in four ways: proceed (let the call continue, optionally with modified arguments), mutate, replace (substitute the result), or abort. Aborting raises HookAborted carrying a reason and a source, which is a typed signal rather than a generic exception. Crucially, the failure policy is asymmetric: HookAborted is the deliberate control-flow path, while any OTHER exception raised inside a hook is fail-open - the hook is treated as a non-event and execution continues, so a broken observability hook cannot take down a run. Hooks also emit a HookDispatchedEvent for telemetry, which makes hook activity observable without instrumenting each hook.
build: Add hday_hooks.InterceptionPoint enum (agent_start, agent_end, llm_before, llm_after, tool_before, tool_after, task_start, task_end, turn_end) and register(point, fn, agents=None, tools=None, crew_wide=False). Implement the four verbs: Hooks.proceed(args=None), Hooks.mutate(args), Hooks.replace(result), Hooks.abort(reason, source) raising HookAborted. The dispatcher catches HookAborted and honours it; it catches every other exception, logs it without payload, and CONTINUES the call (fail-open). Emit a HookDispatchedEvent(point, hook_name, outcome, duration_ms) into the ledger for every dispatch, including fail-open ones.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert Hooks.abort raises HookAborted and the call does not proceed; (b) assert a hook raising ValueError is logged, the call proceeds, and a HookDispatchedEvent with outcome='error' is recorded; (c) assert mutate changes the arguments the executor receives; (d) assert replace short-circuits the executor (spy counter == 0) and its value is returned; (e) assert agents=['lane-a'] scoping means the hook never fires for lane-b; (f) assert exactly one HookDispatchedEvent per dispatch.

name: LLM-collapsed human feedback that routes a flow through declared outcomes
what: A @human_feedback(...) decorator on a flow method declares the outcomes the human can produce: emit=[...] names the branches, llm= names the model that interprets the free-form human reply, and default_outcome= names the fallback when the reply matches nothing. The human types prose; the model collapses it into exactly one of the declared outcomes; the outcome is what @listen/@router conditions branch on. The result is surfaced as a HumanFeedbackResult dataclass carrying both the raw text and the resolved outcome, and there is an async provider form so a webhook or UI can supply the answer without blocking the flow thread. This keeps the flow graph finite (only N branches exist) while letting the human speak naturally.
build: Add hday_gate.human_feedback(emit=[...], llm=None, default_outcome=None) decorating a step. On invocation, emit a feedback request to the cockpit, receive free text (sync provider or async provider for webhook/UI), call the judgment lane with a schema constraining the answer to the declared outcomes, and return HumanFeedbackResult(raw_text, outcome, matched: bool). Steps then declare routing as on(outcome) handlers, so the graph has exactly len(emit) branches. If the model returns nothing matching, use default_outcome and record matched=False in the ledger.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert free text 'yeah go ahead but tighten the intro' collapses to the declared 'approve' outcome via a fake judgment lane; (b) assert text matching nothing yields default_outcome with matched=False; (c) assert the returned object carries both raw_text and outcome; (d) assert only the declared outcomes can route (an undeclared outcome raises); (e) assert the async provider path resolves a webhook-supplied answer without blocking.

name: MCP Registry: server.json metadata, reverse-DNS namespaces, and the aggregator REST API
what: The official centralized metadata repository for publicly accessible MCP servers (preview; backed by Anthropic, GitHub, PulseMCP, Microsoft). Metadata is stored as `server.json` (schema at github.com/modelcontextprotocol/registry/blob/main/docs/reference/server-json/draft/server.schema.json) containing the unique server name (reverse-DNS form, e.g. `io.github.user/server-name`), where to locate the server (npm package name, remote URL), execution instructions (args, env vars), and discovery data (description, capabilities). Namespace authentication ties names to verified GitHub accounts or domains (GitHub, DNS, or HTTP challenges), so only the legitimate owner can publish under a namespace. A REST API plus a published OpenAPI spec (docs/reference/api/openapi.yaml) is the interface other registries implement, so private registries interoperate with existing host support. The registry hosts metadata and delegates security scanning to package registries and downstream aggregators; host applications are explicitly NOT meant to consume it directly but through downstream aggregators (expected pull cadence ~hourly). Private servers are out of scope — self-host a private registry instead. Spam controls: namespace authentication, strict character limits/regex validation, manual takedown; rate limiting and AI spam detection under consideration.
build: `hday_registry.py` (new): a registry client implementing the published OpenAPI surface (search, fetch server.json by name, list versions), with a local cache honouring the ~hourly pull expectation and never fetching on the interactive path. A `Publisher{namespace, verification_method, verified: bool}` normalizer shared with the A2A card verifier so the cockpit's Sources section has one trust vocabulary. Desktop: a 'Discover servers' pane listing registry entries with verified/unverified publisher chips and a one-click install that writes an explicit config entry (never silent). Treat registry metadata as untrusted input: validate against server.json before use, and never auto-execute a command from a registry entry without an approval.
test: tests/test_registry_client.py — assert an unverified namespace renders as unverified and cannot be one-click installed; that a server.json failing schema validation is rejected with a readable error; that registry reads are served from cache inside the TTL window; and that no registry-supplied command is ever executed without a gate decision record.

name: Middleware as typed async hooks that wrap call_next, with per-turn instance state and an introspectable describe()
what: AG2 middleware defines four typed async hooks - on_turn, on_llm_call, on_tool_execution, on_human_input - each receiving the event plus a call_next continuation. A hook may call call_next(...) to continue the chain (possibly with modified arguments), return its own result to replace the call, or raise to stop. Middleware instances hold state that lives for the duration of a turn, so a middleware can accumulate across the hooks it sees within one turn and be re-created for the next. Middleware declares its configuration through describe(), which exposes the settings in a form that can be logged or asserted on - so a middleware's configuration is testable without invoking it, and configuration that must NOT leak (such as per-user approval state) is deliberately kept in context.variables rather than on the instance.
build: Add hday_middleware.py with abstract Middleware exposing async on_turn(event, call_next), on_llm_call(event, call_next), on_tool_execution(event, call_next), on_human_input(event, call_next), plus a state dict created fresh per turn and a describe() returning a frozen config dict. Register middleware per tool (@tool(middleware=[...])), per agent (Agent(middleware=[...])), and per run (middleware=[...] on the call), applied outermost-first in registration order. Anything that must not be introspected (approval memory) goes into the turn context's variables, never onto the instance. Port the honesty guard from a boolean check into an on_tool_execution middleware that can short-circuit by returning a result.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert the four hooks fire in the documented order for a scripted turn and that call_next receives modified arguments when a hook rewrites them; (b) assert a hook returning without calling call_next prevents the inner call (spy counter == 0); (c) assert state accumulated in on_turn is visible in on_tool_execution within the same turn and absent in the next turn; (d) assert describe() on approval_required-style middleware contains only config keys and no approval state; (e) assert nested middleware order is outermost-first.

name: OpenAI Realtime: interruption semantics and MCP-tool approval inside the session
what: Interruption: the reference client's cancelResponse(id, sampleCount) immediately ceases generation AND truncates the played item — removing all audio after sampleCount and clearing the text response — specifically so the model does not 'remember' content it generated ahead of where the user actually heard. Push-to-talk over WebSocket: set turn_detection null; on push down, response.cancel if a response is in flight and conversation.item.truncate to drop unplayed audio; on push up, input_audio_buffer.append, input_audio_buffer.commit, then response.create. Over WebRTC/SIP the input audio buffer must be explicitly cleared (input_audio_buffer.clear) and unplayed output dropped with output_audio_buffer.clear, which also truncates the conversation. MCP: the realtime API reference includes MCP-specific models (realtime_mcp_approval_request among the realtime resource models), i.e. MCP tool calls inside a realtime session carry an explicit approval step in the event model rather than executing silently.
build: `hday_voice.py`: implement truncation faithfully — on barge-in, cancel the response, truncate at the samples actually played, and record the truncated length in the ledger so the transcript the cockpit shows matches what the human heard. Any MCP tool call arriving inside a realtime session must raise an approval request that lands in 'Needs you' like any other interrupt; never auto-approve because the channel is voice. Desktop: a voice session is a source row with a distinct chip and the same a/d keyboard affordances.
test: tests/test_voice_interrupt.py — assert barge-in emits cancel + truncate with the played-sample count and not the full length; that the recorded transcript matches the truncated audio; that an MCP tool call inside a voice session creates a pending approval and is not executed; and that approving by voice and by keyboard produce identical resume payloads.

name: Session storage keyed by session_id with a session_type discriminator, separate run tables, and storage control
what: Persistence is opt-in by attaching a database, and everything then hangs off a session_id. A hydrated session carries session_id, the owner id (agent_id / team_id / workflow_id depending on owner type), user_id, per-owner data blobs (session_data, agent_data, team_data, workflow_data), metadata, runs, summary, created_at and updated_at. The physical layout separates concerns: session metadata lives in a session table (default agno_sessions) while run records live in a separate runs table (default agno_runs) and are loaded into session.runs on hydration - runs is not a column on the session table - and a session_type discriminator column distinguishes agent, team and workflow sessions, so one storage layer serves all three owner types. Tables are created on first relevant operation if absent, session_table and runs_table are independently configurable (documented for environment isolation), and the same get_session(session_id=...) interface exists on Agent, Team and Workflow. There is also documented storage control for choosing what gets persisted, and session summaries for condensing long conversations.
build: Add hday_store.py: Session(session_id, owner_id, owner_type, user_id, session_data, owner_data, metadata, runs, summary, created_at, updated_at) with owner_type in {agent, team, workflow} as a discriminator column. Two tables, hday_sessions and hday_runs, with independently configurable names, created on first use if absent; hydration loads runs into session.runs. Expose get_session(session_id) identically from agent, lane_group and flow objects. Add a storage_control config listing which message classes are persisted (e.g. skip reasoning traces and raw tool payloads) and a session summary job that condenses long sessions.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert runs is not a column on hday_sessions and hydration reconstructs session.runs from hday_runs in order; (b) assert an agent session, a lane_group session and a flow session are distinguishable by owner_type while get_session is the same call shape; (c) assert custom session_table/runs_table names are honoured and a fresh DB creates both tables on first write; (d) assert storage_control excluding tool payloads means the persisted run has the tool call but not its payload; (e) assert a session summary is produced for a session past the configured length.

name: Skills as frontmatter-declared capability bundles with progressive disclosure and invocation control
what: A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md whose frontmatter declares the contract: name, description, and controls including allowed-tools (pre-approve the tools the skill may use), disable-model-invocation (the model cannot auto-invoke it), user-invocable, context (including running the skill inside a forked context), agent, model, and hooks. Skills are discovered from user, project and plugin scopes. Invocation has two independent axes - the model may invoke a skill when the description matches, and the user may invoke it directly - and each axis is switchable, which is what lets you ship a skill that only humans can trigger. Skills can be executed in a subagent context, and a skill's frontmatter can carry hooks, so a skill is a portable unit of instructions + tool permissions + lifecycle behavior.
build: Extend the existing skill loader to parse SKILL.md frontmatter into SkillSpec(name, description, allowed_tools: list[str], disable_model_invocation: bool, user_invocable: bool, context: 'inline'|'fork', agent: str|None, model: str|None, hooks: dict). Register allowed_tools as a pre-approval set in hday_gate that is consulted AFTER deny rules (deny still wins) and only for the duration of the skill's execution. Gate model-side invocation on disable_model_invocation and expose user invocation separately in the cockpit command palette. context='fork' runs the skill body in a fresh subagent with the skill's allowed_tools rather than inheriting the parent's.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a skill with allowed_tools=['read'] gets no approval prompt for read but still hits a deny rule on write; (b) assert disable_model_invocation=True means the model's tool list omits the skill while a direct invocation still succeeds; (c) assert context='fork' starts a subagent whose tool list is the skill's allowed_tools intersected with the registry; (d) assert a skill-declared hook fires only while that skill is executing.

name: Skills over MCP (io.modelcontextprotocol/skills): serving Agent Skills as resources
what: Serves Agent Skills (the agentskills.io SKILL.md format) over MCP: discovery via `skills/list` and retrieval via `skills/get`, with supporting files exposed as MCP resources, directory listing via `resources/directory/read` (including a 'held entry' concept for directory reads), and per-skill `_meta` key conventions. Skills can nest. A pointer can be exposed from server `instructions`. Files are retrieved lazily as needed, so cost scales with files actually used, not skill size. An archive form was considered and deferred (symlink/executable-bit and host-unpacking risk).
build: `hday_protocols.py`: `list_skills()`, `get_skill(name)`, `read_skill_resource(uri)`. Represent each remote skill as a first-class entry in `hday_manifest.py` with `origin: 'mcp:<server>'` so local and remote skills are uniformly listable and a name collision is detectable. Desktop: an extension of the existing panel list showing remote skills with their server chip and a 'pull' action. Do NOT auto-execute or auto-install a remote skill; retrieval is explicit.
test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_skills.py — assert a remote skill and a local skill with the same name are both listed and flagged as a collision rather than one silently winning; that skill files are fetched only when read (count RPCs); and that nested skills resolve their own resources under the right parent.

name: Subagent definition file with a frontmatter contract that constrains tools, model, permissions, skills and hooks
what: A subagent is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter plus a system-prompt body, and the frontmatter is the whole contract: name (required), description (required - the parent uses it to decide when to delegate), tools (an allowlist; omitting it inherits every tool), disallowedTools, model (model | inherit), permission-mode, skills, hooks, and memory. Files are discovered from user, project, and plugin scopes with a documented precedence, and a subagent can be created through the /agents command, the CLI, or by hand. Two invocation paths: automatic (the parent delegates based on the description) and explicit (the user names the subagent). Key operational facts: subagents run with their OWN context window and cannot see the parent's conversation except through what the parent passes in the delegation prompt; they cannot spawn further subagents (no nesting); and there is a documented concurrency limit for parallel subagent execution. Context management is first-class: a subagent can be given a persistent identity (worktree-isolated and/or background) so it survives across turns, and its transcript can be retrieved afterwards, with per-subagent transcript files. There is also a fork mode (CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT) where a subagent inherits the parent's full conversation instead of starting clean.
build: Add hday_manifest.SubagentSpec parsed from .hday/agents/<name>.md YAML frontmatter: name, description, tools (list|None=inherit), disallowedTools, model ('inherit' or explicit), permission_mode, skills, hooks, memory. Lane loader resolves specs across scopes (user < project < plugin) with documented precedence and validates: name unique, description non-empty, tools subset of the registered tool registry, no nesting (a subagent spec must not declare `agents`). Delegation passes an explicit prompt payload because the child context is fresh; a `fork: true` flag makes the child inherit the parent's message list instead. Add a max_concurrent_subagents setting enforced by a semaphore in the dispatcher, and write each child's transcript to runs/agents/<lane>/<run_id>.jsonl retrievable by the cockpit.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a spec with tools=['read','grep'] cannot invoke a write tool even when the parent can; (b) assert omitting tools inherits the full registry; (c) assert a spec declaring nested agents fails manifest validation with a specific error; (d) assert two subagent specs with the same name resolve by scope precedence and the loser is reported; (e) assert max_concurrent_subagents=2 serializes three delegations (assert peak observed concurrency == 2); (f) assert fork=True puts the parent's messages in the child's first request and fork=False does not.

name: Suspend and resume with schema-validated resume data and persisted snapshots
what: A step can pause itself: it declares a resumeSchema in addition to inputSchema/outputSchema, and inside execute it calls suspend() (returning suspend({...})) when its resume condition is unmet. Suspension saves the current execution state as a snapshot in the configured storage provider, so it persists across deployments and restarts. run.resume({step, resumeData}) restarts from that step with resumeData validated against the step's resumeSchema; the step object can be passed for full type-safety or a step id string when the id comes from user input or a database; when only one step is suspended the step argument can be omitted and the last suspended step resumes; and resuming with only a runId requires creating the run instance first via createRun({runId}). Because resume is an ordinary call, it can be invoked from an HTTP endpoint, an event handler, or a timer - which is what makes 'wait for a human, an API callback, or a delay' the same mechanism.
build: Add resume_schema to hday_flow.Step and a suspend(payload) call inside execute. On suspend, persist a Snapshot(run_id, step_id, state, created_at) through the existing storage provider and return a suspended run handle. Implement run.resume(step=None, resume_data=None, run_id=None): validate resume_data against the step's resume_schema (reject with a typed error on mismatch), locate the step by object or by id string, default to the last suspended step when omitted, and require create_run(run_id=...) when only a run id is known. Expose a POST /runs/{run_id}/resume endpoint for the cockpit and a timer-based resume for timeout policies.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert suspend() writes exactly one snapshot and the run reports suspended with the step id; (b) assert resume with resume_data violating resume_schema raises a typed validation error and leaves the snapshot intact; (c) assert resume by step id string and by step object behave identically; (d) assert omitting the step resumes the last suspended step when exactly one is suspended and raises when several are; (e) assert resume from a re-loaded process (serialize, restart, resume) produces the same completion; (f) assert the HTTP endpoint path performs the same validation as the in-process call.

name: Team modes: the orchestration pattern is a swap-in enum, and members are resolved by stable id at run time
what: A team's delegation behavior is selected by a mode enum rather than by rewriting members: TeamMode.coordinate (default) has the leader select members, formulate each member's task, and synthesize results; TeamMode.route has the leader pick one member and return that member's response directly (no synthesis step, lower latency); TeamMode.broadcast sends the same task to every member; TeamMode.tasks has the leader build and execute a shared task list until the goal is complete. Two orthogonal flags survive as legacy: determine_input_for_members=False passes the raw user content to members instead of letting the leader formulate a task (and it applies across coordinate, route and broadcast), and respond_directly=True returns member responses without leader synthesis. Member identity is explicit - members should carry stable id values because member selection and run tracking are keyed on them - and members can also come from callable factories resolved at run time, so the roster is not fixed at construction. The leader can still answer directly or use its own tools in any mode.
build: Add hday_router.TeamMode {coordinate, route, broadcast, tasks} and lane_group(name, members=[...], mode=TeamMode.coordinate, determine_input_for_members=True, respond_directly=False). Require every member to declare a stable id and fail manifest validation if missing or duplicated. Implement members= as a list or as a callable factory resolved at run time. Record the mode and the resolved member ids on every delegation ledger entry so a strategy change is visible in the audit trail.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert route mode returns the member's response unchanged with no synthesis call (assert the leader's synthesis prompt was never built); (b) assert broadcast sends the identical task object to every member and coordinate sends per-member tasks; (c) assert determine_input_for_members=False passes raw user content for coordinate, route and broadcast; (d) assert tasks mode executes a shared list to completion and its final task list is recorded; (e) assert a member without a stable id fails validation and a duplicate id fails validation; (f) assert a callable factory is invoked once per run, not at construction.

name: Tool hooks as ordered wrappers with injected run context, plus observe-only pre/post hooks
what: A tool hook receives the function name, the wrapped function call, and the arguments, and controls execution by what it does with the wrapped callable: calling function_call(**arguments) continues the chain (possibly with mutated arguments), while raising or returning another value stops or replaces the call. Hooks are assigned per agent or per team and apply to every tool call that owner makes, or per tool via the decorator, and a list is applied in order with the FIRST hook as the outermost layer. Hooks can receive a RunContext by declaring a supported parameter name, giving access to session state, dependencies and metadata - the documented pattern is to read a value out of session_state and rewrite an argument before continuing the chain. Alongside wrapping hooks there are observe-only pre_hook and post_hook callbacks that receive the FunctionCall object (function, arguments, result); exceptions in these are logged and execution CONTINUES, and the docs state explicitly that they are not equivalent to a wrapping gate - deliberate aborts need a supported run-control exception such as StopAgentRun.
build: Add hday_tools.hook(fn) with a documented parameter-name convention: agent/lane, team, run_context for injection, name/function_name, function/func/function_call, args/arguments. Wrap order = outermost-first in registration order, and the chain continues only when the hook calls function_call(**arguments); raising aborts, returning a value replaces. Add pre_hook/post_hook decorator kwargs receiving a FunctionCall(function, arguments, result) that are observe-only: exceptions are logged and execution continues, and deliberate aborts must use StopRun from hday.exceptions. Document in the gate module that pre/post hooks must never be relied on to block.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert hooks=[outer, inner] runs outer first and that mutating arguments in outer is visible to inner and to the tool; (b) assert a hook that raises prevents the tool from running and propagates the exception; (c) assert a hook that returns a value replaces the tool result; (d) assert a pre_hook raising ValueError is logged and the tool still runs; (e) assert run_context injection exposes session_state mutations to the tool body; (f) assert StopRun from a post_hook aborts the run (the documented deliberate-abort path).

name: Typed handoff tool with declared destination, argument schema, and history input_filter
what: A handoff is not an internal function call - it is rendered to the model as a tool named transfer_to_<agent_name> (Handoff.default_tool_name()). handoff(agent, tool_name_override=, on_handoff=, input_type=, input_filter=, is_enabled=) declares it. input_type is the Pydantic schema for the handoff tool-call arguments: the SDK publishes it as the tool's `parameters`, validates the returned JSON locally, and passes the parsed value to on_handoff(ctx, input_data). is_enabled is evaluated while preparing available handoffs, before the model returns arguments, so it cannot authorize values inside an argument-bearing handoff; field-level authorization must happen at the top of on_handoff and must raise to refuse (the transfer continues once on_handoff returns normally). input_filter receives HandoffInputData and must return a new HandoffInputData - that is the only supported way to change what history the receiving agent sees. handoff_filters.remove_all_tools strips structured tool items but does not redact tool text already copied into ordinary messages. RunConfig.handoff_input_filter is a run-wide default and a per-handoff input_filter wins over it. Optional history compaction: RunConfig.nest_handoff_history wraps summarizable history into ordered <CONVERSATION HISTORY> segments while preserving lossless message items in place, with RunConfig.handoff_history_mapper as a full override; nesting applies only when neither the handoff's input_filter nor the run's handoff_input_filter is set.
build: Add hday_router.Handoff(destination_lane, tool_name='transfer_to_<lane>', input_model: type[BaseModel]|None, on_handoff: Callable[[RunContext, BaseModel], Awaitable[None]]|None, input_filter: Callable[[HandoffInputData], HandoffInputData]|None, is_enabled: Callable[[], bool]|None). HandoffInputData = frozen dataclass(input_history: list[Msg], pre_handoff_items: list[Msg], new_items: list[Msg], input_items: list[Msg]|None). Render enabled handoffs into the model's tool list with input_model.model_json_schema() as `parameters`. On a transfer_to_* call: validate args -> if invalid, return a tool error and do not transfer -> run on_handoff -> apply input_filter -> build the receiver's messages -> append one handoff record to the unified decision ledger {from_lane, to_lane, tool_name, args_hash, ts, enabled_reason}. Provide hday_router.filters.remove_all_tools as the default filter and RunConfig-equivalent handoff_input_filter on the lane config with per-handoff precedence.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert the rendered tool list contains exactly one transfer_to_gate entry whose parameters equal the input_model schema; (b) feed a malformed arg dict and assert on_handoff was never called and no ledger record was written; (c) with input_filter=remove_all_tools assert tool_call/tool_output items are dropped and plain messages preserved; (d) assert per-handoff input_filter beats the lane-level handoff_input_filter; (e) assert is_enabled=False removes the tool from the list entirely.

name: Workbench: a stateful tool collection behind one list_tools/call_tool interface, with MCP as one implementation
what: A Workbench is an interface to a COLLECTION of tools that share state and resources, distinct from a Tool which wraps one callable. The interface is two methods: list_tools() returns the current tool schemas, and call_tool(name, arguments, cancellation_token) returns a ToolResult (with to_text(), is_error, name). Because the workbench owns the state, tools can share a connection, a sandbox, or a resource pool without the agent knowing. The agent's tool loop is written out explicitly in the reference: create() with tools=await workbench.list_tools(), and while the model returns FunctionCall content, add the AssistantMessage, call the workbench per call, add a FunctionExecutionResultMessage whose entries carry call_id, content=result.to_text(), is_error=result.is_error and name, then re-create. An MCPWorkbench is a provided implementation where an MCP server is the tool collection, so local tools and remote MCP tools are reached through the same two-method interface. Cancellation is threaded through every call via the message context's cancellation token.
build: Add hday_tools.Workbench protocol {list_tools() -> list[ToolSpec], call_tool(name, arguments, cancellation) -> ToolResult} with implementations LocalWorkbench(tools, shared_state), McpWorkbench(client), and NamespacedWorkbench(name, description, members) for deferred loading. ToolResult(name, content, is_error) with to_text(). Rewrite the lane tool loop to the explicit form: create(tools=await workbench.list_tools()) -> while FunctionCall: append assistant message, call each tool, append one result message carrying call_id/is_error/name -> re-create. Thread a CancellationToken through every call and abort the loop on cancel without corrupting the message list.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a Workbench that mutates shared_state is observable from a second tool in the same collection but not from another workbench; (b) assert the result message preserves call_id, name and is_error per call (golden compare against a scripted 2-call response); (c) assert an McpWorkbench and a LocalWorkbench are interchangeable behind a fake-model fixture; (d) assert cancelling mid-loop stops before the next create() and leaves the message list well-formed; (e) assert list_tools() is re-read after a tool-set change without recreating the workbench.

name: constrained-decoding-fsm
what: Outlines accepts an output TYPE alongside the prompt and guarantees the generated text conforms to it. Supported types span the Python ecosystem: native types (int, str, float, bool), typing constructs (Literal, List, Dict, Enum, Union, Optional, Tuple, nested collections), and third-party types such as pydantic models; plus three library-specific ones — Choice(list) for DYNAMIC multiple choice, JsonSchema, Regex, and CFG (context-free grammars). Classification is done with Literal or Enum. Important contract detail: an Outlines generator ALWAYS returns a string — you cast it yourself (e.g. Character.model_validate_json(result)). The docs frame it as 'provide as an output type what you would give as the type hint of the return type of a function'.
build: For the self-hosted/local-model path, render each judgment's output type as a grammar: a Choice built at runtime from the live lane registry for lane selection, a bounded int/float for scores, and a pydantic JSON schema for structured verdicts. Keep the adapter parse chain as a second line of defence for providers without grammar support, and assert in the ledger which enforcement path was used per call.
test: tests/test_constrained_output.py::test_runtime_choice_grammar_rejects_unknown_lane — build the Choice from a 3-lane registry, assert the generated lane is always one of the three and that a removed lane is no longer generatable; assert the returned value is a string that must be cast.

name: content-capture-optin
what: The spec separates metadata from content: message content attributes are Opt-In, and it documents uploading full content to external storage and keeping only a reference on the span (with streaming chunks handled separately).
build: Store content hashes plus a content_ref pointer by default (hday_manifest already computes sha1_10); a --capture-content flag (off by default) writes full text into a local blob dir and records only the ref; a redaction pass strips secret-shaped strings before any hosted push, reusing the patterns in tests/test_integrity_and_secrets.py.
test: Default run contains no command text in the ledger (refs only); with the flag the blob exists and the ref resolves to identical bytes; a seeded AWS-key-shaped string never appears in a pushed payload.

name: dataset-experiments
what: Datasets hold named items (input plus optional expected output); an experiment runs a task over a dataset with evaluators, and each run item links back to the dataset item and the run name so two runs can be compared item-by-item.
build: runs/datasets/gate-cases.jsonl: frozen cases {action, mandate, expected_kind, expected_allow}. A day-experiment command replays the dataset through hday_gate.decide with a pluggable judge (deterministic stub or SystemOneClient), writes one experiment row per run (run name = rules version) under runs/experiments/<run>.json, and prints per-item flips plus pass-rate delta versus the recorded baseline run.
test: Replay a 10-case dataset twice with a stub judge that flips one verdict: diff must show exactly that flip and the right delta; a no-change replay shows zero flips; a missing dataset file exits non-zero with one stderr line.

name: dual-llm-quarantine
what: The dual-LLM pattern separates a privileged LLM that can call tools and see the user's instructions from a quarantined LLM that may process untrusted content but can only return symbolic values (chosen from a fixed set), never free text that the privileged LLM would treat as instructions. The 2025 design-patterns paper catalogues it among six patterns for securing agents against prompt injection.
build: Route untrusted text (tool output, file contents, fetched pages) through a quarantined call whose answer is constrained to a symbol (enum/choice/number, e.g. 'does this text instruct deleting tests? yes/no/unclear'); the privileged gate consumes only the symbol plus provenance and refers to the raw text by hash. Enforce it in hday_gate.decide: the typed phase receives symbols, never raw untrusted text.
test: Schema test: the typed phase's inputs contain no raw untrusted text; a fixture with an injected 'ignore your rules' string inside tool output cannot change the verdict when the quarantined call is stubbed to return the correct symbol; the injection attempt is recorded as a row.

name: entity-graph-memory
what: Mem0 builds a graph where the entities mentioned across memories (people, places, organizations, concepts) become nodes and memories that share an entity become connected. No schema is defined by the developer and there is no external graph store to provision — it is built in and always on. The stated payoff is entity-centric questions ('what do we know about Alice?') answered from many separate conversations, and multi-hop recall linking a fact in one memory to a related fact in another. Entity extraction in the write pipeline is what feeds these nodes.
build: Add an entities index alongside the memory store: {entity_key -> [memory_id]}, populated from the entity-extraction stage, with entity_key normalized (lowercased, trimmed, alias-merged). Add memory_recall_entity(entity, *, depth=1) that walks shared-entity edges and returns the connected memories with their episode ids. Depth is capped and every hop is recorded in the ledger. Start with an inverted index in SQLite; only reach for a real graph store if traversal depth > 2 is ever needed.
test: tests/test_memory_graph.py::test_entity_recall_links_across_sessions — seed two sessions that both mention the same project entity, assert memory_recall_entity returns both memories with distinct source episode ids, and assert depth=2 finds the transitive memory while depth=1 does not.

name: experiment-loop
what: The evaluation loop: run evaluations repeatedly, change exactly one variable per experiment (prompt, model, parameters, scorer), account for nondeterminism, keep the baseline current, and segment results by metadata. Multiple simultaneous changes make results uninterpretable.
build: day-loop command: freeze dataset, run baseline, change exactly one variable (e.g. RISK_THRESHOLD), re-run, print per-item diff plus summary. It refuses (exit 2) when more than one variable differs from the recorded baseline manifest, and appends each iteration to the ledger so the cockpit shows the loop history rather than a single number.
test: A one-variable change produces a diff report; a two-variable change is refused with exit 2; a baseline manifest hash mismatch is detected and reported; nondeterminism is surfaced by re-running the baseline twice and warning when scores differ.

name: genai-attributes
what: A field dictionary for GenAI operations: gen_ai.operation.name (required), gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens/output_tokens, gen_ai.tool.name (required for tool spans), gen_ai.tool.call.id, gen_ai.tool.type, error.type. Message content attributes (gen_ai.input.messages and friends) are marked Opt-In.
build: hday_semconv.py holding an explicit map from ledger row fields to semconv keys (judge calls record provider/model/token usage; tool calls record gen_ai.tool.name plus a stable gen_ai.tool.call.id = uuid5(session+turn+index); errors record error.type). Local-only fields stay under an hday.* prefix; never invent semconv keys for local concepts.
test: Unit: every emitted row maps to the attribute table with no unmapped keys; token fields are ints or absent (never the string 'unknown'); content attributes are absent by default; the map is a single dict, so a drift test fails when a lane adds an unmapped field.

name: genai-metrics
what: Standard instruments: gen_ai.client.operation.duration (histogram), gen_ai.client.operation.time_to_first_chunk, gen_ai.server.request.duration, gen_ai.invoke_workflow.duration, gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration / .inference_calls / .tool_calls, and gen_ai.execute_tool.duration.
build: hday_metrics.py computing rollups over the ledger: gate.decisions by kind (counter), gate.escalation_rate, judge.duration histogram (ms, documented buckets), tool.calls per turn. Expose via a day-metrics command consumed by the ops-shell panel; window and buckets come from config.
test: Bucket boundaries are deterministic for a fixture ledger; an empty ledger yields zeros rather than errors; a malformed row (missing ms) is skipped and counted in a skipped field instead of skewing the histogram.

name: human-approval-gates
what: OWASP's LLM01 mitigations include 'require human approval for high-risk actions: implement human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations to prevent unauthorized actions', alongside least privilege, input/output filtering, and segregating untrusted content. LangGraph implements the mechanism as interrupt(): execution pauses at any point (dynamically, conditionally), the exact state is checkpointed, the payload surfaces to the caller, and the graph resumes with Command - the thread_id is the persistent cursor.
build: hday_approval.py writing approval rows {request_id, action_hash, reason, blast_radius, ttl, status in pending|approved|denied|expired|unreachable}. When no human gate is reachable, record unreachable (never a silent approval) and let policy decide (deny for external/irreversible, allow-plus-record otherwise). The cockpit escalation-matrix panel lists pending approvals with approve/deny commands; approvals expire by TTL and are bound to the action hash they were granted for.
test: An approval for action hash A cannot authorize action hash B; expiry flips pending to expired and the next matching call re-escalates; unreachable rows never become approvals; the panel resolves exactly one request id per approve command; a stale approval row cannot be replayed after TTL.

name: llama-guard-taxonomy
what: Llama Guard is an LLM-based input-output safeguard that classifies both prompts (prompt classification) and model responses (response classification) against an explicit safety taxonomy, emitting a safe/unsafe decision and the violated categories; the taxonomy is customizable by prompting. Llama Guard 3 (Llama-3.1-8B) is aligned to the MLCommons hazard taxonomy, covers 8 languages, was optimized for tool-call safety (search and code interpreter), and its first-token probability can be used as an unsafe-class score with thresholding.
build: rules/taxonomy.yml: violation ids with human names, detectors (regex and/or judge), severity. Each hit emits a binary score per category plus a taxonomy_version on the row; the cockpit aggregates hits by category so a rule that fires constantly becomes visible (noise control). An optional model-classifier lane can cover categories regex cannot see (e.g. 'claims a check passed without running it').
test: Drift test: every violation id in hday_gate's regex tables exists in the taxonomy, and vice versa; a hit without a taxonomy id fails validation; category rollups match a fixture ledger; the taxonomy version is recorded on every hit row.

name: prompt-version-labels
what: Every prompt version gets an automatic version id plus user-assigned labels used to route environments (production, staging), tenants, or experiments (prod-a/prod-b); traces record which version was used, so metrics can be attributed per version.
build: rules/registry.json mapping prompt_id to versions[] with labels; hday_prompts.load(prompt_id, label) (pure, import-safe) returns {text, version, label}; every ledger row carries prompt_version and prompt_label; day-sections shows the active label per section and day-section-set switches a label for the next turn only (never retro-labels old rows).
test: Unit: load('gate_rubric','production') and ('staging') return different versions; rows carry the version actually used; switching a label changes only subsequent rows; an unknown label raises a loud load error rather than falling back to latest.

name: sandbox-runtime-os-isolation
what: Anthropic's sandbox-runtime (srt) enforces filesystem, network and Unix-socket restrictions on arbitrary processes at the OS level using native primitives (sandbox-exec on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux) plus proxy-based network filtering, with a secure-by-default posture, and is explicitly aimed at sandboxing agents, local MCP servers and bash commands. Violation monitoring taps the macOS sandbox violation log (macOS-only).
build: Wire srt (or bubblewrap directly on this Linux host) as the execution wrapper for terminal tool calls: default-deny filesystem outside the workspace, network allowlist through the configured proxy, no Unix sockets. The gate's blast_radius value selects the profile (local < workspace < machine < external), and every launch records the profile plus any violation in the ledger.
test: Integration: a curl to a non-allowlisted host fails inside the wrapper and is recorded; a write outside the workspace fails; an ordinary in-workspace read/test still passes (no over-restriction); violation records render in the cockpit. Note the macOS violation log is not available here - on Linux rely on bubblewrap failures plus proxy logs.

name: scorer-scope
what: Scorers grade the span or trace they are attached to and are themselves logged as score spans; they can be code or LLM-judges, run alongside the task, and carry name plus metadata so results are filterable.
build: hday_scorers.py with a registry: code scorers (regex_phase_correct, evidence_present, cost_within_budget) and judge scorers (reason_quality, mandate_match), each declaring scope in {row, run}. score_row()/score_run() write score rows with scope plus scorer version; the cockpit adds a per-lane score column and a run rollup. Scope is enforced, not advisory.
test: Scoring one row leaves run aggregates unchanged; a run-scope scorer cannot attach to a row (rejected); a scorer that raises is recorded as unjudged and never breaks the turn.

name: self-check-rail
what: NeMo configurations can enable self-check output rails using the application's own LLM - the README's example config lists `self check facts` and `self check hallucination` as output flows alongside moderation and sensitive-data masking with entity lists.
build: hday_selfcheck.py: before the gate settles a pass, collect the turn's evidence rows and ask the judge a typed question per claim ('does evidence X support claim Y?') using noul plus a choice; unsupported claims force the verdict to unjudged/deny with a reason naming the claim. Bounded to N claims per turn, fail-open loudly.
test: With a stub judge: a claim with no matching evidence is rejected; a claim with matching evidence passes; partial judge answers leave the unanswered claims marked unjudged rather than assumed true; the bound is enforced (claim N+1 is reported as unchecked).

name: tau-bench-passk
what: tau-bench emulates dynamic conversations between a simulated user and an agent with domain APIs and policy guidelines; success is scored by comparing the final database state against the annotated goal state, and pass^k measures the probability that all k independent trials succeed (reliability), not the average. Reported: gpt-4o succeeded on under 50% of tasks and pass^8 under 25% in retail.
build: day-reliability command: for a scenario card (action + mandate + expected verdict + expected side effects), run k trials (default 4, configurable) with the live judge, compare final observable state (git refs, file hashes, ledger rows) to the expected state, and record pass^k as a score on the scenario. Cards with pass^k < 1 surface in the cockpit as unreliable rules.
test: With a stub judge that answers correctly with probability p: pass^k is exactly 1 for p=1 and 0 for p=0, and strictly below 1 for a flaky stub; a scenario with a correct verdict but a missing side effect is still scored as a failure.

name: trajectory-evals
what: agentevals scores the agent trajectory (the list of intermediate messages and tool calls) rather than only the final answer, with LLM-as-judge trajectory evaluators that return {key, reasoning, score} (e.g. trajectory_accuracy) and exact/strict matching of tool sequences. Agent-as-a-Judge extends step-level scoring to intermediate steps.
build: day-traj-eval over a ledger slice: (a) deterministic strict match of the decision/tool sequence for known scenarios, (b) a judge scorer on reason quality with a fixed rubric that must return reasoning alongside the score. Store both as evaluation-result events on the turn span. The cockpit shows trajectory score next to the verdict, so a gap between them is visible.
test: A fixture ledger with a correct verdict but a skipped evidence step scores below the pass bar in trajectory mode and above it in verdict-only mode (proving the metrics differ); a judge response without reasoning is recorded as unjudged, not scored.

name: webarena-functional-validators
what: WebArena builds a highly realistic and reproducible self-hosted environment (fully functional websites across e-commerce, forum, collaborative development and content management, plus tools and knowledge bases) and evaluates the functional correctness of task completion rather than text similarity.
build: Validators per ops action, declared next to the task card: git ref exists and matches the workspace hash; file content equals expected; a ledger row with the expected kind is present; a panel command returns the expected JSON shape. day-verify runs validators instead of trusting text, and a failed validator blocks the 'verified' claim.
test: Negative controls are mandatory: each validator must fail when the underlying state is absent and pass after the action is applied in a tmp workspace; a validator that returns truthy for an empty state is rejected in review tests.

name: Agent-to-agent registries: GCP Agent Registry and AGNTCY Agent Directory / OASF
what: Two live 2026 agent-registry efforts. GCP Agent Registry: a managed registry for agents, endpoints, MCP servers, tools, bindings, and skills, with a documented data model, automatic vs manual registration, endpoint registration and discovery, MCP-server/tool management, skill registration with revisions, publisher review, search for agents/tools/skills, RBAC, audit logging, and its own Agent Registry MCP server. Its agent identifier is a URN (the OTel agent-spans doc cites `urn:agent:projects-123:projects:123:locations:us-east1:aiplatform:reasoningEngines:456` as a gen_ai.agent.id example) — i.e. the registry identifier IS the telemetry identity. AGNTCY (Linux Foundation): an open collective building Internet-of-Agents infrastructure — Agent Directory Service (a FEDERATED registry for publishing, verifying, and discovering agents and multi-agent applications), OASF (Open Agentic Schema Framework: an extensible, OCSF-inspired record model where agent records are annotated with skills, domains, and modules; a hosted schema server at schema.oasf.outshift.com with validation, decoding, and translation services), SLIM (secure low-latency messaging with pub/sub, streaming, MLS encryption), decentralized Identity (identifiers, verifiable credentials, policy-based access), SHADI (hardened agent runtime), plus observability/eval and CSIT tooling.
build: `hday_registry.py`: a second backend alongside the MCP registry implementing (a) GCP Agent Registry lookup for agents/endpoints/skills with RBAC-scoped results, and (b) AGNTCY Agent Directory lookup returning OASF records. Normalize both, plus A2A agent cards and MCP server.json, into one `RemoteEntity{id, kind: agent|server|skill|tool, display_name, publisher, registry_source, verified, capabilities}` type that the Sources panel and `hday_router.py` both consume. Use the registry identifier as gen_ai.agent.id in `hday_telemetry.py` so telemetry and registry entries join. Treat OASF records as untrusted; validate before display.
test: tests/test_registry_normalize.py — assert an MCP server.json, an A2A agent card, a GCP registry agent, and an OASF record all normalize into RemoteEntity with no field loss for {id, kind, publisher, verified}; that the registry id used in telemetry matches the one shown in the UI; that a record failing validation is dropped with a logged reason rather than partially rendered; and that routing never selects an entity whose verified flag is false when policy requires verification.

name: Crews versus flows: autonomous collaboration as one node inside a deterministic orchestration graph
what: The architecture draws a hard line between two execution models and then composes them. A Crew is an autonomous, role-based unit: agents with roles and goals collaborate under a process (sequential, or hierarchical where a manager LLM or manager agent plans and delegates), and the crew decides its own internal path. A Flow is an event-driven graph: methods are marked @start, @listen(...) and @router, conditions compose with or_()/and_(), and the flow owns explicit state that is passed between steps. The composition rule is that a crew can be kicked off as a step inside a flow, and a flow can be invoked from within a crew - so autonomy is a bounded node inside a deterministic graph rather than the top-level control structure. Flows additionally support persistence: a persisted flow started with a stable id resumes prior state, while a distinct restore-from id forks a new run from a previous state, and a flow can be run synchronously or streamed.
build: Add hday_flow.py: Flow with @start, @listen(*events), @router decorators, or_()/and_() condition combinators, and a typed FlowState object threaded through steps. Add a CrewStep node type that wraps a group of lanes with a declared process ('sequential' | 'hierarchical' with manager_lane) and returns a single result to the flow. Enforce the boundary in the manifest: a CrewStep may not declare flow-level routing, and a Flow may not be started from inside a CrewStep except as a declared sub-flow. Support flow persistence with kickoff(state_id=...) to resume and restore_from_state_id=... to fork.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert or_(a, b) fires on either event and and_(a, b) only after both, in either order; (b) assert a CrewStep returns exactly one result object to the flow regardless of how many lanes ran inside it; (c) assert manifest validation rejects a CrewStep declaring flow-level routing; (d) assert kickoff with an existing state_id resumes rather than restarting (assert step-execution counts); (e) assert restore_from_state_id produces a new state_id with fork lineage.

name: Declared tool surface: hosted tools, deferred loading via namespaces + ToolSearchTool, and agents-as-tools with approval
what: Four distinct tool classes share one declaration site on Agent(tools=[...]). (1) Hosted tools run on the provider side: WebSearchTool, FileSearchTool, CodeInterpreterTool, HostedMCPTool, ImageGenerationTool. (2) Local/runtime tools require an implementation you supply: ComputerTool (Computer/AsyncComputer interface), ApplyPatchTool (ApplyPatchEditor interface), ShellTool (local OR hosted container - with a hosted environment you must not set executor, needs_approval, or on_approval). (3) Deferred loading: @function_tool(defer_loading=True), tool_namespace(name=, description=, tools=[...]), and HostedMCPTool(tool_config={..., 'defer_loading': True}) are searchable surfaces; the agent then needs exactly one ToolSearchTool() to let the model load them on demand. Namespaces can mix immediate and deferred tools - non-deferred members stay callable immediately. ToolSearchTool(execution='client') is rejected by the standard Runner (client-executed tool_search_call raises). (4) allowed_callers controls how a tool may be invoked: omitted = direct model calls only, ['programmatic'] = program-only, ['direct','programmatic'] = both; ProgrammaticToolCallingTool() must appear at most once and requires at least one programmatically callable tool or a searchable surface. For @function_tool(allowed_callers=[...]) a structured return annotation (Pydantic/TypedDict/dataclass) becomes a strict output schema validated before the value returns to the program. Separately, Agent.as_tool() turns a whole agent into a tool and accepts max_turns, run_config, hooks, session, needs_approval, plus structured input via parameters / input_builder / include_input_schema, output shaping via custom_output_extractor, streaming observation via on_stream, and runtime gating via is_enabled. The docs are explicit that is_enabled controls visibility and dispatch and does NOT replace authorization on arguments or the accessed resource.
build: In hday_tools.py split tool registration into classes: HostedTool (no local executor, provider-side), LocalTool(executor, needs_approval, on_approval), DeferredTool(namespace), and AgentTool (sub-lane). Implement tool_namespace(name, description, tools) grouping deferred tools, plus ToolSearchTool() which searches namespace names/descriptions and loads matching tools into the active set. Implement allowed_callers on the tool record and reject a tool_search_call emitted with execution='client' in the runner (raise, do not execute). Implement lane.as_tool(tool_name, description, parameters, input_builder, include_input_schema, custom_output_extractor, on_stream, needs_approval, is_enabled) where needs_approval routes into the existing gate escalation path and is_enabled is a static-config predicate only - document in the gate module that argument-level authorization belongs in the tool body or the guardrail, never in is_enabled.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a namespace with 3 deferred and 1 immediate tool exposes exactly 1 tool before ToolSearchTool runs and 4 after; (b) assert exactly one ToolSearchTool is accepted and a second is rejected; (c) assert a client-executed tool_search_call raises instead of executing; (d) assert allowed_callers=['programmatic'] makes the tool invisible to direct calls but reachable from the program runner; (e) assert as_tool(needs_approval=True) produces an interruption record and resumes only after approve(); (f) assert is_enabled=False removes the agent tool from the model's tool list.

name: Generative UI specs: A2UI surfaces/actions and MCP-UI iframes as the two renderable targets
what: AG-UI is explicitly NOT a generative-UI spec — it is the bidirectional runtime connection that carries one. Three sibling specs: A2UI (Google, declarative LLM-friendly, JSONL-based and streaming, platform-agnostic; current production release v0.9.1 standardizing on `application/a2ui+json`, v1.0 candidate adds client-to-server RPC (`actionResponse`), action IDs, and renames theme to surfaceProperties; v0.9 introduced `createSurface`, client-side functions, custom catalogs, and a prompt-first philosophy; renderers exist for Angular, Flutter, Lit, Markdown). MCP-UI (Microsoft + Shopify; iframe-based, extends MCP; client/server SDKs, 5.2k stars, Ruby/Python SDKs in progress). Open-JSON-UI (OpenAI, declarative). A2UI transports: A2A extension (stable), AG-UI (stable, CopilotKit is AG-UI's creator and primary consumer), REST/WebSockets/SSE proposed. A2UI's design rules: declarative data not executable code, agents may only use pre-approved components from the client's catalog (no UI injection), flat streaming JSON for incremental LLM generation, adjacency-list component model, data binding, and progressive rendering. AG-UI's own generative-UI draft proposes a two-step `generateUserInterface` tool ({description, data, output}) delegated to a secondary LLM, with documented limits: OpenAI's 1024-char tool-description cap, unreliable $ref/oneOf support across providers, and context-window pressure (dedicated UI agents outperform combined ones).
build: `desktop/plugin.js`: an `a2ui` renderer implementing the adjacency-list model with a hermes-day catalog (card, table, diff, progress, chart, form, action-button) and `application/a2ui+json` ingestion from an AG-UI CUSTOM event or a tool result; an `mcp-ui` renderer reusing the sandboxed-iframe machinery from the MCP Apps pattern. A surface is a named container in the rail; `createSurface` and `actionResponse` (v1.0) drive client->server actions. TUI and Discord surfaces implement a degraded catalog (text/table/diff only) and declare that in capabilities — never silently render nothing. Route every generated-UI action through the gate with origin='genui'. Keep the catalog closed: an unknown component type renders as a labeled placeholder, never as raw HTML.
test: tests/test_genui_render.py + plugin.js harness — assert an unknown component type renders a placeholder and increments a counter (never raw HTML); that the same A2UI payload renders to a table on desktop, plain text on TUI, and a degraded form on Discord per each surface's declared catalog; that a surface action produces a gate record with origin='genui'; and that a payload missing a required component reference fails closed.

name: Graph workflows with explicit string routes, fan-out/join, and human-input nodes
what: Graph-based workflows define agent logic as nodes and edges with explicit routing; the Go reference describes a graph engine (workflowagent plus workflow.Edge) that maps directly to Python's Workflow(edges=[...]), with edges declared as {From, To, Route} where a string route such as StringRoute("output-1") selects the next node from a node's returned value, plus Chain(...) for sequences and a parallel fan-out/join path. LlmAgents can appear as nodes but must be configured single-turn/task mode. Nodes can be functions, tools, LLM agents or human input, and the human-input page documents requesting input with a message and payload plus tool-confirmation approval prompts inside LLM agents. The docs frame graphs as the deterministic option, dynamic workflows as programmatic orchestration, and template workflows as higher-level blocks.
build: Add a route table to hday_router.py: lanes declare {from: node, on: route_string, to: node} edges (plus Chain helper and a join node that waits for all inbound branches), and the gate's verdict strings become the route keys, so dispatch is a lookup instead of nested conditionals. Add an approval node type that suspends the graph until a human response arrives, and emit the route table as a rendered diagram/JSON artifact so reviewers can see the whole dispatch surface.
test: tests/test_hday_router.py: a graph with a classifier node routing on three string verdicts; assert each verdict reaches only its declared target, an undeclared verdict raises a typed 'unrouted_verdict' error instead of falling through, a fan-out/join waits for both branches before the join node runs, and the exported route table round-trips (JSON -> graph -> same routing decisions for all fixture verdicts).

name: Hierarchical memory: LLM-inferred scopes, composite scoring with tunable decay, and private per-agent views
what: Memory is one system with hierarchical scopes rather than several stores: the built-in scopes are short-term, long-term, entity and external, and writes are routed into the right scope by an LLM that infers where a fact belongs. Retrieval is scored by a composite rather than raw similarity - semantic similarity combined with recency and importance weights, with a tunable recency half-life in days - so a recent but only loosely similar item can outrank an older near-exact match. The API is uniform across scopes (remember, recall, forget, extract_memories, tree) and a scope(path) accessor exposes a private view so one agent can be given its own memory namespace without a second store. Extraction happens automatically after a task and recall is injected automatically before one, so the agent does not have to manage memory explicitly.
build: Extend hday_ctxscore into hday_memory.py with scopes short_term, long_term, entity, external and a router that uses the judgment lane to classify a candidate fact into a scope (with a deterministic fallback rule). Scoring: score = w_semantic * cosine + w_recency * 0.5**(age_days / recency_half_life_days) + w_importance * importance, all weights and the half-life configurable in the lane manifest. Implement remember/recall/forget/extract_memories/tree, auto-extract after each task and auto-inject a recall block before each task, and a scope(path) accessor returning a private view bound to one lane.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert the composite score ordering flips when recency_half_life_days is lowered (fixture with one fresh low-similarity and one old high-similarity item); (b) assert scope('lane-a') cannot read an item written to scope('lane-b') (expect empty result); (c) assert the deterministic fallback router classifies a fixture fact into the expected scope when the judgment lane is stubbed to fail; (d) assert extract_memories runs after a task and the injected recall block appears before the next task's prompt; (e) assert tree() returns the scope hierarchy with counts matching writes.

name: Hub-and-spoke network: envelopes with Resume/Rule, WAL, append-only audit log with an open kind set, pre-decision arbiter and post-hoc listeners
what: The network model puts a hub between agents: agents do not address each other, they register with the hub and traffic moves as envelopes. Identity is a Passport plus a Resume (capabilities claimed and observed), which is what lets the hub route by capability rather than by name. Channels are created from adapter manifests with declared participants and expectations, and channel traffic is a write-ahead log. Two asymmetric seams surround every decision: a HubArbiter is consulted BEFORE the hub commits a register / channel-open / send / dispatch decision (so a policy can veto a state transition), while HubListeners are read-only observers that the hub fans state transitions out to AFTER the fact.
