The audit log is itself a HubListener registered first, so every state transition lands as one structured record before any other listener sees it; records are plain dicts with at least kind and at, the kind set is explicitly open for tenants to extend, it supports live tail via subscribe(cb)/unsubscribe(cb), and it can be replaced with a tenant subclass (replace_audit_log) which is registered as the first listener so audit writes still complete before other listeners observe the event. Observability is layered: pure evaluators over channel state return zero or more Violation records, and a violation handler decides what happens (audit / warn / auto_close).
build: Add hday_hub.py: Envelope(sender, recipient, channel_id, kind, payload, id, ts); Passport(agent_id, name) and Resume(claimed_capabilities, observed_capabilities); Channel(manifest, participants, wal: list[Envelope]). Implement HubArbiter.approve(decision) -> Decision|Veto consulted before register/channel_open/send/dispatch, and HubListener.on_event(record) fanned out after commit. Make AuditLog a HubListener that the hub registers FIRST, appending one dict per transition to ledger/audit.jsonl with at least {kind, at}; expose read_all(), append(record), subscribe(cb)/unsubscribe(cb) with subscriber exceptions logged and swallowed, and replace_audit_log(custom) that re-registers the replacement at position 0. Export AUDIT_KIND_* constants and allow plugins to append new kinds. Add Expectation(name, on_violation in {'audit','warn','auto_close'}, params) evaluated by pure functions over channel state on a sweeper tick.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a vetoing arbiter prevents the state change and writes no transition record; (b) assert ordering: with a replacement audit log plus a second listener, the audit record is written before the second listener observes the event (assert call order in a spy list); (c) assert a subscriber that raises does not stop other subscribers; (d) assert a custom kind appended by a plugin is preserved by read_all(); (e) assert expectation_sweep_interval=0 disables the background loop and a manual tick fires the expected Violation and handler action.

name: Human-in-the-loop as a persisted pause with a three-level requirement tree and a continue_run resumption loop
what: When a workflow pauses for HITL it exposes the pause through three nested objects and the caller reads them to find out what is being asked, resolves the innermost ones, and calls continue_run. WorkflowRunOutput carries is_paused and pause_kind ('step' | 'executor' | None) plus requirement collections that name what is pending: steps_requiring_confirmation (confirm/reject), steps_requiring_user_input (values), steps_requiring_output_review, steps_requiring_route (route selection) and steps_requiring_executor_resolution (an agent/team tool needing resolution). Below that, a StepRequirement object describes one step's requirement (requires_confirmation and friends), and below that executor-level requirements describe a tool-level gate (for example tool_execution.requires_confirmation, or confirmation/confirmed pairs to approve a @tool(requires_confirmation=True)). The documented driver is a loop: while run_output.is_paused, resolve the pending requirements, then run_output = workflow.continue_run(run_output). Because pause state is part of the run output that is persisted, a pause survives the process and can be resumed later.
build: Extend the gate/runner with RunOutput.is_paused, pause_kind in {'step','executor',None}, and requirement collections steps_requiring_confirmation / _user_input / _output_review / _route / _executor_resolution. Add StepRequirement(step_id, requires_confirmation, requires_user_input, requires_route, ...) and an executor-requirement shape for tool gates (tool_execution.requires_confirmation; confirmation + confirmed to approve). Persist pause state with the run so it survives restart, and provide the documented driver loop: while run_output.is_paused: resolve pending requirements; run_output = continue_run(run_output). Surface the requirement tree in the cockpit so the UI renders what is pending rather than a generic 'blocked'.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a step-level confirmation pause sets pause_kind='step' and populates steps_requiring_confirmation only; (b) assert a @tool(requires_confirmation=True) gate sets pause_kind='executor' and populates the executor requirement; (c) assert resolving only the inner requirements and calling continue_run resumes correctly, and that calling continue_run with an unresolved requirement raises; (d) assert pause state survives a serialized restart (write, reload, continue_run, same outcome); (e) assert the loop terminates exactly when no requirements remain.

name: Lifecycle hook system: many events, matcher groups, five handler types, exit-code and JSON verdict semantics
what: Hooks fire at named lifecycle points and are configured as event -> matcher groups -> handlers. The event surface is broad and includes PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted, Stop, StopFailure, UserPromptSubmit, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, Notification, ConfigChange, InstructionsLoaded, CwdChanged, FileChanged, PreModelSwitch, PostModelSwitch, Elicitation, ElicitationResult, WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove, TeammateIdle and MessageDisplay. A handler is one of five types - shell command, HTTP endpoint, MCP tool call, LLM prompt, or subagent - so the extension point is not tied to the shell. The matcher field filters activation: a plain value or |-separated alternatives is compared against the event's matcher field (tool_name for tool events); a matcher containing other characters is treated as a JavaScript regular expression tested with RegExp.prototype.test, which matches anywhere in the value, so ^Edit$ is needed for whole-string matching; some events have no matcher support and a matcher on them is silently ignored; MCP tools match as mcp__<server>__<tool> and a server-wide match requires the .* suffix (mcp__memory alone is an exact string that matches nothing). Input arrives as JSON on stdin (command hooks) or as the POST body (HTTP hooks); output can be plain text or JSON with fields including permissionDecision, and additionalContext can inject text back into the model's context. Exit codes carry semantics, and there is an `if` field for a second, narrower filter beyond the matcher, plus async hooks and a `once`-style single-fire option. Config lives in user settings, project settings, or a plugin's hooks/hooks.json, and the same events fire in terminal, IDE, desktop and cloud sessions.
build: Add hday_hooks.py with HOOK_EVENTS enum covering the subset we can actually emit: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, ConfigChange, InstructionsLoaded, FileChanged, PreModelSwitch, PostModelSwitch. Config shape mirrors the reference: {event: [{matcher: str, if: str|None, hooks: [{type: 'command'|'http'|'python'|'prompt'|'subagent', ...}]}]}. Implement match_event(event, value) with the documented rule: if the matcher contains only [A-Za-z0-9_|] treat it as exact/|-alternatives, otherwise compile as a regex and use search() semantics. Deliver JSON input on stdin for command hooks and as a POST body for http hooks; parse stdout as text or JSON and honour permissionDecision and additionalContext. Implement exit-code mapping and an `async: true` flag that does not block the turn.
test: Deterministic: (a) matcher table test: 'Bash' matches only Bash; 'Edit.*' matches Edit and NotebookEdit; '^Edit$' does not match NotebookEdit; 'mcp__memory' matches nothing while 'mcp__memory__.*' matches mcp__memory__read; a matcher on an event without matcher support is ignored and the hook still fires; (b) assert a JSON stdout of {permissionDecision: 'deny'} blocks the tool and that plain-text stdout does not; (c) assert additionalContext text appears in the next model request; (d) assert an async hook returns immediately while its side effect lands later; (e) assert a hook raising an exception does not abort the turn unless its event is declared blocking.

name: MCP client hardening: dynamic tool updates, reconnection, push messages over channels, and backgrounding
what: The MCP integration layer documents four behaviors that matter more than the happy-path connect. (1) Dynamic tool updates: when a server changes its tool set, the client picks up the change instead of requiring a reconnect, and the tool list is re-resolved. (2) Automatic reconnection with backoff: a dropped server connection is retried and the session is restored rather than surfacing as a hard failure to the model. (3) Push messages: a server can push messages into the conversation through a channel, which is how an MCP server drives the agent rather than only answering it. (4) Automatic backgrounding: a long-running tool call is moved to the background and the agent continues, with the result delivered when it lands. Tool naming is mcp__<server>__<tool>, and plugin-bundled servers get a scoped segment mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>__<tool> so matchers written against the bare server key never fire for them.
build: Build hday_mcp.Client with: (a) a tool-list revision counter - on a list_changed notification, re-resolve tools and diff (added/removed) into the ledger and the model's tool list; (b) a reconnect supervisor with exponential backoff and a max-attempts budget, re-establishing the session before re-resolving tools, and recording each attempt as a ledger entry; (c) a channel abstraction where a server-pushed message is injected as a user-role message with source=mcp:<server> at a defined point in the turn; (d) automatic backgrounding: a tool call exceeding background_after_ms returns a handle to the model and delivers the result as a follow-up message, with the pending handle visible in the cockpit. Name tools mcp__<server>__<tool> and mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>__<tool>, and make the hook matcher require .* for server-wide matches.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a simulated list_changed adds one tool and removes one, and the model's tool list matches the diff with two ledger entries; (b) assert a dropped connection retries with monotonically increasing backoff up to the budget and then raises a typed error; (c) assert a pushed message appears at the declared injection point and carries source=mcp:<server>; (d) assert a tool sleeping past background_after_ms returns a handle, the turn continues, and the result arrives as a follow-up; (e) assert mcp__plugin_my-plugin_db__query matches only the scoped matcher.

name: OpenAI Realtime event model: the session/conversation/response event grammar
what: A WebSocket (or WebRTC/SIP) event protocol where every message is a typed event with an explicit `type` string; the reference client dispatches them as `server.{event_name}` and `client.{event_name}` and exposes a raw `realtime.event` stream carrying {time (ISO), source ('client'|'server'), event}. Client events include session.update, input_audio_buffer.append/commit/clear, conversation.item.create, conversation.item.truncate, response.create, response.cancel, output_audio_buffer.clear. Server events include session.created (which echoes the server's default instructions when the client set none), conversation.item.created, conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.completed (with a usage object billed against the ASR model, not the realtime model), input_audio_buffer.speech_started / speech_stopped / committed / cleared / dtmf_event_received, response.* deltas, and rate_limits/error events. Session config is set ahead of or during the connection via session.update: instructions, voice, tools (type 'function' + JSON-Schema parameters), turn_detection ({type:'server_vad', prefix_padding_ms default 300, silence_duration_ms default 500, threshold default 0.5} or null to disable VAD), input_audio_transcription ({model:'whisper-1'}), max_output_tokens (1..4096 or 'inf'). Item types in the conversation cache are message | function_call | function_call_output, with delta carrying exactly one of audio (Int16Array), transcript (string), or arguments (string). Audio is pcm16 @ 24 kHz by default.
build: `hday_voice.py` (new): a thin event router that normalizes Realtime events into the same CockpitEvent union as the AG-UI adapter (session.created -> session-ready, input_audio_buffer.speech_started -> user-interrupt, response.* -> assistant stream, function_call items -> TOOL_CALL_*). Voice approvals reuse the interrupt machinery: a spoken 'approve' resolves the same open interrupt the keyboard does, and the resume payload is identical. Configure turn_detection explicitly (never rely on defaults) and set max_output_tokens so a read-out of a long queue cannot run away. Keep the API key server-side; the desktop surface must never hold it (the reference client warns explicitly against browser-side keys).
test: tests/test_voice_event_router.py — assert each normalized event maps to exactly one CockpitEvent variant; that a spoken approval produces the same resume payload as the keyboard path (byte-identical); that turn_detection is always explicitly set in session.update; and that no API key is ever serialized into the plugin's client-side config.

name: Permission modes as a session baseline, layered with allow/ask/deny rules and a protected-path floor
what: A session runs in exactly one permission mode - Manual (prompt), acceptEdits, plan (read-only planning), auto (classifier-reviewed), bypassPermissions - selected by --permission-mode, by permissions.defaultMode in user or managed settings, or from the in-session mode indicator, and there is a documented precedence for which pick outranks which. Layered on top of the mode is a rule system (allow / ask / deny) where deny rules apply in every mode, and rules match commands as written rather than as resolved - a documented limitation of bash rule matching. An administrator can forbid a mode outright (disableAutoMode: 'disable' removes auto from the mode cycle and a session started with --permission-mode auto starts in Manual instead; a running session leaves auto when the setting reaches it and displays 'auto mode disabled by settings'). Working directories define the default trust boundary: reads outside them are normally prompt-free in auto mode, but the first such read prompts once and the answer can be recorded (keep allowing / block from now on, which sets permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories=true in user settings and makes file tools refuse such reads in every later session and every mode / ask again next time). Auto mode adds a classifier layer whose verdicts are explicitly enumerated: blocked-by-default (curl|bash, sending sensitive data to external endpoints, production deploys and migrations, mass deletion on cloud storage, granting IAM or repo permissions, force push, git reset --hard / checkout -- . / restore . / clean -fd / stash drop / stash clear, terraform/pulumi/cdk/terragrunt destroy, writing to a secret manager, changing DNS or TLS, merging a PR no human approved, disarming a safety guard flag, launching an agent loop without approval or sandbox, commenting out or force-passing a test or assertion that guards security behavior) and allowed-by-default (local file operations in the working directory, installing dependencies declared in lock files, reading .env and sending credentials to their matching API, read-only HTTP requests, pushes to any branch of the working repo). Critically, boundaries stated in conversation are treated as a block signal and are re-read from the transcript on each check, so a boundary can be LOST to context compaction; approvals stated in conversation only clear a block when the message names the action AND the specific thing that makes it dangerous (naming the verb alone clears nothing).
build: Add to hday_gate: PermissionMode enum {manual, accept_edits, plan, auto, bypass} resolved by precedence (CLI flag > session override > profile setting > default) with a managed-settings disable flag per mode. Add a RuleLayer(allow=[], ask=[], deny=[]) where deny is evaluated first and applies in every mode, and rules match the command as written. Add working_directories plus block_reads_outside_working_directories as a persisted floor that file tools honour in every mode. Port the auto-mode classifier as a typed list: BLOCKED_BY_DEFAULT and ALLOWED_BY_DEFAULT pattern groups in hday_gate.policy, evaluated as data (so tests can assert membership) rather than as prose. Implement conversational boundaries as first-class session state (not transcript-scraped): Boundary(text, scope, active, lifted_by) stored on the session AND mirrored into the ledger, because our compaction is real and the reference documents that transcript-scraped boundaries get lost. Require approvals to carry a specificity record {action, dangerous_aspect} and reject approvals that name only the verb.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert a deny rule blocks in every one of the five modes; (b) assert disable_auto_mode removes auto from resolution and downgrades an explicit auto request to manual; (c) assert block_reads_outside_working_directories persists after a simulated process restart and refuses reads in a different mode; (d) assert a boundary recorded then a compaction pass does not clear it (contrast: assert the transcript-scrape implementation would have lost it); (e) assert approve(action='force-push') without dangerous_aspect does not clear the block, and approve(action='force-push', dangerous_aspect='branch main') does; (f) assert each BLOCKED_BY_DEFAULT pattern is exercised by at least one fixture command.

name: Six-seam processor pipeline with an abort tripwire that can request a retry
what: Processors attach to an agent as inputProcessors / outputProcessors and expose up to six interception methods at different granularities: processInput (once at the start of agent execution; receives messages, systemMessages and an abort() function; returns a replacement message array or {messages, systemMessages}), processInputStep (at EVERY step of the agentic loop including tool-call continuations, enabling per-step model switching or tool-choice changes), processLLMRequest (rewrite the request immediately before the provider call, with prompt, model, stepNumber, steps, state and abort()), processOutputStep (after each LLM step, to validate and optionally request a retry), processOutputStream (per streamed chunk, with per-chunk drop versus abort()), and processOutputResult (the final result). abort() is the tripwire and emits a normal tripwire response that stops the call; abort('reason', {retry: true}) requests a retry instead of a hard stop. Output methods share a state object that lives for the lifetime of one request, keyed by the processor's id so each processor sees only its own data, created fresh for every generate()/stream() call. Execution order relative to memory is documented and matters: an output guardrail that calls abort() skips memory processors so the rejected messages are not saved. prepareStep() is a shorthand that wraps processInputStep() for the common case.
build: Add hday_processors.py with a Processor base exposing async process_input, process_input_step, process_llm_request, process_output_step, process_output_stream, process_output_result, each receiving (payload, abort, state) and returning a replacement payload or None. abort(reason, retry=False) raises/returns a Tripwire that either stops the call or requests one more attempt. state is a dict created per request and namespaced by processor id. Wire input_processors and output_processors on the lane config, document and enforce the ordering rule that an output tripwire skips memory writes so rejected content is never persisted, and add prepare_step(fn) as the shorthand for process_input_step.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert process_input_step fires once per loop iteration including after tool calls, while process_input fires exactly once (count via spy); (b) assert state written in process_output_stream is readable in process_output_result and is empty in a second request; (c) assert state namespacing: two processors with different ids never see each other's keys; (d) assert abort(retry=True) causes exactly one retry and abort() without retry stops; (e) assert an output tripwire prevents the memory write (assert the store is unchanged); (f) assert prepare_step is equivalent to a process_input_step processor.

name: Trace as a typed span tree with custom span types and additive processors
what: One trace is a tree of typed spans. A Trace has trace_id (format trace_<32 alphanumeric>) and a name; each Span has trace_id, span_id, parent_id, started_at/finished_at, and span_data, a typed payload (AgentSpanData, GenerationSpanData, FunctionSpanData, GuardrailSpanData, HandoffSpanData, ...). The runner auto-instruments: Runner.{run,run_sync,run_streamed} is wrapped in trace(), each agent run in agent_span(), each LLM generation in generation_span(), each function tool call in function_span(), each guardrail in guardrail_span(), each handoff in handoff_span(); custom_span() exists for anything else. trace() is usable as a context manager (`with trace('Joke workflow') as t:`) and wrapping multiple run() calls in one trace() groups them into a single trace - which is the documented way to express 'these runs are one unit of work'. Export is processor-based: BatchTraceProcessor batches to a BackendSpanExporter with a size trigger and a final flush at process exit; add_trace_processor() ADDS an observer alongside the default, set_trace_processors() REPLACES the set. Processors are independent observers and the default provider catches a processor's callback exceptions so one failing processor does not stop the others - therefore a redaction processor registered before an exporter does NOT protect that exporter; when export depends on redaction, redaction and delivery must live inside one application-owned exporter. flush_traces() blocks until buffered spans are exported and should be called after trace() closes. RunConfig.trace_include_sensitive_data=False disables capturing generation/function inputs and outputs.
build: Add hday_trace.py: dataclasses Trace(trace_id, name, started_at, finished_at, spans) and Span(trace_id, span_id, parent_id, started_at, finished_at, span_type, span_data: dict). Span constructors mirror the reference set: agent_span, generation_span, function_span, guardrail_span, handoff_span, custom_span, all context managers that set parent_id from a contextvar. Wrap every lane dispatch in trace() and every gate decision in guardrail_span() carrying the GuardrailResult. Export via TraceProcessor protocol with add_trace_processor (additive, default ledger writer stays registered) and set_trace_processors (replace). Enforce the reference's safety rule: the ledger exporter must redact before it writes and must never rely on a separate redaction processor - if redaction raises, discard the batch and log a fixed message with no payload. Add RunConfig.trace_include_sensitive_data and flush_traces().
test: Deterministic: (a) run a two-lane turn and assert the resulting trace has one root agent_span per lane with correct parent_id chaining and exactly one guardrail_span per gate call; (b) assert wrapping two lane runs in one trace() yields a single Trace with two root agent spans; (c) assert add_trace_processor leaves the ledger writer registered while set_trace_processors removes it; (d) inject a redaction failure and assert nothing was written and the log line contains no payload substring; (e) assert trace_include_sensitive_data=False nulls generation span inputs/outputs.

name: Workflow as a typed chain DSL where step ids are the data keys
what: A workflow is built by chaining typed steps: createStep({id, inputSchema, outputSchema, execute}) and then .then(step), .parallel([...]), .branch([...]), .map(fn), terminated by .commit(). Because steps are declared with zod input and output schemas, the graph is type-checked at composition time, and step ids are the addressing scheme for data: after .parallel() or .branch() the result is an object keyed by child step id, a following step reads the previous step's value through inputData, and a specific result is retrieved with getStepResult(step). .branch() requires every branch to share the same inputSchema and outputSchema because branching must keep schemas consistent, only the first branch whose condition is true executes, and its output is keyed by that step's id. .map() exists precisely to reshape the keyed output of parallel/branch into the input shape the next step needs, and it also applies after .then(). Failure handling is a declared property of the parallel step rather than ad-hoc try/catch.
build: Add hday_flow.Step(id, input_schema, output_schema, execute) and a Workflow builder with .then(step), .parallel([steps]), .branch([steps]) (each carrying a condition), .map(fn), .dowhile(...), .foreach(...), .commit(). Validate at composition time that adjacent schemas are compatible and that all .branch() members share input and output schemas. Outputs of parallel/branch are dicts keyed by child step id, and expose get_step_result(step). Persist the executed step ids and their schema-validated outputs in the ledger so a run can be replayed step by step.
test: Deterministic: (a) assert composing .then(a).then(b) with incompatible a.output_schema/b.input_schema raises at build time, not at run time; (b) assert .branch() with mismatched member schemas is rejected; (c) assert only the first matching branch executes and the output dict is keyed by that step's id; (d) assert .parallel() output is keyed by every child id and get_step_result returns the same object; (e) assert .map() after .parallel() reshapes into the next step's input_schema and a mismatch fails validation; (f) assert a declared failure policy on .parallel() is honoured when one child raises.

name: camel-capabilities
what: CaMeL wraps the LLM in a protective system layer: it extracts control and data flows from the trusted query so untrusted data can never influence program flow, and uses capabilities to prevent exfiltration of private data over unauthorized data flows by enforcing security policies when tools are called. Reported result: 77% of AgentDojo tasks solved with provable security versus 84% for an undefended system.
build: Add a capability table to the gate: each tool/action declares {required_capability, allowed_sources, egress: bool}. Values derived from private sources (env, secrets, ledger) carry a taint label and are rejected if the target action is an egress sink without an explicit capability; deny rows record the capability rule id. Start with the egress axis only (network send, git push) as the smallest useful slice.
test: A tainted value into an egress tool without capability is denied with the rule id; the same value into a local tool is allowed; a capability grant for one call does not persist to the next (no ambient authority); a control fixture without the check would allow the egress, proving the check is load-bearing.

name: community-summaries-label-propagation
what: Beyond entities and facts, the graph contains COMMUNITY nodes holding summaries derived through an iterative map-reduce-style summarization of member nodes. Communities are named with key terms and subjects from their summaries, and those names are embedded and stored so a query can reach a community. Updates are dynamic: when a new entity node is added, the system surveys the communities of neighbouring nodes, assigns the new node to the community held by the PLURALITY of its neighbours, then updates the community summary. The paper notes the tradeoff — dynamic updating is efficient but the resulting communities gradually drift, which is why the map-reduce rebuild exists alongside it.
build: Add a periodic (cron) community pass over the decision ledger: cluster recent entries by shared entities/tags, summarize each cluster with the cheap model, store {community_id, name, summary, member_ids, embedding}. Incremental path: a new entry joins the community held by the plurality of its entity neighbours. Keep the derived-at timestamp and a drift counter so a full rebuild can be scheduled when the incremental assignments diverge. Expose communities as a retrieval channel for digest/cockpit 'what's been happening' views.
test: tests/test_communities.py::test_plurality_assignment_and_drift_flag — build three clusters, add a node adjacent to two of them, assert it joins the plurality community; force many incremental assignments and assert the drift counter trips the rebuild recommendation.

name: control-flow-integrity
what: The design-patterns paper's family for injection-resistant agents: action-selector (the LLM only translates a prompt into a pre-defined action over untrusted data, with no feedback loop), plan-then-execute (tool outputs may return to the agent but cannot influence the choice of actions - explicitly framed as control-flow integrity), LLM map-reduce (each chunk processed in isolation with no shared state), and context-minimization (the user prompt is removed from context once it has been translated into a tool call).
build: hday_plan.py: at turn start the router/gate emits a plan (ordered intended actions with their blast radii) derived from the mandate and tool groups, stored in the session ledger. During the turn, a tool call that is neither in the plan nor explainable by a plan step is flagged as a plan_deviation row and, for risky combinations, denied or escalated. Pair with context-minimization: after a mandate has been translated into plan steps, drop the raw user prompt from the judge's context.
test: A plan of [read, test] followed by an unplanned rm is flagged; a call matching a planned step is not flagged; plan deviations appear in the cockpit; read-only planned steps are never falsely denied; the prompt-removal step is asserted (judge context contains plan + symbols, not the raw prompt).

name: privilege-control-progent
what: Progent secures agents through privilege control: privilege is a security policy of symbolic rules over tool names and arguments, specifying which calls are allowed for task completion and which are blocked; every tool call is checked against the policy by a deterministic procedure enforcing least privilege; an LLM generates the initial policy from the user's task and the policy is updated dynamically as execution context evolves.
build: rules/policy.yml per task class: symbolic rules such as tool: terminal, allow: [read-only command patterns], deny: [rm, git push, curl]. The policy is selected or generated at turn start from the mandate, narrowed by the gate, and every decision records the policy id and matched rule id; mid-turn policy updates are explicit ledger rows, never silent.
test: A call outside the policy is denied with its rule id; a call inside it is allowed without invoking the judge (cost assertion); a policy that permits nothing denies everything (fail-closed control); policy generation from a fixture mandate is deterministic; a policy update mid-turn is recorded and cannot retroactively allow an earlier call.

name: episodic-memory-schema
what: Episodic memory preserves successful interactions as learning examples. The documented schema is a typed Episode with four fields — observation ('the situation and relevant context'), thoughts ('key considerations and reasoning process'), action ('what was done in response'), result ('what happened and why it worked'). Extraction is configured by create_memory_manager(model, schemas=[Episode], instructions='Extract examples of successful interactions...', enable_inserts=True) and returns typed records (ExtractedMemory with an id and the Episode content). The docs stress the contrast with semantic memory: episodic captures the situation, the reasoning and WHY it worked, not just the fact.
build: Add an episodic store whose rows are typed Episodes {observation, thoughts, action, result, outcome: success|failure, lane, tools_used, source_episode_id}. Populate it from finished turns (post_tool_call / turn-complete) only when the outcome is verified — tie it to the existing evidence verdict so unverified turns never become 'learning examples'. Recall episodes by situation similarity and inject at most 2 into pre_llm for a matching lane.
test: tests/test_episodic.py::test_only_verified_turns_become_episodes — feed one verified and one no-evidence turn, assert only the verified one yields an Episode row, and assert every Episode carries a non-empty result field.

name: immutable-signature-optimizer-safety
what: Every mutation method (with_instructions, with_updated_fields, prepend, append, insert, delete) deep-copies the field dict, applies the change and returns a NEW Signature class — the original is untouched. The stated reason: optimizers run many candidate variants of the same program, and in-place mutation would let candidates clobber each other through shared state. Two more rules matter: field names and desc/prefix are INERT to instruction optimizers (GEPA rewrites only the docstring, because field names are the program's public interface — caller code reads result.haiku), and equality for comparing variants is Signature.equals(other), not ==, which compares class identity. Persistence round-trips only the mutable parts: dump_state()/load_state() save instructions plus each field's annotation, prefix, desc and field-type tag.
build: Make hermes-day's instruction blocks immutable values: with_instructions(block, text) returns a new block object; a candidate is a (base_hash, diff) pair. Never let an optimiser touch tool names, lane names or field names — only the instruction text, with the same explicit rationale documented in the module. Persist candidates as dump_state()-style dicts (instructions + field metadata) so a promoted prompt can be loaded without re-declaring code.
test: tests/test_prompt_immutability.py::test_candidate_mutation_cannot_touch_the_live_prompt_or_field_names — apply a candidate that tries to rename a field and assert the rename is rejected; assert the live prompt object's hash is unchanged after evaluating 3 candidates.

name: prompt-guard-injection-classifier
what: Prompt Guard is an 86M classifier trained on a large corpus of attacks that detects both explicitly malicious prompts (jailbreaks) and benign-looking data containing injected instructions; Meta recommends fine-tuning it on application-specific data and layering it with other protections. The model card is access-gated on Hugging Face (terms acceptance required).
build: Optional hday_inject_scan.py lane: run a local classifier over chunks entering context; a flag marks the chunk hide/quarantine and writes a ledger row with lane=classifier plus the score. Content is never silently dropped - a flagged chunk is recorded and can be reviewed. Threshold lives in rules/rails.yml.
test: With a stub classifier: a flagged chunk is marked and recorded (never deleted); threshold changes are reflected in the ledger; a classifier error leaves chunks whole with an unjudged row (fail-open loudly).

name: reask-validation-loop
what: Frames self-critique as ordinary validation: 'Instead of framing self-critique or self-reflection in AI as new concepts, we can view them as validation errors with clear error messages that the system can use to self-correct.' Validators are pydantic validators (field_validator / AfterValidator / BeforeValidator) that raise ValueError; the failure is caught and the model is re-asked. The documented mechanics behind the scenes: the client appends the assistant message, then appends a user message reading 'Please correct the function call; errors encountered:\n{e}' — i.e. the raw pydantic error text is the repair prompt — and loops up to max_retries (example sets 2). The docs describe this as a defence against two failure forms: pydantic validation errors (code- or LLM-based) and JSON decoding errors.
build: Implement hermes-day judgments as pydantic models with real validators (e.g. a risk score bounded 0..1, a lane name that must exist in the registry, a verdict that must cite at least one evidence id) and a reask loop that replays the pydantic error text verbatim, capped by the retry budget above. Log every reask with the validator that fired, so 'which rule does the model keep violating' becomes a queryable fact rather than a hunch.
test: tests/test_reask.py::test_invalid_judgment_is_reasked_with_the_pydantic_error_text — return an out-of-range risk score, assert the follow-up request contains the validator's message, assert the loop stops at the budget and raises, and assert the ledger records the fired validator.

name: gaia-levels
what: GAIA is 466 real-world questions requiring reasoning, multi-modality, browsing and tool use, with unambiguous answers scored exactly; human respondents scored 92% versus 15% for GPT-4 with plugins, and answers to 300 questions are withheld to power a leaderboard.
build: A tiered ops task set under runs/tasks/: tier-1 single-tool (answer a fact from a panel command), tier-2 multi-step (diagnose and fix a seeded breakage), tier-3 long-horizon (multi-turn mission). Every task declares an exact expected answer or state; roughly 30% of tasks are held out of the repo and used only for periodic honest re-checks.
test: Harness lint: every task file has an exact expected answer and a tier (free-text expectations fail lint); the repo suite never reads holdout files (path guard test); scoring is exact-match with a stated pass bar, no fuzzy matching.

name: online-scoring-rules
what: Online scoring rules run scorers on live traffic with: scope (trace or span), an idle timeout (default 30s after the last span before a trace-scoped rule fires), SQL filter criteria, and a sampling rate (percentage of matching traces). Scorer-written spans do not restart the idle timer, and a trace that receives new spans can be scored again.
build: day-online-eval background task: select rows where kind in {deny, unjudged} OR hash(row_id) % 10 == 0; wait idle_s (default 30) so the turn has settled; run judge scorers; write score rows. Sampling rate, filters and idle are read from rules/rails.yml. A crashing scorer logs once and marks rows unjudged; it never raises into the hot path.
test: Sampling 0.0 scores only filtered rows; 1.0 scores all eligible rows; rows younger than idle_s are deferred; a trace that gains rows after scoring is re-scored; a crashing scorer leaves decision rows untouched.

name: swe-bench-verified
what: SWE-bench scores a patch by running the repository's own tests (execution-based, not text similarity): 2,294 real GitHub issues across 12 Python repos in the original set. SWE-bench Verified is a 500-sample subset screened by human annotators for well-specified issues and appropriately scoped tests, with easy (196 sub-15-minute) and hard (45 over-one-hour) slices; OpenAI and the SWE-bench authors shipped a containerized Docker evaluation harness.
build: Give every rule/instinct a machine-checkable task card: {workspace fixture, action, fail_to_pass check, pass_to_pass set}. day-suite runs the cards in a sandboxed workspace and reports per-card pass/fail plus any pass-to-pass regressions the action introduced. Difficulty labels (fast <15 min vs slow) decide what runs per commit versus nightly.
test: The suite is its own test: a card whose action is reverted must fail its fail-to-pass check; an unrelated card must still pass (no collateral); a deliberately broken gate rule must be caught by at least one card, or the card set is provably too weak.
